### 3.4. Assessment of Risk of Bias of the Included Studies and Publication Bias

Each study was evaluated using the Cochrane Collaboration tool for assessing the risk of bias. For each domain, studies were judged to be at either high (red), unclear (yellow) or low (green) risk of bias; see [Figure 11](#fig_body_display_jcm-14-07710-f011), [Figure 12](#fig_body_display_jcm-14-07710-f012) and [Figure 13](#fig_body_display_jcm-14-07710-f013). Two studies showed a low risk of randomization bias [[21](#B21-jcm-14-07710),[23](#B23-jcm-14-07710)]. In the remaining studies, the method used for randomization was not mentioned; therefore, these studies were judged to have an unclear risk of selection bias. Studies which failed to describe the methods used for random sequence generation, allocation or blinding were reckoned to have an unclear risk of selection, performance and detection bias, respectively. No studies were judged as having a high risk of performance and detection bias due to the lack of blinding.

### 3.5. Grade of Evidence

The GRADE assessment revealed that the certainty of evidence for l-theanine for cognitive enhancement in these settings was consistently low or very low, mainly due to the small sample sizes, inconsistency and imprecision ([Table 5](#table_body_display_jcm-14-07710-t005)). Overall, while the acute administration of l-theanine may improve cognition, the confidence of these findings is limited.

### 3.6. Studies Included in the Qualitative Analysis

Three studies were excluded from the statistical analysis; however, the results of these may also contribute to the whole picture of the clinical efficacy of l-theanine. args.summary:
This is a systematic review and meta-analysis (published in the Journal of Clinical Medicine, October 2025) evaluating the effect of L-theanine on cognitive performance in healthy adults, based on randomized placebo-controlled clinical trials. The study was conducted by researchers at the University of Szeged, Hungary.

**Methodology:** Five RCTs involving 148 healthy adults were included in the quantitative analysis. The search was conducted across PubMed, Cochrane Central, Embase, and Web of Science until July 2024. The Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool (version 2.0) was used, and a random effects model was applied. Outcomes measured included simple reaction time, Stroop test results, and rapid visual information processing/recognition visual reaction time.

**Key Results:**
- **Simple reaction time:** L-theanine (50–400 mg) showed no significant effect on reaction time to a simple stimulus (MD: −0.46 ms; 95% CI [−15.65; 14.73]).
- **Stroop test:** Non-significant improvement for congruent stimuli (MD: −37.38 ms; 95% CI [−86.39; 11.62]) and non-significant deterioration for incongruent stimuli.
- **Rapid visual information processing/recognition visual reaction time:** A dose-dependent significant improvement was observed at higher doses (MD: −15.20 ms; 95% CI [−28.99; −1.41]), but not at lower doses.

**Conclusions:** The beneficial effects of L-theanine on cognitive performance could not be confirmed across all test methods. The compound may only affect certain cognitive domains. Results were limited by the low number of trials, heterogeneity of test preparations, and small sample sizes. The GRADE assessment rated the certainty of evidence as low or very low. Further trials using standardized products with larger sample sizes are needed.

# What are the effects of combining Caffeine and L-Theanine?

## The Combination of Caffeine and L-Theanine

L-theanine and [caffeine](https://usecadence.com/blogs/science/an-introduction-to-caffeine "Caffeine") is a novel nootropic stack that is growing increasingly popular within communities looking to improve mental and physical performance. They are combined for their synergistic effects on cognitive function and energy. L-theanine, an amino acid found in tea leaves, promotes relaxation and reduces stress by modulating neurotransmitter activity, while caffeine, a well known stimulant, increases alertness and energy levels by blocking adenosine receptors in the brain. When taken together, these compounds can balance each other out, mitigating the jittery effects of caffeine while aiding its positive impacts on focus and mental clarity.

Research has shown that this combination can improve attention, reaction time, and cognitive performance more effectively than either substance alone. [Einöther & Martens, 2013](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24172303/) reported that 100 mg of caffeine paired with 200 mg of L-theanine improved both speed and accuracy in cognitive tasks. This synergy makes the combination particularly beneficial for tasks requiring sustained attention and mental endurance, especially during intense workouts, particularly those that involve changing stimuli such as CrossFit and Hyrox. Whilst you're here, be sure to take a look at our [Energy Hydration Sachets](https://us.usecadence.com/products/race-500-sachets "Energy Hydration Sachets"), which contain a 1:2 ratio of caffeine (100mg) and l-theanine (200mg). Also be sure to take a look at our [Energy Hydration Drink](https://us.usecadence.com/products/energy-hydration-drink-peach "Energy Hydration Drink"), with the same 1:2 ratio of caffeine (120mg) and L-theanine (240mg).

### Caffeine and L-Theanine for Cognitive Function

As discussed, L-theanine and caffeine work synergistically, a mechanism which can improve cognitive function through several, complex neurophysiological mechanisms. L-theanine reduces fMRI BOLD expression, decreasing brain activity during mind wandering and increasing vigilance to detect distractor stimuli, while also lowering the responsiveness of regions processing visual stimuli to distractors ([Kahathudawa et al., 2018](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29420994/)). This may help maintain focused attention and whilst also reducing susceptibility to distractions. Additionally, L-theanine modulates EEG alpha oscillations, decreasing background alpha oscillations associated with relaxation and increasing attention-related alpha oscillations, thus promoting a state of alert relaxation conducive to better cognitive performance ([Gomez-Ramirez et al., 2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10548-008-0068-z)).

L-theanine also influences neurotransmitter systems by increasing dopamine levels and decreasing the release of serotonin, noradrenaline, and GABA ([Kimura et al., 1971](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/4397636/)). This modulation may contribute to better mood and alertness without overstimulation. Furthermore, L-theanine acts as a glutamate inhibitor, preventing excessive excitatory activity in the brain and promoting a balanced neural environment ([Kakuda et al., 2002](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12596867/)).

Caffeine, on the other hand, increases the levels of several neurotransmitters, including dopamine, serotonin, glutamate, and noradrenaline ([Solinas et al., 2002](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12151508/)). This leads to heightened arousal, improved mood, and better cognitive processing. The combination of L-theanine and caffeine leverages these complementary effects, with L-theanine providing a calming influence which counteracts the jitteriness of caffeine, resulting in improved attention, faster reaction times, and better overall cognitive performance.

## Caffeine & L-Theanine Research Review

The growing body of evidence to support caffeine supplementation alongside theanine has been summarised in Table 1 below, but will also be discussed at length in the following section.

A review of 11 randomised, placebo controlled studies by [Camfield et al., 2014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24946991/) explored the synergistic impact of L-theanine and caffeine on cognitive function and mood. The outcome measures of mood were alertness, calmness, and contentedness, derived from the Bond-Lader scales, and state anxiety, from the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory. Cognitive measures assessed were attentional switch, intersensory attention, and rapid visual information processing. The research found that measures such as attention switching accuracy, unisensory visual attention, unisensory auditory attention all improved following caffeine and L-theanine supplementation.

Research by [Owen et al. (2010)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18681988/) looked at supplementation of 50mg of caffeine, with and without 100mg of L-theanine, looking for the effects on cognition and mood. The researchers compared the effects of these subjects with placebo in 27 participants, looking at the effects on word recognition, rapid visual information processing, critical flicker fusion threshold, attention switching and mood. The results found that caffeine and L-theanine had the greatest effect, improving measures across the board such as subjective alertness, speed and accuracy on an attention switching task, as well as reduced susceptibility to distracting information in a memory task.

[Haskell et al. (2008)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18006208/) carried out a randomised, placebo-controlled, double blind, balanced crossover study which investigated the acute cognitive and mood effects of L-theanine (250mg), caffeine (150mg) as well as their combination. The study measured salivary caffeine levels, headache ratings, reaction time and sentence verification accuracy, amongst other cognitive measures. They found that caffeine on its own led to a faster reaction time, visual processing accuracy and improved self-reported mental fatigue. The combination of L-theanine and caffeine improved these same measures, and more, including reduced headache & tiredness rating, and increased alertness ratings.

Research in the same year from [Rogers et al. (2008)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17891480/) also looked at the effects of caffeine and L-theanine supplementation at doses of 250mg of caffeine (a high dose) and 200mg of theanine. They discovered that theanine antagonised the effect of caffeine on increasing blood pressure, however no other significant effects were found.

Research led by [Dodd et al. (2015)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25761837/), a double blind, placebo controlled study, looked at the effects of caffeine and L-theanine on cerebral blood flow, cognition and mood. The results showed that caffeine reduced oxygenated haemoglobin and increased deoxygenated haemoglobin, thus improving attention and mood. Meanwhile the combination of caffeine and L-theanine eliminated the vasoconstrictive and behavioural effects of just caffeine.

[Foxe et al. (2012)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22326943/) studied 27 participants performing the Sustained Attention to Response Task over two hour sessions. The effects of caffeine (50mg) and L-theanine (100mg) supplementation both on their own and in combination was examined. The results showed that both caffeine and L-theanine and L-Theanine significantly reduced error rates compared to placebo, but their combination didn’t necessarily provide additional benefits in this particular study.

[Suzanne J. L. Einöther et al. (2010)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20079786/) investigated the effects of L-theanine (97mg) and caffeine (40mg) in combination against placebo, looking at the effects on attention tasks and self reported alertness. The study found that the combination significantly improved task switching performance, but not subjective alertness.

[Kelly et al. (2008)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18641209/) examined the cognitive effects of combining 100 mg of L-theanine and 50 mg of caffeine. Their participants underwent tasks involving cued shifts of attention whilst their brain activity was recorded. The combination of L-theanine and caffeine increased hit rate and target discriminability compared to placebo, whilst caffeine alone improved discriminability, but not hit rate. L-theanine on its own had no effect.

Interestingly, research by [Chanaka N. Kahathuduwa et al. (2020)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-70037-7) investigated the impact of L-theanine and caffeine on cognitive function in children with ADHD. In this randomised controlled trial, participants received a combination of L-theanine and caffeine. The combination of the two compounds together improved cognition composite scores and performance in tasks, indicating better attention and impulse control, whilst also reducing task-related reactivity in the brain.

## Caffeine & L-Theanine Dosage Ratios

Current research on the optimal dosage and timing of caffeine and L-theanine supplementation suggests that a 2:1 ratio of L-theanine to caffeine is effective in optimising cognitive function and increasing energy. [Owen et al. (2010)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18681988/) demonstrated that this 2:1 ratio improved cognitive measures across the board such as subjective alertness, speed and accuracy on an attention switching task, as well as reduced susceptibility to distracting information in a memory task.

Another study by [Foxe et al. (2012)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22326943/) looked at the same ratio and found cognitive benefits to both caffeine and L-theanine. Research by [Einöther et al., (2010](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0195666310000267)) looked into the effects of taking 97mg of L-Theanine and 40mg of caffeine (approx 2:1 ratio) compared to placebo. The combination of L-theanine and caffeine significantly improved attention on an attention switching task as compared to the placebo.

## Supplementing Caffeine & L-Theanine

Current research suggests that combining caffeine with L-theanine may mitigate the sleep impairments often associated with caffeine supplementation alone. Caffeine is known to improve alertness and cognitive performance, but its stimulating effects can also interfere with sleep quality and increase sleep latency. However, L-theanine, an amino acid found in tea, has calming properties that can counterbalance caffeine's stimulatory effects.

Research has found that a combination of 250mg of L-theanine and 150mg of caffeine improved cognitive performance, and the study’s reviews of more literature suggests that the combination is indicative of relaxation without drowsiness, leading to decreased negative impact on sleep typically observed with caffeine alone ([Haskell et al., 2008](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18006208/)). Another study reported similar benefits, with L-theanine supplementation improving sleep efficiency and reducing sleep disturbances ([Hidese et al., 2019](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/acta-neuropsychiatrica/article/effects-of-chronic-ltheanine-administration-in-patients-with-major-depressive-disorder-an-openlabel-study/0373674887BEA9598D911C7B274A3432)). These findings suggest that L-theanine can offset caffeine's adverse effects on sleep, allowing for the cognitive benefits of caffeine without compromising sleep quality, making it a good option for those individuals who train later in the day, requiring the performance enhancing benefits of caffeine.

With regards to timing, the existing research suggests that taking caffeine combined with L-theanine in the morning is likely to improve focus and reduce stress. This timing leverages the wakefulness-promoting effects of caffeine whilst L-theanine may mitigate potential anxiety and jitteriness, setting a calm yet alert tone for the day. Alternatively consuming 30-60 minutes prior a cognitively or physically demanding task, or workout can benefit. This is because caffeine reaches peak plasma levels within 30 minutes, and L-theanine's calming effects can smooth out caffeine's stimulating effects, resulting in improved attention and reduced mind-wandering ([Sohail et al., 2021](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8794723/#:~:text=The%202008%20study%20by%20Haskell,in%20subjects%20administered%20L%2Dtheanine.)).

Research suggests that there are upper limits to the safe daily intake of caffeine and L-theanine. For caffeine, the FDA advises a maximum daily intake of 400 mg for most adults, equivalent to about four to five cups of coffee. Consuming more than this can lead to adverse effects such as insomnia, jitteriness, and increased heart rate ([FDA, 2021](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/spilling-beans-how-much-caffeine-too-much)). Studies indicate that doses above 400 mg of caffeine daily may exacerbate anxiety and disrupt sleep patterns ([Nawrot et al., 2003](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12519715/)).

For L-theanine, studies have shown that doses up to 1,200 mg per day are generally well-tolerated without significant adverse effects. According to a review, the FDA has granted L-theanine GRAS (Generally Recognized As Safe) status at doses up to 250 mg per serving, with no known toxicity at higher levels used in studies ([Borzelleca et al., 2006](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16759779/)). However, beneficial effects on cognitive function and relaxation are typically observed with doses between 200-400 mg.

As always, we recognise that we are all genetically different and metabolise caffeine differently, so we recommend that you assess tolerance with 100mg of caffeine first and monitor effects. If you want information on how much caffeine or L-theanine you should take, we recommend that you speak to a medical professional.

## Conclusion

In conclusion, the synergistic effects of caffeine and L-theanine offer both the cognitive and stimulatory physical benefits of caffeine and the calming effects of L-theanine for improved attention, reaction time and overall cognitive performance without the jitteriness often associated with caffeine alone. This combination may be particularly useful for tasks which require sustained focus and mental endurance in an athletic setting.

## Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

### What are the main benefits of combining caffeine and L-theanine?

Combining caffeine and L-theanine may improve cognitive function and energy levels more effectively than either compound alone. The combination has been shown in studies to improve attention, reaction time and overall mental clarity, with L-theanine potentially mitigating the jitteriness normally associated with caffeine.

### How does L-theanine help counteract the negative effects of caffeine?

L-theanine is an amino acid found in tea leaves. It promotes relaxation and may reduce stress by modulating neurotransmitter activity. When taken with caffeine, it may help balance caffeine’s stimulatory effects, promoting a state of calm and alertness.

### What is the optimal dosage ratio of L-theanine to caffeine for cognitive benefits?

The bodies of research which find beneficial properties of the combination generally incorporate a 2:1 ratio of L-theanine to caffeine, with positive effects including improvements in attention and accuracy in cognitive tasks.

### Can combining caffeine and L-theanine improve sleep quality?

Combining a low dose of caffeine with L-theanine may mitigate the sleep impairment effects often associated with caffeine alone. L-theanine’s calming properties may counterbalance caffeine’s stimulatory effects, allowing those who incorporate the combination to benefit from the cognitive enhancements without compromising on sleep quality.

### When is the best time to take caffeine and L-theanine?

Taking caffeine and L-theanine in the morning may improve focus and reduce stress throughout the day. Furthermore, consuming both 30-60 minutes before a cognitively demanding task or workout can improve performance by leveraging the positive effects of both.

# L-Theanine and Caffeine Stack: 4 Ratios Ranked by Clinical Evidence (2026)

By Kate Andrews

[0 comments](#blog-post-comments)

![L-Theanine and Caffeine Stack: 4 Ratios Ranked by Clinical Evidence (2026)](//noobru.com/cdn/shop/articles/pexels-l-theanine-and-caffeine-stack-1781291125999.jpg?v=1781291130&width=1500)

**James Sheridan**  
 Health & Nutrition Writer · BSc Biomedical Science · 8+ years in evidence-based supplementation  
 Medically reviewed by [Dr Sarah Chen, MB ChB](https://noobru.com/pages/editorial-team) · Last updated: 12 June 2026

The **L-theanine and caffeine stack** is probably the most well-evidenced nootropic pairing in existence — yet most guides stop at "take them together" without explaining *which* ratio suits *which* situation. A [2008 double-blind crossover study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18681988/) published in *Nutritional Neuroscience* found that combining L-theanine and caffeine improved both speed and accuracy on attention-switching tasks compared with either compound alone — but the dose ratio matters far more than most people realise. Below, we rank the four most common ratios by clinical evidence strength and map each to the real-world scenario where it performs best in 2026.

## What Is the L-Theanine and Caffeine Stack?

L-theanine is an amino acid found naturally in tea leaves (*Camellia sinensis*) that promotes alpha brain-wave activity — the electrical pattern associated with calm alertness. Caffeine is the world's most widely consumed stimulant, blocking adenosine receptors to reduce drowsiness and increase wakefulness.

Taken individually, each has clear benefits and clear drawbacks. Caffeine alone can cause jitteriness, elevated heart rate, and anxiety. L-theanine alone may promote relaxation but lacks the acute drive many people want for demanding tasks.

The stack works because the two compounds are mechanistically complementary. L-theanine modulates GABA, serotonin, and dopamine pathways, effectively smoothing the rough edges of caffeine's stimulatory action without dulling its cognitive benefits\*. The result — supported by multiple peer-reviewed trials — is what researchers call "calm focus": alert and attentive, but not wired\*.

## The Evidence: What Do Clinical Studies Actually Show?

The L-theanine and caffeine combination has more high-quality human trial data than almost any other nootropic stack. Here are the three most relevant studies.

### 1. The 2008 Attention-Switching Trial

A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study by Haskell et al. ([PubMed 18681988](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18681988/)) found that 250 mg L-theanine combined with 150 mg caffeine significantly improved both speed and accuracy on attention-switching tasks. Participants also reported feeling more alert yet less "headachy" — a proxy for reduced caffeine side effects\*.

**Quotable takeaway:** "L-theanine doesn't dull caffeine — it sharpens what caffeine starts."

### 2. The 2019 Systematic Review

A systematic review by Camfield et al. published in *Nutrition Reviews* ([PubMed 31758189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31758189/)) examined 11 studies on the L-theanine and caffeine combination. The authors concluded that the pairing reliably improved attention and task-switching performance, with the strongest effects appearing at L-theanine doses ≥200 mg alongside moderate caffeine (100–160 mg).

### 3. L-Theanine and Anxiety Reduction

A 2019 randomised, placebo-controlled trial by Hidese et al. ([PubMed 30580081](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30580081/)) demonstrated that 200 mg/day of L-theanine for eight weeks reduced stress-related symptoms and improved sleep quality and cognitive function. While that study did not include caffeine, it reinforces L-theanine's independent anxiolytic value — and explains why adding it to a caffeine routine may address the anxiety and sleep-disruption downsides many caffeine users experience\*.

### 4. Supporting Evidence: Rhodiola rosea

Research into Rhodiola rosea, often discussed alongside this stack, has shown significant reductions in mental fatigue and improvements in short-term memory during stressful conditions ([PubMed 22228617](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22228617/)). This matters because many people who seek out the L-theanine and caffeine stack are trying to solve the same problem: maintaining cognitive performance under pressure\*.

## Four Common Ratios, Ranked by Evidence and Use Case

Not every L-theanine-to-caffeine ratio is created equal. Here is how the most commonly recommended combinations compare, based on clinical literature and practical user reports.

| Ratio (L-Theanine : Caffeine) | Typical Dose | Evidence Strength | Best Use Case |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **2:1** | 200 mg : 100 mg | Strong — most studied ratio | Deep work, writing, complex problem-solving |
| **1:1** | 100 mg : 100 mg | Moderate — used in some trials | Quick tasks, meetings, email sprints |
| **3:1** | 300 mg : 100 mg | Limited — mainly anecdotal | High-anxiety individuals, evening study |

### 2:1 — The Gold Standard

The **2:1 ratio (200 mg L-theanine to 100 mg caffeine)** is the most commonly used in clinical trials and the one endorsed by the majority of nootropic researchers. If you are new to the stack, start here. It offers the best balance of alertness and calm for sustained cognitive work\*.

### 1:1 — The Quick-Burst Blend

The 1:1 ratio suits people who want a bit more stimulation and less sedation. It is useful for short, high-intensity cognitive bursts — think a 45-minute sprint through a presentation deck — rather than hours of sustained focus.

### 3:1 — The Anxiety-Sensitive Option

Occasionally recommended for people who are sensitive to caffeine or who tend toward anxiety. The evidence here is largely observational rather than from controlled trials, but the logic is sound: more L-theanine means more GABA modulation and more alpha-wave activity to offset a smaller caffeine stimulus.

### 1:2 — The Pre-Workout Flip

This ratio flips the balance for physical performance contexts, where a higher caffeine dose may help with power output and endurance while L-theanine takes the edge off pre-competition nerves\*. It is the least studied for cognitive outcomes but the most practical for gym use.

## Timing: When to Take the Stack for Maximum Effect

Take the L-theanine and caffeine stack 30 to 45 minutes before you need peak focus. L-theanine crosses the blood-brain barrier within approximately 30 minutes, while caffeine reaches peak plasma concentration in around 45 minutes. Consuming both at the same time aligns their onset windows neatly.

A few timing principles worth noting:

* **Morning deep work:** Take the stack with or shortly after breakfast. The combination may help you enter a focused state faster without the cortisol spike that a strong black coffee on an empty stomach can trigger\*.
* **Afternoon slump:** A lower-dose version (100 mg L-theanine, 50 mg caffeine) taken around 1:00–2:00 PM may help counteract the post-lunch dip without disrupting sleep later\*.
* **Pre-workout:** 30 minutes before training, consider the 1:2 ratio. This is particularly useful for sports demanding both physical exertion and tactical awareness.
* **Cut-off time:** Caffeine has a half-life of roughly five to six hours. Avoid the stack within six hours of bedtime — even with L-theanine's calming effect, the caffeine will still circulate.

## What Else Complements the Stack?

The L-theanine and caffeine pairing is powerful on its own, but several other evidence-based compounds can extend its benefits when the task demands it:

* **Rhodiola rosea:** An adaptogen shown to reduce mental fatigue and support short-term memory under stress. Adding it to the stack may improve resilience during prolonged work sessions\*.
* **Alpha GPC:** A choline donor that increases acetylcholine availability. Research suggests it may enhance cognitive output when combined with stimulatory compounds\*.
* **Phosphatidylserine:** A phospholipid that supports neuronal membrane integrity and may help modulate the cortisol response to stress\*.
* **N-Acetyl L-Tyrosine:** A precursor to dopamine and norepinephrine — the catecholamine neurotransmitters most depleted by stress and sleep deprivation.

 What is the best L-theanine to caffeine ratio?

The most studied ratio is **2:1** — typically 200 mg L-theanine with 100 mg caffeine. This balance improved attention accuracy and speed while reducing caffeine's jittery side effects in a [2008 double-blind crossover trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18681988/) published in *Nutritional Neuroscience*.

  Can I take L-theanine and caffeine every day?

Both compounds have strong safety profiles at standard doses. Most studies use daily dosing for four to eight weeks without adverse effects. However, cycling caffeine intake — for example, five days on, two days off — can help prevent tolerance build-up.

  How long does the L-theanine and caffeine stack take to work?

Most users report noticeable effects within 30 to 60 minutes. L-theanine crosses the blood-brain barrier within about 30 minutes, and caffeine reaches peak plasma levels in roughly 45 minutes, so taking them together aligns their onset well.

  Does L-theanine cancel out caffeine?

No. L-theanine modulates caffeine's stimulatory effects rather than blocking them. You still get alertness and energy from caffeine, but the anxiogenic edge — jitters and racing heart — is smoothed out, resulting in calm, focused energy\*.

  Can I just drink green tea instead of supplementing?

Green tea naturally contains both compounds but in low, variable amounts — roughly 25 mg L-theanine and 30 mg caffeine per cup. You would need six to eight cups to reach clinically studied doses, and the ratio sits closer to 1:1 rather than the optimal 2:1.

## L-Theanine and Coffee: The Perfect Stack for Focus Without Anxiety

By Potential Editorial

![L-theanine and coffee stack for calm focus - molecular structure with coffee cup](//potentialfuel.com/cdn/shop/articles/Deepika_green_tea_leaves_high_resolution_8k_--ar_43_--v_7_1_5eb45b5d-af8a-43ad-b1eb-6c9e93c8971e.png?v=1775045128&width=1232)

# L-Theanine and Coffee: The Perfect Stack for Focus Without Anxiety

You know the feeling. The first sip of coffee lands and you feel sharp, awake, capable of anything. Thirty minutes later, your heart is racing, you are bouncing between browser tabs, and the focus you were chasing has curdled into low-grade anxiety.

The problem was never caffeine. It was caffeine *alone*.

There is one compound that changes the equation entirely: **L-theanine** - an amino acid found naturally in tea leaves that, when paired with caffeine, delivers clean focus without the jitters, the crash, or the 2 PM wall. This combination is not a biohacking secret anymore. It is the single most studied nootropic stack in the world, backed by decades of clinical research.

This guide covers everything: what L-theanine is, how it works with caffeine at a neurochemical level, the exact dosages that research supports, and the simplest way to build this stack into your daily coffee habit.

## What Is L-Theanine?

L-theanine is an amino acid found almost exclusively in the *Camellia sinensis* plant - the same plant that gives us green tea, black tea, and oolong. It was first identified by Japanese scientists in 1949 and has since become one of the most studied natural compounds for cognitive performance and stress management.

Unlike most amino acids, L-theanine crosses the blood-brain barrier efficiently. Once there, it influences several neurotransmitter systems directly - which is why its effects are felt within 30 to 50 minutes of consumption, not hours or days.

### Key properties of L-theanine

* **Non-sedating relaxation**: Reduces stress and anxiety without making you drowsy
* **Alpha brain wave promotion**: Increases alpha-frequency brain activity, the same pattern associated with calm alertness and meditation
* **Neurotransmitter modulation**: Influences GABA, serotonin, and dopamine levels
* **GRAS status**: Generally Recognized as Safe by the FDA with no known adverse effects at typical doses
* **No tolerance buildup**: Unlike many cognitive enhancers, L-theanine does not lose effectiveness with daily use

## How L-Theanine Works: The Mechanism of Action

To understand why L-theanine and caffeine work so well together, you need to understand what each one does on its own.

### What caffeine does to your brain

Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors. Adenosine is the molecule that accumulates throughout the day and signals to your brain that it is time to feel tired. When caffeine blocks those receptors, you feel alert and energized.

But caffeine does not stop there. It also triggers a release of adrenaline and cortisol - your fight-or-flight hormones. At moderate doses (150mg and above), this can tip over into anxiety, restlessness, and the classic coffee jitters. Your focus narrows in the wrong direction: instead of deep work, you get hypervigilance.

### What L-theanine does to your brain

L-theanine takes a different path. It promotes the production of **GABA** (gamma-aminobutyric acid), an inhibitory neurotransmitter that calms neural activity. It also modulates serotonin and dopamine - neurotransmitters involved in mood, motivation, and reward.

Most notably, L-theanine increases **alpha brain wave activity**. A 2008 study published in *Nutritional Neuroscience* by Nobre et al. demonstrated that just 50mg of L-theanine significantly increased alpha wave production within 45 minutes of ingestion, particularly in participants who reported higher baseline anxiety [1]. Alpha waves are the brain state associated with relaxed concentration - the feeling of being in flow without effort.

### The magic of combining them

When you take L-theanine and caffeine together, something remarkable happens. Caffeine provides the alertness and energy. L-theanine smooths out the rough edges - the anxiety, the jitters, the scattered attention. You get stimulation without overstimulation.

This is not speculation. It is one of the most replicated findings in nutritional neuroscience.

## What the Research Says: Clinical Evidence

The caffeine and L-theanine combination has been studied extensively in randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials - the gold standard of clinical research.

### Study 1: The landmark combination study (Haskell et al.)

The most cited study on this stack was published in *Biological Psychology* and is indexed as PMC4480845. Haskell and colleagues tested the effects of caffeine, L-theanine, and their combination on cognitive performance in healthy adults.

**Key findings:**

* Caffeine alone improved alertness and reaction time but increased self-reported headache and jitteriness
* L-theanine alone improved calmness and reduced tension
* The combination improved both speed and accuracy of attention-switching tasks, while reducing the negative side effects of caffeine alone

The researchers concluded that the combination "leads to benefits in mental performance and mood that are greater than those observed for either compound alone" [2].

### Study 2: Attention and task-switching (Owen et al., 2008)

Owen and colleagues published a study in *Nutritional Neuroscience* examining 50mg caffeine combined with 100mg L-theanine. Even at these modest doses, participants showed significant improvements in accuracy during demanding cognitive tasks and reported fewer instances of mind-wandering compared to the placebo group [3].

### Study 3: Alertness and cognitive performance (Giesbrecht et al., 2010)

A study in *Nutritional Neuroscience* by Giesbrecht et al. tested the combination across a battery of cognitive assessments. The caffeine-L-theanine group showed improved alertness and attention, with the L-theanine component specifically reducing the susceptibility to distracting stimuli during focused work [4].

### Study 4: Stress response (Kimura et al., 2007)

Kimura and colleagues demonstrated that 200mg of L-theanine reduced both psychological and physiological markers of stress - including heart rate and salivary immunoglobulin A - during an acute stress task. Participants who received L-theanine reported feeling significantly calmer than the placebo group [5].

### Study 5: Sustained attention meta-analysis (Kahathuduwa et al., 2017)

A systematic review and meta-analysis published in *Nutritional Neuroscience* analyzed multiple trials and concluded that the caffeine-L-theanine combination reliably improves sustained attention and overall cognitive performance, with L-theanine specifically counteracting caffeine-induced reductions in calmness [6].

### The bottom line from research

Across these studies and others, the pattern is consistent: **caffeine gives you energy, L-theanine gives you control over that energy.** Together, they produce a state of focused calm that neither can achieve alone.

## The Optimal Caffeine to L-Theanine Ratio and Dosage

Research consistently points to a **1:1 to 1:2 caffeine-to-L-theanine ratio** as the sweet spot.

| Ratio (Caffeine : L-Theanine) | What to Expect | Best For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1:1 (e.g., 70mg : 70mg) | Balanced focus with moderate calming | Daily work, meetings, creative tasks |
| 1:2 (e.g., 100mg : 200mg) | Stronger calming effect, very smooth focus | High-stress days, anxiety-prone individuals |
| 2:1 (e.g., 200mg : 100mg) | More stimulation, mild calming | Physical performance, early mornings |

Most clinical trials showing the strongest cognitive benefits used doses in the range of **50-250mg caffeine paired with 100-200mg L-theanine**. The most frequently studied and recommended combination is approximately **100mg caffeine with 100-200mg L-theanine**.

### Recommended daily dosage

* **L-theanine**: 100-200mg per serving
* **Caffeine**: 50-100mg per serving (roughly one cup of coffee)
* **Frequency**: Safe for daily use; clinical studies running several weeks reported no adverse effects
* **Timing**: Effects begin within 30-50 minutes and last 3-5 hours

A standard cup of coffee contains about 80-100mg of caffeine. Pairing it with an equal or double amount of L-theanine gives you the clinically validated ratio.

## How to Get Your L-Theanine: A Source Comparison

There are three practical ways to pair L-theanine with your daily caffeine.

| Source | L-Theanine per serving | Caffeine per serving | Ratio achieved | Convenience | Consistency | Additional benefits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Green tea** | 20-30mg | 25-50mg | ~1:0.5 | High | Low (varies by brew) | Antioxidants (EGCG) |
| **L-theanine capsule + coffee** | 100-200mg (capsule) | 80-100mg (coffee) | 1:1 to 1:2 | Medium (two products) | High | Precise dosing |
| **Functional coffee with built-in L-theanine** | 70mg+ | 70mg+ | ~1:1 | Highest (one step) | Highest (pre-measured) | Protein, enzymes, nutrition |

### Green tea

Green tea is the original caffeine-L-theanine stack. The problem is dosage. A typical cup of green tea delivers only 20-30mg of L-theanine - well below the 100-200mg range used in clinical studies. You would need to drink 4-7 cups of green tea to reach the dose that research actually validates. And at that point, you are also consuming 100-350mg of caffeine, which defeats the purpose.

### L-theanine supplements + coffee

This is the biohacker approach: take a 200mg L-theanine capsule with your morning coffee. It works. The dosing is precise, and you can dial in the exact ratio you want.

The downside is friction. You need to remember the capsule, carry it separately, and purchase two products.

### Functional coffee with L-theanine built in

This is the approach that eliminates all friction. A functional coffee that already contains the optimal dose of L-theanine - combined with caffeine from real coffee - gives you the clinically studied stack in a single cup.

No pills. No measuring. No second product. Just coffee that works the way coffee should have worked all along.

## L-Theanine Benefits Beyond Focus

While the caffeine-L-theanine combination is best known for cognitive performance, L-theanine has a broader range of documented benefits.

### Stress and anxiety reduction

L-theanine's ability to promote GABA production and increase alpha brain wave activity makes it a natural anxiolytic - a compound that reduces anxiety without sedation. Kimura et al. (2007) showed that L-theanine reduced both the subjective feeling of stress and the physiological markers of the stress response [5].

For coffee drinkers who have quit or cut back because of anxiety, adding L-theanine can make coffee viable again.

### Sleep quality

This sounds counterintuitive for a compound taken with caffeine, but L-theanine on its own has been shown to improve sleep quality - not by inducing drowsiness, but by reducing the mental chatter and racing thoughts that delay sleep onset. A 2019 study in *Nutrients* found that L-theanine supplementation improved sleep quality scores in a randomized controlled trial [7].

When paired with caffeine in the morning, L-theanine does not interfere with sleep. It simply ensures that the caffeine wears off cleanly, without the residual restlessness.

### Immune function

Emerging research suggests that L-theanine may support immune function by enhancing the activity of gamma-delta T cells, a type of immune cell involved in the first line of defense against pathogens. While this research is still developing, it adds another dimension to L-theanine's profile as a functional ingredient.

## Why Coffee Drinkers in India Should Care

India is the third-largest coffee-consuming country in Asia, and the market is growing fast - particularly among urban professionals aged 25 to 40 who drink coffee not for tradition but for performance. The morning cup is a productivity tool.

But here is the gap: most Indian coffee drinkers experience some version of the jitters-crash cycle without knowing there is a well-researched solution. L-theanine is widely used in Japan, South Korea, and the United States, but awareness in India is still low.

This is changing. The functional beverage market in India is projected to grow significantly through 2028, driven by consumers who want their daily habits to do more - more nutrition, more focus, fewer trade-offs.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is L-theanine and where does it come from?

L-theanine is a naturally occurring amino acid found primarily in tea leaves (*Camellia sinensis*). It was first isolated from green tea in 1949 by Japanese researchers. It is also found in small amounts in certain mushroom species. In functional foods and supplements, L-theanine is typically derived from green tea extract or produced through fermentation.

### Can I take L-theanine with coffee every day?

Yes. L-theanine has GRAS (Generally Recognized as Safe) status and has been consumed daily through tea for centuries. Clinical studies lasting several weeks have reported no adverse effects at doses of 100-400mg per day. Unlike some cognitive enhancers, L-theanine does not build tolerance - it remains effective with daily use.

### What is the best L-theanine to caffeine ratio?

Research supports a 1:1 to 2:1 ratio of L-theanine to caffeine. For example, if your coffee contains 70-100mg of caffeine, pairing it with 70-200mg of L-theanine delivers the combination most consistently shown to improve focus and reduce jitteriness in clinical trials.

### How long does it take for L-theanine to work?

L-theanine crosses the blood-brain barrier and begins to take effect within 30 to 50 minutes of consumption. When taken with caffeine (which is absorbed in 15-45 minutes), the two compounds reach peak effect around the same time, which is why the combination feels so synergistic.

### Does L-theanine reduce the effectiveness of caffeine?

No. L-theanine does not block or reduce caffeine's stimulant effects. Instead, it modulates the anxiety and jitteriness that can accompany caffeine while preserving - and in some studies enhancing - caffeine's positive effects on alertness, reaction time, and attention.

### Is L-theanine safe for people with anxiety?

L-theanine has anxiolytic (anxiety-reducing) properties and is generally well-tolerated by people with anxiety. However, if you are taking prescription medication for anxiety or any other condition, consult your physician before adding any new supplement to your routine.

### Can L-theanine help with coffee-related sleep problems?

L-theanine itself does not cause drowsiness, but it can improve sleep quality by reducing the mental restlessness that sometimes lingers after caffeine consumption. For best results, consume your caffeine-L-theanine stack in the morning or early afternoon and avoid caffeine within 6-8 hours of bedtime.

## Explanation

Doctors and researchers increasingly support the L-Theanine and Caffeine stack as a safe, effective way to boost focus and clarity without the jittery side effects of caffeine alone. Backed by clinical studies and physician recommendations, this combination offers a balanced cognitive lift for students, professionals, and anyone needing sustained mental performance.

What Is the L-Theanine and Caffeine Stack?  
L-Theanine is an amino acid found naturally in tea leaves. It promotes relaxation without drowsiness by increasing alpha brain waves and modulating neurotransmitters such as GABA, dopamine, and serotonin. Caffeine is a well-known stimulant that blocks adenosine receptors, reducing feelings of tiredness and improving alertness. When taken together in the right ratio—typically 2:1 L-Theanine to caffeine—the two compounds work synergistically to sharpen focus, enhance mood, and smooth out caffeine's harsher effects.

Why Doctors Approve the L-Theanine and Caffeine Stack  
Physicians recommend this stack for several key reasons:

1. Enhanced Cognitive Performance  
   • Improved attention span: Studies show that combining 100 mg of L-Theanine with 50 mg of caffeine boosts reaction time and accuracy on attention tasks.  
   • Better multitasking: Clinical trials report faster information processing and reduced mental fatigue during prolonged cognitive work.
2. Reduced Jitters and Anxiety  
   • Balanced stimulation: L-Theanine's calming action counteracts caffeine-induced jitteriness, nervousness, and rapid heartbeat.  
   • Gentle mood lift: Rather than the abrupt "coffee crash," users experience a steady sense of calm alertness.
3. Favorable Safety Profile  
   • Low toxicity: Both ingredients are Generally Recognized As Safe (GRAS) by the U.S. FDA at recommended doses.  
   • Minimal side effects: Occasional mild headaches or gastrointestinal upset are rare and often dose-related.
4. Natural and Accessible  
   • Plant-derived: L-Theanine comes from green tea; caffeine can be sourced from coffee beans or tea leaves.  
   • Cost-effective: Over-the-counter supplements cost less than prescription alternatives for focus and mood.

Evidence from Clinical Research  
Numerous peer-reviewed studies support the benefits of the L-Theanine and Caffeine stack:

* A randomized, double-blind trial published in Nutrition Neuroscience found that the 2:1 ratio enhances alpha brain wave activity and improves task performance more than caffeine alone.
* Research in Biological Psychology demonstrated that participants receiving both compounds exhibited reduced stress responses (cortisol levels) compared to those on caffeine only.
* A systematic review in the Journal of Functional Foods concluded that L-Theanine mitigates caffeine's side effects while maintaining cognitive gains.

Mechanisms of Action  
Understanding how L-Theanine and caffeine interact helps explain why doctors endorse the stack:

* Adenosine Receptor Modulation: Caffeine blocks adenosine, preventing drowsiness.
* Neurotransmitter Balance: L-Theanine increases GABA and serotonin, promoting relaxation and mood stability.
* Brain Wave Enhancement: L-Theanine fosters alpha waves, linked to relaxed but alert mental states.
* Synergistic Effect: Combined, they produce greater improvements in attention and reaction time than either alone.

Who Can Benefit Most?  
While generally safe for healthy adults, certain populations may derive particular benefit:

• Students preparing for exams  
• Professionals in high-demand cognitive roles  
• Gamers seeking sustained mental sharpness  
• Shift workers needing alertness without anxiety  
• Individuals sensitive to caffeine's side effects

Safe Usage Guidelines  
To maximize benefits and minimize risks, doctors advise following these guidelines:

• Dosage: Aim for roughly 200 mg of L-Theanine paired with 100 mg of caffeine (about one strong cup of coffee) per dose.  
• Timing: Take the stack 30–60 minutes before mentally demanding tasks.  
• Frequency: Limit to 1–2 doses per day to avoid tolerance and sleep disturbances.  
• Hydration: Drink plenty of water, as caffeine can have mild diuretic effects.  
• Monitoring: Track how you feel—adjust doses if you notice headaches, insomnia, or GI upset.

Potential Side Effects and Precautions  
Though side effects are uncommon at recommended doses, stay alert for:

• Mild headaches or dizziness  
• Stomach discomfort or acid reflux  
• Increased heart rate or blood pressure in sensitive individuals  
• Insomnia if taken too late in the day

If you have any heart conditions, high blood pressure, or are pregnant or breastfeeding, speak with your doctor before using the L-Theanine and Caffeine stack.

When to Seek Medical Advice  
This stack is not a substitute for medical assessment. If you experience concerning symptoms—such as chest pain, severe palpitations, or unrelenting anxiety—please consult a healthcare professional immediately. You can also use Ubie's [free AI-powered symptom checker](https://ubiehealth.com/) to quickly evaluate your symptoms and get guidance on whether you need in-person care.

Incorporating the Stack into Your Routine

1. Start Low: Begin with 100 mg L-Theanine + 50 mg caffeine and assess tolerance.
2. Combine with Healthy Habits: Pair with regular sleep, exercise, and balanced nutrition.
3. Cycle Usage: Take breaks (e.g., 5 days on, 2 days off) to prevent tolerance buildup.
4. Source Quality Supplements: Choose reputable brands with third-party testing.

Real-World Success Stories  
Many users, from college students to busy professionals, report:

• Sustained concentration during long study or work sessions  
• Reduced "caffeine crash" mid-afternoon  
• Better mood and less stress under deadline pressure  
• Increased productivity without overstimulation

Doctors often see patients exchanging high-dose caffeine or prescription stimulants for this gentler alternative, leading to fewer side effects and improved overall well-being.

Key Takeaways  
• The L-Theanine and Caffeine stack offers balanced cognitive enhancement.  
• Clinical studies confirm improved focus, reduced anxiety, and a favorable safety profile.  
• Proper dosing and timing maximize benefits while minimizing risks.  
• Always consider underlying health conditions and consult a doctor if needed.

Final Recommendations  
The L-Theanine and Caffeine stack is a medically endorsed, science-backed approach to sharpening mental performance. If you're curious whether it's right for you, start with a low dose and track your response. For any serious or persistent symptoms, or if you have heart issues or other chronic conditions, speak to a healthcare professional.

Remember, no supplement replaces a healthy lifestyle and regular medical care. If you're ever uncertain about symptoms you're experiencing, try Ubie's [free AI symptom checker](https://ubiehealth.com/) to get personalized insights before deciding your next steps. Always speak to a doctor about anything that could be life-threatening or serious.

## Abstract

L-theanine, an amino acid found in tea, and caffeine, found in tea and coffee, are claimed to enhance attention. We conducted a double-blind, placebo-controlled, counterbalanced, two-way crossover trial to determine the acute effects of a high-dose L-theanine–caffeine combination on neurobehavioural (reaction time) and neurophysiological (P3b cognitive event-related potential (ERP)) measures of selective attention in acutely sleep-deprived healthy adults. Thirty-seven overnight sleep-deprived healthy adults (aged 22–30 years, twenty-one men) completed a computerised traffic-scene-related visual stimulus discrimination task before and 50 min after ingesting 200 mg L-theanine–160 mg caffeine combination or a placebo. The task involved selectively responding to imminent accident scenes (20 % probability) while ignoring randomly intermixed, more frequent safe scenes (80 % probability). A 32-channel electroencephalogram was recorded concurrently to derive ERP. The L-theanine–caffeine combination significantly improved the hit rate (*P* = 0·02) and target-distractor discriminability *(P* = 0·047), compared with the placebo. Although both L-theanine–caffeine combination (△ = 52·08 ms, *P* < 0·0001) and placebo (△ = 13·97 ms, *P* = 0·024) improved reaction time to accident scenes, the pre-post-dose reaction time improvement of the L-theanine–caffeine combination was significantly greater than that of placebo (△ = 38·1 ms, *P* = 0·003). Compared with the placebo, the L-theanine–caffeine combination significantly increased the amplitudes and reduced the latencies of P3b ERP component. Our findings suggest that L-theanine–caffeine combination improves the accuracy and speed of deploying selective attention to traffic scenarios in sleep-deprived individuals. This improvement is brought about by greater and faster neural resource allocation in the attentional networks of the brain.

In recent years, there has been growing interest in the use of food supplements to support cognitive performance. L-Theanine, also called γ-glutamylethylamide or γ-ethylamino-L-glutamic acid, is a non-protein-forming amino acid found specifically in the tea leaves (*Camellia sinensis*). Caffeine (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine) is present in coffee, tea and cocoa. A cup of tea contains 4–22 mg of L-theanine and 25–50 mg of caffeine, depending on the variety and brewing time([Reference Einöther and Martens1](#ref1),[Reference Chin, Merves and Goldberger2](#ref2)) . Purified forms of L-theanine and caffeine are now available as nootropic supplements in the market.

The pharmacology of L-theanine and caffeine has been extensively studied. Ingested L-theanine is absorbed into the bloodstream through the small intestine via a sodium-coupled active transporter([Reference Eschenauer and Sweet3](#ref3),[Reference Türközü and Şanlier4](#ref4)) . The peak plasma concentration of L-theanine occurs around 45–50 min after ingestion. It crosses the blood–brain barrier using a leucine-preferring transport system([Reference Nathan, Lu and Gray5](#ref5)).

L-Theanine is structurally similar to glutamic acid, the precursor of the neurotransmitter glutamate. Animal studies indicate that L-theanine is a low-affinity glutamate receptor partial agonist([Reference Kakuda, Yanase and Utsunomiya6](#ref6)). It also enhances the release and concentration of dopamine([Reference Yokogoshi, Kobayashi and Mochizuki7](#ref7),[Reference Yamada, Terashima and Wada8](#ref8)) and serotonin([Reference Canli, Omura and Haas9](#ref9)), which play crucial roles in various cognitive processes. High doses of L-theanine have been demonstrated to be safe in humans. No significant adverse effects were reported with doses of up to 450–900 mg in patients with generalised anxiety disorder([Reference Sarris, Byrne and Cribb10](#ref10)). Similarly, children with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder who were administered 400 mg of L-theanine daily for 6 weeks reported no significant adverse effects([Reference Lyon, Kapoor and Juneja11](#ref11)).

Caffeine is rapidly absorbed into the bloodstream through the intestine, with complete absorption within 45 min after ingestion([Reference Carrillo and Benitez12](#ref12)). Peak plasma caffeine concentration is observed in 1-hour post-ingestion([Reference McLellan, Caldwell and Lieberman13](#ref13)). Caffeine readily crosses the blood–brain barrier([Reference Bryan14](#ref14)). Caffeine is an adenosine receptor antagonist. It increases the dopaminergic and cholinergic transmission in the brain. It is recognised as a central nervous system stimulant that enhances alertness, vigilance and attention([Reference McLellan, Caldwell and Lieberman13](#ref13),[Reference Smith15](#ref15)) . Caffeine is considered safe in moderate amounts in healthy adults, with no significant adverse effects. However, high doses (400 mg per day equivalent to about 5·7 mg/kg body weight for a 70 kg adult) can lead to adverse effects([16](#ref16)), characterised by nervousness, irritability, insomnia, sensory disturbances, diuresis, arrhythmia, tachycardia, hyperventilation and gastrointestinal disturbances([Reference Nawrot, Jordan and Eastwood17](#ref17)). Both L-theanine and caffeine are completely cleared from the plasma within 24 h([Reference Nawrot, Jordan and Eastwood17](#ref17),[Reference Unno, Suzuki and Kakuda18](#ref18)) .

The present study focuses on the effects of L-theanine–caffeine combination on selective attention. Selective attention is the process of allocating attention among relevant inputs, thoughts and actions while simultaneously ignoring irrelevant or distracting stimuli([Reference Gazzaniga and Ivry19](#ref19),[Reference Lezak, Howieson and Bigler20](#ref20)) . Selective attention is applied in daily activities and plays a critical role in time-constrained activities like driving: For instance, a driver who approaches a traffic intersection must focus on traffic lights while ignoring distractions like pedestrians standing on pavements and roadside billboards.

Purified L-theanine and caffeine have been administered in various doses to evaluate their effects on cognitive functions. Caffeine is widely recognised for its ability to enhance selective attention in a dose-dependent manner([Reference McLellan, Caldwell and Lieberman13](#ref13),[Reference Einother and Giesbrecht21](#ref21)) . High-dose L-theanine improves neurobehavioural measures (reaction times and task accuracy) of selective attention([Reference Haskell, Kennedy and Milne22](#ref22)–[Reference Dassanayake, Kahathuduwa and Weerasinghe26](#ref26)). For instance, Higashyama *et al.* ([Reference Higashiyama, Htay and Ozeki23](#ref23)) reported that 200 mg of L-theanine enhanced auditory reaction time in participants with higher anxiety propensity. Similarly, Kahathuduwa *et al.* ([Reference Kahathuduwa, Dassanayake and Amarakoon24](#ref24),[Reference Kahathuduwa, Dhanasekara and Chin27](#ref27)) showed that the same dose of L-theanine improves recognition visual reaction time in healthy volunteers. High-dose L-theanine seems to enhance attentional processing in a dose-dependent manner([Reference Kahathuduwa, Weerasinghe and Dassanayake25](#ref25),[Reference Dassanayake, Kahathuduwa and Weerasinghe26](#ref26)) , yet the amount of L-theanine in a single cup of tea seems to be insufficient to significantly enhance attention([Reference Kahathuduwa, Dassanayake and Amarakoon24](#ref24)). Previous research also shows that the degree of attentional improvement caused by the L-theanine–caffeine combination is greater than the degree of improvement caused by either compound alone, suggesting a synergistic effect([Reference Kahathuduwa, Dassanayake and Amarakoon24](#ref24),[Reference Kahathuduwa, Dhanasekara and Chin27](#ref27)–[Reference Giesbrecht, Rycroft and Rowson30](#ref30)) .

Neural mechanisms underlying the attentional effects of L-theanine and caffeine have been investigated with electroencephalography (EEG), cognitive event-related potentials (ERP) and functional MRI. In a high-density EEG-mapping study, Gomez-Ramirez *et al.* ([Reference Gomez-Ramirez, Higgins and Rycroft31](#ref31)) observed that a 250 mg dose of L-theanine induced a phasic increase in alpha power in brain regions associated with visual processing during task anticipation while suppressing background *α* activity. This was indicative of enhanced target–distractor discrimination. ERP are EEG signals evoked by a stimulus or neural process and can be extracted through filtering out background EEG activity and averaging the number of EEG epochs time locked to the event of interest. The P3b component, a late ERP marker of attentive processing, is widely used in cognitive psychophysiology. P3b is a positive deflection that peaks around 300 ms post-stimulus, with a prominent centro-parietal scalp distribution([Reference Sutton, Braren and Zubin32](#ref32)–[Reference Polich and Criado34](#ref34)). In a classic oddball paradigm, P3b appears in response to infrequent targets (i.e. oddball), but not for frequent standard stimuli. The key indices measured in P3b are its amplitude and latency: Amplitude refers to the difference between the mean pre-stimulus baseline voltage and the highest positive peak of the P3b ERP waveform. It is an index of the extent of neural resources allocated for attentional processing. P3b latency is the time elapsed from the onset of the stimulus to the point of the P3b peak. It is an index of the speed of attentional deployment and context updating. L-Theanine, caffeine and L-theanine–caffeine combination are known to elicit a larger P3b amplitude than placebo([Reference Kahathuduwa, Dassanayake and Amarakoon24](#ref24)). Additionally, high-dose L-theanine (400 mg) has been reported to significantly reduce P3b latency([Reference Dassanayake, Kahathuduwa and Weerasinghe26](#ref26)). Functional MRI studies further elucidate the role of L-theanine and caffeine in enhancing selective attention. Kahathuduwa *et al.* ([Reference Kahathuduwa, Dhanasekara and Chin27](#ref27)) observed that L-theanine reduces blood oxygenated Hb level-dependent (BOLD) responses to distractor stimuli in brain regions governing visual attention, and both L-theanine and caffeine significantly decrease functional MRI responses in the right precuneus, a key region within the default mode network associated with mind wandering. This evidence suggests that the L-theanine–caffeine combination enhances attentional focus by suppressing mind wandering and deviation of attention to distracters([Reference Kahathuduwa, Dhanasekara and Chin27](#ref27)).

The research studies discussed above on the acute attentional effects of L-theanine–caffeine combination have primarily concentrated on healthy volunteers tested under optimal conditions, using abstract task paradigms. In everyday life, however, people consume L-theanine and caffeine often when they feel tired or sleep deprived and when they have to attend to demanding everyday activities like driving. Our recent work shows that high-dose L-theanine improves accuracy and reaction time in a traffic-related attention task in sleep-deprived healthy adults([Reference Karunaratne and Dassanayake35](#ref35)). Given that the L-theanine–caffeine combination has greater attentional effects than L-theanine alone, we hypothesised that the L-theanine–caffeine combination may enhance attention more effectively in individuals experiencing sleep deprivation. To test this hypothesis, we investigated whether an orally administered combination of 200 mg of L-theanine and 160 mg of caffeine could enhance neurobehavioural measures (reaction time and response accuracy) and neurophysiological measures of selective attention in a traffic-scene-related visual recognition reaction task in sleep-deprived healthy young adults. To this end, we conducted a double-blind, placebo-controlled, counterbalanced, crossover trial, comparing the effect of the L-theanine–caffeine combination with that of a placebo. The primary neurophysiological outcome measure of interest in this study was the P3b ERP component, which is found to be sensitive to attentional deficits of sleep deprivation([Reference Poh, Chong and Chee36](#ref36),[Reference Peng, Dai and Ba37](#ref37)) and attentional enhancement by L-theanine and caffeine([Reference Kahathuduwa, Dassanayake and Amarakoon24](#ref24),[Reference Dassanayake, Kahathuduwa and Weerasinghe26](#ref26)) .

## Materials and methods

### Participants

A sample of thirty-six participants was required to observe an effect size (Cohen’s d) of 0·5([Reference Cohen38](#ref38)), with an *α* error of 0·05 and a power of 80 %. A sample size of 40 was decided upon, assuming a 10 % attrition rate. We screened a total of forty-one healthy young adults to assess their eligibility for the study, excluded one respondent who was colour blind and recruited forty young adults (age: 22–30, twenty-one males). All had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and normal hearing. None of the participants had significant neurological/psychiatric illnesses. None were on medications that have neurological effects, used alcohol regularly or used tobacco products or recreational psychoactive drugs. All participants consumed less than four cups of tea or coffee per day. The study received approval from the Research Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Medicine, University of Peradeniya and was conducted in accordance with the World Medical Association Declaration of Helsinki([39](#ref39)). Informed written consent was obtained from all participants who met the eligibility criteria. Each participant was compensated with 3000 Sri Lankan rupees (10 USD) for their participation. The trial protocol has been registered in the Sri Lanka Clinical Trial Registry (registration number: SLCTR/2023/006, [https://slctr.lk/trials/slctr-2023–006](https://slctr.lk/trials/slctr-2023-006)).

### Study design and treatment

This study was a double-blind, placebo-controlled, counterbalanced, two-way crossover trial. The study was conducted in the Clinical Neurophysiology and Cognitive Neuroscience (CLINCON) laboratory at the Department of Physiology, Faculty of Medicine, University of Peradeniya. We compared a high-dose L-theanine–caffeine combination (200 mg L-theanine + 160 mg caffeine) with a placebo (360 mg of starch) on their effects on reaction time measures and concurrently recorded ERP in a traffic-scene-based recognition visual reaction task. The rationale for selecting 200 mg of L-theanine and 160 mg of caffeine was based on previous experimental evidence and safety guidelines([Reference Sarris, Byrne and Cribb10](#ref10),[16](#ref16),[Reference Kahathuduwa, Dassanayake and Amarakoon24](#ref24),[Reference Karunaratne and Dassanayake35](#ref35),[Reference Hindmarch, Quinlan and Moore40](#ref40)) . These selected doses are also consistent with the amounts found in many commercial nootropic supplements and functional beverages, thus increasing the ecological validity of the study. To minimise order effects, we counterbalanced the treatment sequence by assigning half of the participants to receive the active treatment first, followed by the placebo, while the other half received the treatments in the reverse order. L-Theanine and caffeine were obtained as a commercial preparation in 100 % purified powdered form (Green Labs Nutrition) and stored in airtight packaging prior to preparation. The specific doses of L-theanine (200 mg), caffeine (160 mg) and starch (360 mg) were measured with a digital microscale having a sensitivity of 1 mg. Each measured L-theanine–caffeine combination and placebo was incorporated into transparent gelatine capsules. The participants were asked to swallow the capsule with 100 ml of water. The two treatments were indistinguishable from one another, and we did not reveal the administered dose to the participants. One investigator (GN) conducted all the tests and processed EEG/ERP data. The capsules were dispensed by a third person, so the investigator was also blind to the treatment conditions.

### Tests and measurements

We administered a traffic-scene-based visual oddball task originally developed by Martin *et al.* ([Reference Martin, Siddle and Gourley41](#ref41)) in which the participant had to respond to imminent accident scenes while ignoring safe scenes ([Figure 1](#f1)). The task and its validity in psychopharmacology have been described in detail by the original authors([Reference Martin, Siddle and Gourley41](#ref41),[Reference Martin and Siddle42](#ref42)) and, more recently, by Karunaratne and Dassanayake([Reference Karunaratne and Dassanayake35](#ref35)). Visual stimuli were presented on a standard 14·5” PC screen with a resolution of 1024 by 768 pixels, and the responses were recorded using the Presentation® (Neurobehavioural Systems, Inc.) software on a WindowsTM-based personal computer. The participants performed the task in a seated position, fixating their eyes at the centre of the screen placed at a distance of 60 cm. Each visual stimulus, a 384-by-256-pixel traffic scene as a car driver would see through the windscreen, was presented in the centre of the screen for 200 ms. The stimuli were presented with an inter-stimulus interval of 1613 ms. There was a 20 % probability for a given stimulus to be an imminent accident scene (i.e. target stimulus) and an 80 % probability for it to be a safe (non-accident) traffic scene (i.e. standard stimulus). The participants were holding the press pad and pressed the response button as fast as they could with the thumb of their dominant hand for the targets while ignoring the standard stimuli. A total of 450 stimuli (90 targets and 360 standards) were presented throughout the task in two blocks, each block consisting of forty-five targets and 180 standards randomly intermixed within the task block to prevent participants from predicting their sequence. Each task block was run for about 7 min, and the whole task took about 15 min.

Concurrent EEG was recorded during the task to derive ERP and study the underlying neurophysiological processes. A BioSemi Active Two EEG/ERP acquisition system with ActiView software (BioSemi) was used to acquire EEG data. Continuous EEG data were acquired from a thirty-two-channel electrode cap configured to international 10–20 scalp electrode placement standards([Reference Klem, Lüders and Jasper43](#ref43)), with the placement of two pairs of additional horizontal and vertical electrodes for electro-oculography, and two electrodes over left and right mastoids (M1 and M2) for re-referencing. During the acquisition of data, the EEG signals were digitised at a rate of 1024 Hz. Electrode offset at each site was maintained within ±40 mV. The high-pass filter was set at 0·1 Hz and the low-pass filter at 30 Hz. EEG data were recorded using common average referencing in the BioSemi Active Two system. A detailed description of this electrode referencing system can be found on the product website (<https://www.biosemi.com/faq/cms&drl.htm>).

After acquiring the continuous EEG data, subsequent stages of EEG data processing were done offline using an automated script in EEG Display version 6.4.11 (Functional Neuroimaging Laboratory, University of Newcastle): Bipolar horizontal (HEOG) and vertical EOG (VEOG) channels were generated using the eye electrode recordings. Active EEG site recordings were re-referenced to the average of the left and right mastoids. Continuous EEG recordings were subjected to blink artifact reduction, creating a blink model using the VEOG recordings and epoched (–100 to 1000 ms) time-locked to stimulus (i.e. target or standard) onset. All epochs with voltage deviations beyond ± 40 μV were rejected, and the rest were baseline-corrected and averaged separately for standard and target trials. Automatic peak detection was performed on averaged ERP waveforms to measure amplitudes and latencies. In each averaged ERP recording, we concentrated on the attentive component (P3b) of ERP. The P3b component was extracted by isolating the maximum positive peak in a latency window of 280–600 ms.

### Testing protocol

The testing protocol has been adapted from one that we used recently to study the attentional effects of L-theanine on sleep-deprived individuals([Reference Karunaratne and Dassanayake35](#ref35)). The test preparation timeline commenced 8 d before testing ([Figure 2](#f2)). Participants were instructed to get at least 6 h of sleep per night for the first 7 d before the experiment. Participants abstained from alcohol for at least 48 h and tea, coffee or other caffeinated beverages for 24 h before testing. On the day before testing, the participants continued their daily activities as usual and had a 2-hour siesta after lunch. After this, the participants stayed awake for 17 h until the testing session on the following day. The research team maintained frequent contact with the participants to ensure that they were strictly following the above instructions. Testing was performed in the mornings, starting at 08.00.

The daily testing protocol is outlined in [Figure 3](#f3). Upon arrival at the laboratory on each testing day, participants were assessed for compliance with the preparation guidelines, and they were queried about their subjective feeling of sleepiness. Then the participants were allowed to relax for 10 min. Participants were then introduced to the traffic task, in which they were instructed on the importance of both speed and accuracy of responses. Initially, participants underwent pre-dose testing, which involved performing the traffic task while EEG recordings were taken. This consisted of a 2-minute practice session followed by the actual task, which lasted approximately 15 min. Subsequently, they consumed the treatment prepared for the session and remained seated for 50 min, watching a non-stimulating wildlife documentary. Following this, participants did the post-dose testing, which was the same as the pre-dose test. The interval between two testing days ranged from 3 to 7 days. On the second testing day, participants followed the same protocol, but with alternative treatment.

### Data analysis

The data of all participants (across two counterbalanced arms) were pooled together for data analysis. The neurobehavioural outcome measures were hits (correct responses to targets, i.e. imminent accident scenes), misses (missed responses to targets), false alarms (active responses made for safe scenes) and mean hit reaction time (time from onset of the target stimulus to the response). Additionally, A′ (A prime) – a non-parametric measure of target-distractor discriminative sensitivity – was calculated based on the probability of hits and false alarms([Reference Stanislaw and Todorov44](#ref44)). In this paradigm, A’ reflects an individual’s ability to accurately distinguish between imminent accident scenes from safe scenes. Higher A’ values indicate better discrimination performance. The neurophysiological outcome measures were the peak amplitudes and latencies of the P3b ERP component in predetermined centro-parietal CZ, CP1, CP2, PZ, P3 and P4 scalp sites, where the P3b ERP is expected to be most prominent([Reference Polich and Criado34](#ref34)).

The accuracy measures (viz. probability of hits, probability of false alarms and A′) had highly skewed distributions and were analysed using the Wilcoxon signed rank test. The hit reaction time and P3b EPR latencies and amplitudes were normally distributed, and their variances across treatment and time conditions were similar, conforming to the normality and homoscedasticity assumptions. Consequently, treatment (L-theanine and placebo) × time (pre-dose and post-dose) two-way, within-subject ANOVA tests were conducted to analyse the treatment and time effects on hit reaction time, P3b ERP amplitude and P3b latency. Subsequent pairwise pre- *v*. post-dose comparisons of group means (i.e. change from baseline) of hit reaction times and latencies and amplitudes of P3b ERP for each treatment were performed, using paired *t* tests. The level of significance was set at a *P* value of 0·05. Given the active treatment *v*. placebo comparison and the P3b scalp sites were determined *a priori* based on the study hypothesis, we did not adjust the *P* values for multiple comparisons. All the statistical analyses were done using Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS™) version 21.0. (IBM Corp.).

## Results

### Participant characteristics

Out of the forty eligible participants, three were excluded after allocation ([Figure 4](#f4)): One was excluded since the participant did not adhere to the test preparation protocol. The second participant blinked too often during the test sessions, and the EEG data were contaminated with too many eye-blink artefacts. The third participant’s data were excluded from the analysis due to contamination of the EEG recording with excessive drift artefacts. The data of the remaining thirty-seven overnight-sleep-deprived healthy young adults (mean age = 25·86, sd = 2·21, 21 males) were analysed. Thirty-four participants were right handed and three were left handed on self-report.

### Neurobehavioural data

The main neurobehavioural outcome measures were pre- and post-dose hits, false alarms, target-distractor discrimination sensitivity (A’) and hit reaction time. [Table 1](#tbl1) summarises the results of the accuracy data. A significant improvement in the probability of hits (*P* = 0·005) and A′ (*P* = 0·008) was observed with the L-theanine–caffeine combination. No significant changes in either the probability of hits (*P* = 0·881) or A′ (*P* = 0·762) were observed with the placebo. There was a significant improvement in the probability of hits (*P =* 0·02*)* and A’ (*P* = 0·047) by the L-theanine–caffeine combination compared with the placebo. Neither the L-theanine–caffeine combination nor the placebo significantly changed the false alarm rate (*P* > 0·05).
