## Abstract

Adenosine receptors mainly control synaptic function, and excessive activation of adenosine receptors may worsen the onset of many neurological disorders. Accordingly, the regular intake of moderate doses of caffeine antagonizes adenosine receptors and affords robust neuroprotection. Although caffeine intake alters brain functional connectivity and multi-omics analyses indicate that caffeine intake modifies synaptic and metabolic processes, it is unclear how caffeine intake affects behavior, synaptic plasticity and its modulation by adenosine. We now report that male mice drinking caffeinated water (0.3 g/L) for 2 weeks were behaviorally indistinguishable (locomotion, mood, memory) from control mice (drinking water) and displayed superimposable synaptic plasticity (long-term potentiation) in different brain areas (hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, amygdala). Moreover, there was a general preservation of the efficiency of adenosine A1 and A2A receptors to control synaptic transmission and plasticity, although there was a tendency for lower levels of endogenous adenosine ensuring A1 receptor-mediated inhibition. In spite of similar behavioral and neurophysiological function, caffeine intake increased the energy charge and redox state of cortical synaptosomes. This increased metabolic competence likely involved a putative increase in the glycolytic rate in synapses and a prospective greater astrocyte–synapse lactate shuttling. It was concluded that caffeine intake does not trigger evident alterations of behavior or of synaptic plasticity but increases the metabolic competence of synapses, which might be related with the previously described better ability of animals consuming caffeine to cope with deleterious stimuli triggering brain dysfunction.

## 1. Introduction

The regular intake of moderate doses of coffee is increasingly recognized to decrease the incidence of numerous chronic diseases, namely, upon aging (e.g., [[1](#B1-biomolecules-13-00106),[2](#B2-biomolecules-13-00106)]). Notably, caffeine, the most widely consumed psychoactive drug worldwide, recapitulates the reduction in overall mortality (e.g., [[3](#B3-biomolecules-13-00106),[4](#B4-biomolecules-13-00106)]), which supports the contention that caffeine might be a prime effector of the impact of coffee on human health, although other coffee constituents such as chlorogenic acids might also contribute to the health benefits afforded by the regular consumption of moderate doses of coffee (e.g., [[5](#B5-biomolecules-13-00106)]). Caffeine mostly acts through the antagonism of adenosine receptors [[6](#B6-biomolecules-13-00106)]. In particular, the impact of caffeine on information flow in brain circuits is fully accounted by the combined antagonism of adenosine A1 receptors (A1R) controlling basal synaptic transmission and of adenosine A2A receptors (A2AR) controlling synaptic plasticity [[7](#B7-biomolecules-13-00106)]. As occurs for A2AR antagonists, moderate doses of caffeine afford a robust neuroprotection in different animal models of neuropsychiatric diseases, ranging from Alzheimer’s disease [[8](#B8-biomolecules-13-00106),[9](#B9-biomolecules-13-00106)], Parkinson’s disease [[10](#B10-biomolecules-13-00106)], ischemia [[11](#B11-biomolecules-13-00106),[12](#B12-biomolecules-13-00106)], epilepsy/convulsions [[13](#B13-biomolecules-13-00106),[14](#B14-biomolecules-13-00106),[15](#B15-biomolecules-13-00106)], traumatic brain injury [[16](#B16-biomolecules-13-00106),[17](#B17-biomolecules-13-00106)], diabetic encephalopathy [[18](#B18-biomolecules-13-00106),[19](#B19-biomolecules-13-00106)], spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 [[20](#B20-biomolecules-13-00106),[21](#B21-biomolecules-13-00106)], multiple sclerosis [[22](#B22-biomolecules-13-00106),[23](#B23-biomolecules-13-00106)], attention deficit and hyperactivity disorder [[24](#B24-biomolecules-13-00106),[25](#B25-biomolecules-13-00106)] or depressive-like mood dysfunction [[26](#B26-biomolecules-13-00106),[27](#B27-biomolecules-13-00106),[28](#B28-biomolecules-13-00106)].

Importantly, the neuroprotective effects of caffeine require its prolonged intake whereas the acute administration of caffeine to naïve animals often has effects opposite to these afforded by a continuous intake of caffeine (reviewed in [[29](#B29-biomolecules-13-00106),[30](#B30-biomolecules-13-00106)]): the acute administration of caffeine aggravates convulsions through inhibitory A1R [[31](#B31-biomolecules-13-00106),[32](#B32-biomolecules-13-00106)], as well as brain traumatic or ischemic damage [[12](#B12-biomolecules-13-00106),[33](#B33-biomolecules-13-00106),[34](#B34-biomolecules-13-00106)]; in contrast, a regular exposure to caffeine has a neuroprotective effect through the attenuation of facilitatory A2AR signalling [[9](#B9-biomolecules-13-00106),[15](#B15-biomolecules-13-00106),[27](#B27-biomolecules-13-00106),[35](#B35-biomolecules-13-00106)]. Thus, it appears that repeated exposure to caffeine might induce a form of brain preconditioning, with reported alterations of brain functional connectivity [[36](#B36-biomolecules-13-00106),[37](#B37-biomolecules-13-00106),[38](#B38-biomolecules-13-00106)], brain metabolism (e.g., [[18](#B18-biomolecules-13-00106),[39](#B39-biomolecules-13-00106),[40](#B40-biomolecules-13-00106),[41](#B41-biomolecules-13-00106)]) and levels of adenosine [[42](#B42-biomolecules-13-00106)], as well as of A1R and A2AR in the adult brain (e.g., [[43](#B43-biomolecules-13-00106),[44](#B44-biomolecules-13-00106)]).

These long-term adaptive effects caused by long-term exposure to caffeine were assessed in whole brain preparations, whereas the onset of brain dysfunction involves synaptic dysfunction (reviewed in [[45](#B45-biomolecules-13-00106),[46](#B46-biomolecules-13-00106),[47](#B47-biomolecules-13-00106),[48](#B48-biomolecules-13-00106)]). Accordingly, the targets of caffeine in the brain (A1R and A2AR; see [[49](#B49-biomolecules-13-00106)]) are mostly located in synapses [[50](#B50-biomolecules-13-00106),[51](#B51-biomolecules-13-00106)], and neuronal adenosine receptors are involved in brain damage in noxious conditions [[27](#B27-biomolecules-13-00106),[52](#B52-biomolecules-13-00106),[53](#B53-biomolecules-13-00106)] through a control of the dysfunction and damage of synapses (reviewed in [[30](#B30-biomolecules-13-00106)]), which only represent circa 1–2% of the brain parenchyma [[54](#B54-biomolecules-13-00106)]. However, it is unknown if the prolonged exposure to caffeine alters the efficiency of the adenosine neuromodulation system in excitatory synapses of the brain.

Thus, we investigated in adult mice how the prolonged exposure to caffeine affects synaptic transmission and the function of adenosine receptors in synapses of different brain regions, and we also tested if there were caffeine-induced alterations of primary metabolism, which are known to impact on synaptic function and susceptibility to noxious brain stimuli (reviewed in [[55](#B55-biomolecules-13-00106),[56](#B56-biomolecules-13-00106)]).

## 2. Results

### 2.1. Altered Caffeine Levels upon Regular Intake of Caffeine over Time

We first assessed the levels of caffeine in the plasma and in the brain parenchyma of adult mice after an acute and upon regular intake of caffeinated water (0.3 g/L). As shown in [Figure 1](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f001), the plasma levels of caffeine after 24 h of access to caffeinated water were 2.47 ± 0.30 μM in the plasma (n = 8), and ranged from 4.92 ± 0.67 μM in the cerebral cortex, 6.08 ± 0.30 μM in the hippocampus and 7.06 ± 0.71 μM in the striatum (n = 8); this shows that caffeine levels were higher in the brain parenchyma than in the plasma, as expected from the higher lipophilicity of the brain parenchyma compared with the plasma. Notoriously, the levels of caffeine were higher in all compartments after 15 days of regular intake of caffeine, reaching levels of 4.89 ± 0.57 μM in the plasma (n = 8), and higher levels (p < 0.05, n = 8; Student’s t test) in the cerebral cortex (11.75 ± 0.79 μM), hippocampus (11.64 ± 1.24 μM) and striatum (14.41 ± 0.71 μM) ([Figure 1](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f001)).

### 2.2. Lack of Evident Behavioral Modifications upon Caffeine Intake

We then characterized some behavioral features of mice regularly consuming caffeinated water. After 13–18 days of caffeine intake, mice displayed no modification of locomotion (number of crossings during 10 min in an open field, [Figure 2](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f002)A) nor of sensorimotor integration (number of rearing events during 10 min in an open field, [Figure 2](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f002)B) nor of anxiety-like behavior (percentage of time spent in the center of an open field during 10 min, [Figure 2](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f002)C). The lack of an altered anxiety-like behavior was further confirmed in an elevated plus maze, where mice drinking caffeine or water (as control) spent a similar percentage of time in the open arms ([Figure 2](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f002)D). Other mood-related behaviors were also unaltered upon regular intake of caffeine, as assessed by the similar immobility time accounted for mice drinking caffeine or water (as control) in a forced swimming test ([Figure 2](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f002)E). We next probed for possible alterations of reference memory performance upon regular consumption of caffeine: we observed no alterations in the percentage of time spent in the novel arm in a modified Y-maze ([Figure 2](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f002)F), as well as no alterations in the discrimination index in an object displacement test ([Figure 2](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f002)G) between mice drinking caffeinated water or water (n = 8 in all behavioral tests).

### 2.3. Impact of Caffeine Intake on Adenosine Modulation of Synaptic Transmission and Plasticity in the Hippocampus

Since caffeine mostly acts through the antagonism of adenosine receptors involved in the control of synaptic transmission and plasticity [[7](#B7-biomolecules-13-00106)], we next investigated if the regular consumption of caffeine modified the control of synaptic transmission and plasticity that is modulated in different brain regions by adenosine A1 receptors (A1R) and adenosine A2A receptors (A2AR), respectively [[7](#B7-biomolecules-13-00106),[57](#B57-biomolecules-13-00106),[58](#B58-biomolecules-13-00106),[59](#B59-biomolecules-13-00106)]. In Schaffer fibers-CA1 pyramid synapses of mouse hippocampal slices, the activation of A1R by 2-chloroadenosine [[60](#B60-biomolecules-13-00106)] caused a larger inhibition of synaptic transmission in mice drinking caffeine than in control mice ([Figure 3](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f003)A,B). Additionally, the tonic activation of A1R by endogenous adenosine was lower in mice drinking caffeine than in control mice, as concluded from the lower (p < 0.05; Student’s t test) disinhibition of synaptic transmission by a supramaximal concentration of the selective A1R antagonist DPCPX (100 nM; [[61](#B61-biomolecules-13-00106)]) in mice drinking caffeine than in control mice ([Figure 3](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f003)C,D). Finally, there was no significant difference (p = 0.315; Student’s t test) of the magnitude of long-term potentiation (LTP) in hippocampal slices from mice drinking caffeine (60.6 ± 11.2% over baseline, n = 9) or water (81.1 ± 16.3% over baseline, n = 10) ([Figure 3](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f003)E,F). Moreover, there was a tendency for a decreased impact of A2AR in the control of synaptic plasticity, since a supramaximal concentration of the selective A2AR antagonist SCH58261 (50 nM; [[62](#B62-biomolecules-13-00106)]) significantly (p < 0.05; Student’s t test) decreased LTP magnitude in control mice, whereas there was only a tendency (p = 0.083; Student’s t test) for an inhibition of LTP magnitude in mice drinking caffeine ([Figure 3](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f003)F).

### 2.4. Impact of Caffeine Intake on Adenosine Modulation of Synaptic Transmission and Plasticity in the Prefrontal Cortex

In synapses between projections of layer 2/3 and pyramidal neurons of layer V of slices from the prefrontal cortex (PFC), the activation of A1R by 2-chloroadenosine caused a similar concentration-dependent inhibition of synaptic transmission in mice drinking caffeine and in control mice ([Figure 4](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f004)A,B). However, the tonic activation of A1R by endogenous adenosine was lower in mice drinking caffeine than in control mice, as concluded from the lower (p < 0.05; Student’s t test) disinhibition of synaptic transmission by the selective A1R antagonist DPCPX (100 nM) in mice drinking caffeine than in control mice ([Figure 4](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f004)C,D). Finally, there was no significant difference (p = 0.879; Student’s t test) of the magnitude of LTP in PFC slices from mice drinking caffeine (71.8 ± 16.0% over baseline, n = 8) or water (62.7 ± 9.27% over baseline, n = 8) ([Figure 4](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f004)E,F) and there was no difference in the impact of the selective A2AR antagonist SCH58261 (50 nM) on LTP between both groups of mice ([Figure 4](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f004)F).

### 2.5. Impact of Caffeine Intake on Adenosine Modulation of Synaptic Transmission and Plasticity in the Amygdala

In synapses between cortico-thalamic projections and the lateral amygdala, the activation of A1R by 2-chloroadenosine caused a similar concentration-dependent inhibition of synaptic transmission in mice drinking caffeine and in control mice ([Figure 5](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f005)A,B). There was also no modification of the tonic activation of A1R by endogenous adenosine as concluded from the similar (p = 0.931; Student’s t test) disinhibition of synaptic transmission by the selective A1R antagonist DPCPX (100 nM) in mice drinking caffeine and in control mice ([Figure 5](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f005)C,D). Finally, there was no significant difference (p = 0.613; Student’s t test) of the magnitude of LTP in amygdala slices from mice drinking caffeine (41.9 ± 11.2% over baseline, n = 8) or water (45.6 ± 9.56% over baseline, n = 7) ([Figure 5](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f005)E,F) and there was no difference in the impact of the selective A2AR antagonist SCH58261 (50 nM) on LTP between both groups of mice ([Figure 5](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f005)F).

### 2.6. Impact of Caffeine Intake on Metabolic Features of Cortical Synapses

Since omic studies identified adaptive changes of primary metabolism upon regular intake of caffeine [[41](#B41-biomolecules-13-00106)], we next enquired if the regular intake of a moderate dose of caffeine would affect the metabolic properties of cortical synapses that are a major determinant of synaptic function and resilience under noxious conditions [[55](#B55-biomolecules-13-00106),[56](#B56-biomolecules-13-00106)]. The study was carried out in synaptosomes from the mouse cerebral cortex, which is the largest brain region to provide sufficient material to complete the study. As shown in [Figure 6](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f006)A, there was an increased energy charge of synaptosomes (purified synapses) from mice drinking caffeine compared with control mice. Furthermore, there was an increased redox capacity, as assessed by the larger MTT reduction, in synaptosomes from mice drinking caffeine compared with control mice ([Figure 6](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f006)B). This was coupled with a tendency (p = 0.051; Student’s t test) towards a greater glycolytic index in synaptosomes from mice drinking caffeine compared with control mice ([Figure 6](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f006)C). In spite of this apparent increase in the glycolytic index, the analysis of the incorporation of 13C in acetate showed that synaptosomes from mice drinking caffeine preserved the same ability (p > 0.05; Student’s t test) of synaptosomes from control mice to preferentially metabolize lactate (increased levels of [2-13C]acetate originating from [3-13C]lactate) rather than using glycolytic products (lower levels of [1,2-13C2]acetate originating from [U-13C]glucose) ([Figure 6](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f006)D).

**Figure 6.**
Impact of caffeine intake on primary metabolism in the cerebral cortex. Male adult mice (10 weeks old) consumed either caffeine (0.3 g/L, blue symbols and bars) or water (control, black symbols and bars) for 15 days before sacrifice and preparation of either cerebrocortical synaptosomes or slices (400 μm). Compared with control mice (10 weeks old) drinking water (black symbols and bars), cerebrocortical synaptosomes from mice consuming caffeine displayed a larger energy charge (**A**), assessed by HPLC quantification; a greater redox potential, assessed by a MTT reduction assay (**B**); a tendency for an increased glycolytic index, assessed by NMR quantification of the ratio between [U-13C]lactate production (in glucose equivalents) and [U-13C]glucose consumption (**C**); and a preserved production of acetate, assessed by NMR quantification of [1,2-13C2]acetate and [2-13C]acetate originating, respectively, from [U-13C]glucose and [3-13C]lactate (**D**). Data are mean ± SEM of 4-9 experiments (number of different animals tested); \* p < 0.05 using Student’s t test with Welsh correction. Compared with control mice (black symbols and bars), cerebrocortical slices from mice consuming caffeine displayed a preserved glycolytic index (**E**), a reduced contribution of lactate for the pool of acetyl-CoA (**F**), and a preserved Krebs cycle turnover (**G**), which was estimated by the ratio of C4Q and C4D45 analysis of the glutamate C4 resonance and its multiplets, as illustrated in the representative NMR spectra (**H**,**I**). Data are mean ± SEM of 6–8 experiments (number of different animals tested); # p = 0.051 \* p < 0.05 and \*\* p < 0.01 using Student’s t test.

In cortical slices, there was no evident modification (p > 0.05; Student’s t test) of the glycolytic index in caffeine-drinking mice compared with control mice ([Figure 6](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f006)E), indicating that the putative increased glycolysis in caffeine-drinking mice occurred specifically in synapses. It was also observed that the contribution of lactate for the pool of acetyl-CoA was decreased in slices from caffeine-drinking mice compared with control mice ([Figure 6](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f006)F). Finally, 13C-isotopomeric analysis indicated that there was a similar turnover of the citrate (Krebs) cycle in cortical slices from control and caffeine-treated mice ([Figure 6](#fig_body_display_biomolecules-13-00106-f006)G).

## 3. Discussion

The regular intake of moderate doses of caffeine affords a robust neuroprotection that has been mainly associated with the ability of caffeine to antagonize adenosine receptors involved in the control of synaptic transmission, synaptic plasticity and synaptotoxicity [[30](#B30-biomolecules-13-00106)]. Furthermore, a multi-omics study revealed that the regular consumption of caffeine promotes adaptive modifications in the hippocampus with signatures indicative of an altered primary metabolism and an altered efficiency of synaptic plasticity [[41](#B41-biomolecules-13-00106)]. However, the present study refuted the hypothesis that caffeine intake may trigger a modification of synaptic transmission or synaptic plasticity in different brain regions (hippocampus, prefrontal cortex and amygdala), while demonstrating that these regions preserved a similar pattern of modulation by adenosine A1 and A2A receptors irrespective of the regular exposure to caffeine. In contrast, we observed that the regular intake of caffeine altered cortical synaptic metabolism, bolstering the energy charge and the redox state of cortical synapses. This might be associated with a greater coupling of astrocytic and synaptic metabolism as indirectly inferred from the reduced usage of lactate by slices (predominantly extra-synaptic and astrocytic compartments) relieving a greater potential supplementation of lactate to support synaptic metabolism.

The behavioral analysis of mice regularly consuming a moderate dose of caffeine showed a global preservation of locomotion, mood and memory, largely in accordance with our previous similar reports in both mice (e.g., [[19](#B19-biomolecules-13-00106),[27](#B27-biomolecules-13-00106)]) and rats (e.g., [[15](#B15-biomolecules-13-00106),[18](#B18-biomolecules-13-00106)]). args.summary:
This is a scientific research article published in Biomolecules (2023) titled "Effects of Chronic Caffeine Consumption on Synaptic Function, Metabolism and Adenosine Modulation in Different Brain Areas." The study investigated how prolonged caffeine intake affects synaptic function, behavior, and metabolism in adult male mice.

Key findings:
- Mice drinking caffeinated water (0.3 g/L) for 2 weeks showed no behavioral differences (locomotion, mood, memory) compared to controls.
- Synaptic plasticity (long-term potentiation/LTP) in the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and amygdala was similar between caffeine-treated and control mice.
- Adenosine A1 and A2A receptor modulation of synaptic transmission and plasticity was largely preserved, though there was a tendency for lower endogenous adenosine levels in some brain regions.
- Caffeine intake increased the energy charge and redox state of cortical synaptosomes, suggesting improved metabolic competence.
- There was evidence of increased glycolytic rate in synapses and potential greater astrocyte-synapse lactate shuttling.

The authors concluded that chronic caffeine intake does not trigger evident alterations of behavior or synaptic plasticity but increases the metabolic competence of synapses, which may relate to the previously described neuroprotective effects of caffeine against deleterious brain stimuli.

The article is open access, published under CC BY license, and has received 27 citations with over 20,000 article views.

# Mastering Caffeine Cycling for Performance and Productivity

By[David William Rosales](https://davidwilliamrosales.com)    Updated on

You could make the case that **caffeine has had the biggest impact on modern society compared to every other drug.**

[According to 2020 data](https://www.ncausa.org/newsroom/nca-releases-atlas-of-american-coffee), 62% of Americans drink coffee daily. And 90% of adults in the world consume some form of caffeine every day.

But that’s only the surface. As Michael Pollan discusses in *Caffeine: How Caffeine Created the Modern World*, the drug allowed **workers to work longer hours with fewer breaks, accelerating industrialization.**

As he says, “Caffeine helps us to cope with the world caffeine helped us to create.” From office culture, to “third spaces” like coffee shops, undertoning much of our societal fabric is sipping on a caffeinated beverage.

Michael did a nice short video on this for Wired.

**While daily caffeine use is king, I gravitate towards an unconventional approach: caffeine cycling.**

This practice challenges the norm of daily caffeine consumption, and views caffeine not as a friend or foe, but as a tool. It’s not about eliminating caffeine entirely but rather about strategically timing its intake. The goal? To maximize its benefits while minimizing dependence and tolerance.

## **What Is Caffeine Cycling**?

Caffeine cycling involves **strategic alternating periods of caffeine use.**By alternating periods of caffeine use with intervals of reduced intake or abstinence, **you can reset your caffeine sensitivity.** This method promises not just a return to those initial, potent effects of caffeine but also a deeper understanding of how this powerful stimulant interacts with our bodies.

In my personal experience, it has led to some of my best workouts, most productive writing sessions, and straight-up euphoric experiences (like drinking 3 cappuccinos in Bologna, Italy) that brought nearly as much happiness as anything I’ve ever experienced.

![](https://i0.wp.com/davidwilliamrosales.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/B5137321-850C-4466-8378-9A4CA6512E17.jpg?resize=1024%2C768&ssl=1)

Not Italy, but writing and reading while sipping on a cappuccino after cycling is a peak life experience in my opinion.

Let’s get into **why caffeine cycling provides different effects and the exact protocols I follow.**

## **How Caffeine Works in the Body**

Caffeine, a natural stimulant most commonly found in coffee, tea, and cacao plants, works its magic by interacting with our central nervous system. At the heart of its mechanism is its ability to mimic a neurotransmitter called adenosine.

Under normal circumstances, adenosine binds to receptors in the brain, promoting relaxation and sleepiness. However, when caffeine enters the scene, it competes with adenosine for these same receptors.

By blocking adenosine, caffeine prevents this neurotransmitter from causing drowsiness. This blockage leads to increased neuronal firing in the brain, which the pituitary gland perceives as an emergency, thus stimulating the release of adrenaline. This adrenaline rush is what gives you the familiar caffeine boost – increased alertness, heightened awareness, and a burst of energy.

Basically. Caffeine –> blocks adenosine –> releases adrenaline –> you feel like a god.

## **Understanding Caffeine Tolerance and Dependence**

However, if you consume caffeine on a daily basis, it leads to tolerance. This means that over time, the same amount of caffeine will have a diminished effect. The science behind this is quite straightforward. With consistent caffeine intake, the body responds by increasing the number of adenosine receptors in the brain. This adaptation means that more caffeine is required to block a significant proportion of these receptors and achieve the desired stimulating effect.

Even if you have caffeine everyday, **you’ll still block adenosine receptors, but your body won’t release the high amounts of adrenaline.**

For example, [one clinical trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8549061/) found that **after just six days of daily use, the body’s adrenaline response to caffeine decreases.**

This is the key for understanding the value of caffeine cycle. If you take caffeine daily, rather than feeling alert and energized thanks to increased adrenaline, you’ll just feel… normal. That’s cool, but if you want to feel more alert and perform your best, it means you’ll have to cycle it.

If you take caffeine daily, your body will also rely on it for normal functioning. If you suddenly reduce or stop caffeine intake, you may experience withdrawal symptoms like headaches, fatigue, irritability, and difficulty concentrating. This dependence signifies the body’s adaptation to regular caffeine exposure.

#### **The crux of caffeine cycling is to reduce caffeine intake to help reset the body’s response to it, maintaining its effectiveness as a stimulant and minimizing the risks of tolerance and dependence.**

Even for those who have developed a dependence on caffeine, its consumption in the evening can still significantly disrupt sleep patterns *and* still keep people awake in the mornings. Caffeine’s ability to block adenosine receptors doesn’t diminish with dependence. Therefore, consuming caffeine later in the day can prevent the natural buildup of adenosine, which is crucial for initiating sleep. For example, [one study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3805807/) showed significant negative sleep effects when taking caffeine six hours before bed.

This disruption can lead to difficulties in falling asleep, reduced sleep quality, and shorter sleep duration, even in individuals who consider themselves tolerant to caffeine’s effects. The impact on sleep is particularly important to consider, and generally not talked about enough in my opinion.

### **The Challenge in Researching Caffeine**: We’re All Dependent

One of the significant hurdles in fully understanding caffeine’s effects is the widespread caffeine dependence among the general population.

So when researchers select random people, many of them are regular caffeine drinkers. This means studying the effects of caffeine without caffeine tolerance is hard.

Despite having hundreds of studies on caffeine **it’s still unclear whether performance improvements are a result of caffeine, or because the participants are dependent and can’t function normally without it.**

I make this point because **caffeine cycling and its benefits are still mostly unknown.**I will be relying on my personal experience as much as the research because of this phenomenon.

I also bring this up for any scientists reading this, because it makes caffeine cycling an interesting area of study. By examining how periods of abstinence or reduced intake affect caffeine tolerance and response, researchers can gain insights into the adaptability of the human body to this stimulant.

Such studies could also inform guidelines for optimal caffeine use, balancing the benefits of this popular stimulant with the need to minimize dependence and maximize health.

Alas, we’re not there yet.

## **Benefits of Caffeine Cycling**

With this in mind, here are some of the compelling benefits of caffeine cycling.

#### **Improved Sensitivity to Caffeine**

One of the most immediate benefits of caffeine cycling is the restoration of caffeine sensitivity. When you take a break from caffeine, your body’s adenosine receptors reset, reducing your tolerance.**As a result, when you reintroduce caffeine, you experience a more pronounced effect.**

This heightened sensitivity means you feel more focused and energized with smaller amounts of caffeine. Personally, I’ve found that my best workouts and most productive writing sessions occur when I’ve cycled caffeine and then had a deliciously caffeinated cappuccino or latte.

#### **The Best Work Sessions of Your Life**

Oh boy, I feel heightened just thinking about how I feel drinking coffee after 4 days of NOT drinking it. I save my coffee days for Friday and Saturday mornings, which are my blocked-out writing days.

### **Better Sleep Quality**

Regular caffeine consumption, especially later in the day, can interfere with sleep patterns. By cycling caffeine and incorporating caffeine-free periods, you can significantly improve your sleep quality.

If you drink caffeine regularly and use some kind of sleep tracker, I challenge you to take a break from caffeine and look at your sleep numbers to assess this for yourself.

#### **Reduced Dependence**

Caffeine cycling helps in breaking the cycle of dependence. During off-cycles, your body adjusts to functioning without the stimulant, reducing the risk of experiencing withdrawal symptoms like headaches and irritability in the future. This reduced dependence is crucial for those who wish to use caffeine strategically without being bound to it daily.

#### **Positive Impacts on Mental Health and Cognitive Function**

There’s also a mental health aspect to consider. **Regular and high consumption of caffeine can sometimes exacerbate anxiety and stress.** By cycling caffeine, you can help moderate these effects. Additionally, when your body is not constantly exposed to caffeine, the stimulant’s cognitive-enhancing properties, such as improved concentration and alertness, become more effective when you do consume it (due to more adrenaline, as we talked about.)

## **How Long Should You Cycle Caffeine For?**

[One study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2547026/) suggested that it takes about 8 days to reset adenosine receptors. This is from 1989, but I think it holds up as a good framework.

[Some studies](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8849224/) say it can take up to two months to get full tolerance, but other research says you can reset fully within a few days. Since caffeine metabolism varies by person, this probably does too, **so trust your personal experience here, because we all metabolize caffeine different.**

Based on my personal experience, I find if **I have 1-2 days per week of higher caffeine intake (125mg-250mg) and ease back the other days, I still get the full effect.** Or at least, very close to the full effect.

Keep in mind, I’m not one of those psychos who takes pre-workout with 300-400mg of caffeine, ever. If you’re a high-stim type of person, this many skew your experience.

#### **How Many Days in a Row Can I Drink Caffeine?**

Again, this is personal experience, but research has shown over and over that tolerance builds progressively. I’ve found that day 2 is worse than day 1, day 3 is worse than day 2, and after that, I’m not getting the euphoric feeling I did. So this is not science-backed, but **I think 3 is a good number.** If I have a higher dose of caffeine a fourth day in a row, its effects just don’t hit as hard. I’ve already quoted studies that say this occurs after 5-6 days, but no doubt it’s a gradual tolerance. Day one will be better than day three, and day four will be better than day six. After six days of regular caffeine intake, you’re unlikely to get the full effects.

Okay, now let’s get into actual protocols. I mix and match these depending on what I have going on, the phase of life, the time of year. Look, if [I’m in Barcelona where I spend a few months each year](https://davidwilliamrosales.com/2024/05/20/barcelona-digital-nomad/), then I’ll drink more coffee because it’s a social thing.

If I’m in a busy period for work, I may drink more. If I’m in a slower phase of life, I may hardly drink it. So I’ve experimented with several protocols of varying doses.

## **Real-World Caffeine Cycling Protocols**

I’ll start with my preferred protocol.

### **The Green Tea Protocol**

Green tea is a great tool for caffeine cycling, because it allows you to still get some caffeine even on your off days.

In this protocol, my week is divided into distinct phases of caffeine consumption. From **Monday to Thursday, I opt for green tea (~25mg of caffeine)**. Green tea provides a milder caffeine boost compared to coffee, which I find sufficient for maintaining alertness during the workweek. It’s a gentler stimulant, so it keeps me focused without overstimulation. I also love that it has l-theanine in it for a sense of calm. I’ve also noticed that if I have green tea in the morning, I can nap in the afternoon. If I have coffee, I can’t.

The choice of green tea isn’t just about the caffeine content. Green tea is renowned for its health benefits, including high levels of antioxidants, potential fat-burning properties, and contributions to heart and brain health. I love mixing chia green tea with a bit of milk.

**On Fridays and Saturdays, I switch to coffee (~125mg of caffeine)**. As I said, I do this on my writing mornings, my favorite days of the week. **I just feel like life couldn’t get better on these days.**It makes me really *love* my weekends.

**Sunday is my caffeine-free day.** This day of abstinence resets my caffeine sensitivity. It’s a day for my body to rest from any form of caffeine stimulation, allowing me to start the next week refreshed and ready to benefit fully from green tea’s milder effects.

This Green Tea Protocol strikes a balance between enjoying the benefits of caffeine and avoiding the pitfalls of tolerance and dependence.

Would I feel better on Friday and Saturday if I kept green tea out? Yes. For sure. However, **this allows me to consistently get the good parts of caffeine, without suffering from withdrawal or dependence.**

If I’m doing this regularly, I’ll still try to mix in a 48-72 hour period of no caffeine to get more of a reset.

**Green tea is a great way to help you cycle off of caffeine in general.** It’s much better than going cold turkey.

### **The Weekend Warrior Protocol**

This protocol is designed for those who prefer to reserve their caffeine intake for weekends or specific days when they need an extra boost. This is the protocol for those who like to party. That’s because you can **stay out late, wake up, have your caffeine, and still get your weekend back.**

The downside of this one is… Monday might be tough.

**Monday to Friday: No caffeine.** These days are caffeine-free, allowing your body to reset its caffeine sensitivity and reduce dependence. This period is ideal for focusing on hydration, balanced nutrition, and perhaps herbal teas that do not contain caffeine.

**Saturday and Sunday**: Caffeine consumption days. On these days, you can indulge in your favorite caffeinated beverages, like coffee or energy drinks. This timing is particularly beneficial for those who have high-energy activities planned for the weekend, such as workouts, social events, or intensive work projects.

If this really sucks, you can add some green tea on Monday.

### **The Gradual Reduction Protocol**

Going cold turkey off of daily high caffeine intake is a miserable idea. It’s much smarter to taper off. This one is ideal for those looking to gradually reduce their caffeine intake without going cold turkey.

**Week 1:** Start with your regular caffeine intake.

**Week 2:** Reduce the caffeine amount by one-third. For example, if you usually have three cups of coffee a day, cut down to two.

**Week 3:**Halve your initial caffeine intake. Continuing with the example, this would mean going down to one and a half cups of coffee per day.

**Week 4:** Limit caffeine to a minimal amount, like a single small cup of coffee or tea per day.

**Week 5 and Onward**: Alternate between minimal caffeine weeks and caffeine-free weeks. This approach helps in gradually reducing dependence while still allowing for occasional caffeine enjoyment.

### **The Alternating Week Protocol**

This protocol involves alternating caffeine consumption weekly. It does split up your life into “good weeks” and “not as good weeks.”

**Week 1:** Consume caffeine as per your usual routine.

**Week 2:**Completely abstain from caffeine. This week allows your body to reset and reduces tolerance.

**Repeat:** Continue alternating between caffeine consumption and abstinence weeks. This pattern can help maintain caffeine sensitivity and prevent the build-up of tolerance.

### **The “I Love Mondays” Protocol**

This protocol is ideal for those who want to kickstart their workweek with high energy and gradually taper down their caffeine intake as the week progresses, taking weekends off to reset.

**Monday: High caffeine day.** Start your week with a strong cup of coffee or your preferred high-caffeine beverage. Maybe you’ll train legs on this day. This boost helps tackle the challenges of the workweek with maximum focus and energy, making it perfect for those who have demanding Mondays.

**Tuesday to Thursday: Gradual reduction.** Each day, slightly reduce your caffeine intake. For instance, if you start with two cups of coffee on Monday, go down to one and a half on Tuesday, one on Wednesday, and half a cup or a weaker tea on Thursday. This gradual reduction helps in maintaining focus throughout the week without over-relying on caffeine.

**Friday: Minimal caffeine.**On Friday, opt for a very low-caffeine beverage, like a weak tea or a decaffeinated coffee. This helps in preparing your body for the caffeine-free weekend.

**Saturday and Sunday: Caffeine-free days.**Completely abstain from caffeine during the weekend. This break allows your body to reset its caffeine sensitivity and reduces dependence. It’s a time to enjoy other aspects of life, ensuring a well-rounded approach to work-life balance.

#### Tailoring to Your WOrk Schedule

**The “I Love Mondays” protocol is particularly beneficial if you grind your 9-5.** It aligns caffeine intake with the typical workweek’s demands, ensuring peak performance when it’s most needed, while also promoting a healthier approach to caffeine consumption.

#### One Week Off Per Month Approach

If you’re a regular caffeine drinker and don’t want to give that up, I challenge you to take one week off per month.

This isn’t my favorite approach, because you’ll deal with real caffeine dependence. But by getting seven days off, you’ll reset your adenosine receptors, and then you’ll have a great next few weeks.

As I’ll talk about in the next section, there are some tools that can help you stay alert without caffeine.

### **Alternatives to Caffeine**

During off-cycle periods of caffeine cycling, or for those times when you want to avoid stimulants altogether, some several natural substitutes and supplements can help maintain focus and energy. One particularly effective category is nootropics.

#### Nootropics: The Brain Boosters

Nootropics, often referred to as “smart drugs” are compounds that can improve brain performance. They are particularly useful for enhancing focus, memory, and overall cognitive function.

I look for caffeine-free nootropics which are an excellent choice for those looking to stay productive without the stimulating effects of caffeine.

**Afternoon Use:** I find nootropics especially beneficial in the afternoons, specifically between 2-5 pm. This is often when the post-lunch slump hits, and you need to stay on top of your game without resorting to caffeine, which could disrupt your sleep cycle.

Types of Nootropics: There are various nootropics available. If you’re interested, shoot me a message and I’ll share some of my favorites.

#### **Other Natural Alternatives**

**L-Theanine**: Often found in green tea, L-Theanine can be taken as a supplement. It promotes relaxation without drowsiness, making it a great partner to caffeine or a standalone supplement for focus and calm.

**Cold Showers:** Cold showers or other cold exposure tools increase adrenaline, giving a similar physiological effect as coffee. I won’t lie, I’ve done this on my no-caffeine days before.

**Adaptogens:** These are natural substances that help the body adapt to stress and exert a normalizing effect upon bodily processes. The most popular, and probably the most well-researched too, is ashwagandha. 300-600mg in the morning will provide a subtle boost. It’s no coffee replacement, but it’s better than nothing. It also helps with stress.

I have a greens drink that has 300mg of ashwagandha in it. Lots of greens drink are just powdered grass, but I am a fan of this one. Shoot me a message and I’ll give you the brand.

## **Safe and Responsible Caffeine Use**

While caffeine can be a beneficial stimulant when used correctly, it’s important to approach its consumption with mindfulness and responsibility.

This includes understanding safe consumption levels and being aware of the environmental and ethical implications of caffeine sourcing.

#### **Guidelines for Safe Consumption**

**Moderation is Key:** The general guideline for caffeine consumption is up to 400 milligrams per day for most healthy adults, roughly the amount in four 8-ounce cups of brewed coffee. However, individual tolerance can vary, so it’s important to listen to your body.

**Understand Your Sensitivity:** Some people are more sensitive to caffeine than others. If you experience jitteriness, anxiety, heart palpitations, or insomnia, you may need to reduce your intake.

**Timing Matters:** Avoid caffeine late in the day, as it can interfere with sleep. A safe rule of thumb is to avoid caffeine **after 12pm.**I know this is an aggressive curfew, but it plays it safe.

**Watch for Hidden Sources:** Caffeine isn’t just in coffee and tea; it’s also in chocolate, some soft drinks, energy drinks, and certain medications. Be mindful of all sources to avoid unintentional overconsumption.

### Environmental and Ethical Considerations

This one matters a lot to me for several reasons. My dad’s home country, El Salvador, has a dark history of exploitation by colonizers getting rich by growing coffee on the labor of the locals.

Here are some things to keep in mind when you choose and consume your caffeine.

**Sustainable Sourcing:**Coffee and tea are among the most heavily traded commodities in the world, and their production can have significant environmental impacts. Opt for brands that prioritize sustainable farming practices, such as shade-grown coffee, which preserves biodiversity.

**Fair Trade and Ethical Practices:** Support companies that ensure fair wages and good working conditions for their workers. Look for certifications like Fair Trade or Rainforest Alliance.

**Organic Options:** Whenever possible, choose organic coffee and tea to avoid pesticides and chemicals that can harm the environment and your health.

**Reduce Waste:** Consider the environmental impact of your caffeine consumption habits. Using a reusable cup, avoiding single-use pods, and composting coffee grounds are small steps that can make a big difference.

Being a conscious consumer means not only being aware of how caffeine affects your body but also understanding its broader impact on the world. By choosing sustainable, ethical products and consuming caffeine responsibly, you contribute to a healthier planet and a more equitable industry. Indeed, one small decision won’t save the world, but by **demanding the industry leaders to be better and with collective action,** we can.

# Caffeine Tolerance Reset: Why Your Coffee Stopped Working

Roon Team

![Caffeine Tolerance Reset: Why Your Coffee Stopped Working](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fxwiccqnbhaitvojyabpg.supabase.co%2Fstorage%2Fv1%2Fobject%2Fpublic%2Fneuroshift-blog-images%2Fblog%2Fcaffeine-tolerance-reset.webp&w=1920&q=75)

## The Caffeine Tolerance Trap: Why Your Coffee Stopped Working and How to Reset It (Without Quitting)

Your third cup of coffee hits like your first one used to. Maybe weaker. You're not imagining it. This is the **caffeine tolerance trap**, and if you've been drinking coffee daily for more than a few weeks, you're already in it. The good news: a caffeine tolerance reset doesn't require white-knuckling through a week of headaches. There are faster, smarter protocols, and a new class of compounds that sidestep the tolerance problem entirely.

This article breaks down exactly what's happening in your brain, gives you five evidence-based reset strategies, and explains why the most interesting solution isn't about resetting at all.

**Key Takeaways**

## What Caffeine Tolerance Actually Is (And Why It Happens So Fast)

Caffeine works by blocking **adenosine receptors** in your brain. Adenosine is the molecule that accumulates during waking hours and signals sleepiness. When caffeine parks itself on those receptors, adenosine can't do its job, and you feel alert.

Your brain doesn't like being tricked. Within days of consistent caffeine intake, it responds by [upregulating adenosine receptors](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1846425/), literally building more of them. More receptors means your usual dose of caffeine blocks a smaller percentage of the total. The result: diminishing returns.

According to [Healthline's review of the research](https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/caffeine-tolerance), dependence can develop in as few as **3 days** from doses as low as 100 mg per day. That's a single cup of coffee. For heavy users (400+ mg daily), tolerance to caffeine's stimulant effects can become nearly complete, meaning your morning coffee is mostly just preventing withdrawal rather than giving you a boost.

This is the core problem. You're not drinking coffee for energy anymore. You're drinking it to feel normal. And if you've layered in pre-workout on top of your daily coffee habit, you've likely accelerated the process. A 300 mg pre-workout plus two cups of coffee puts you well over 500 mg daily, which is deep into tolerance territory.

## How Long Does It Take to Reset Caffeine Tolerance?

The short answer: **7 to 14 days** of zero caffeine will return your adenosine receptors to baseline. A [2022 study published in PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8849224/) examined recovery from daily caffeine intake (450 mg/day for 10 days) and confirmed that receptor normalization requires a sustained abstinence period.

According to [StatPearls (NCBI)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430790/), caffeine withdrawal symptoms typically begin **12–24 hours** after your last dose, peak at **20–51 hours**, and resolve within **2–9 days**. The most common symptoms: headache, fatigue, irritability, difficulty concentrating, and depressed mood. Caffeine withdrawal is recognized in the DSM-5 as a clinical syndrome.

The longer answer: how long to reset caffeine tolerance depends on your daily intake, how long you've been consuming, and which protocol you choose.

![Roon focus pouches](/_next/image?url=%2Fcomparison%2Froon.png&w=256&q=75&dpl=dpl_AaV8m2kU6rgrxGaD1Yx68W5DqMdY)

Roon focus pouches

Clean, all-day focus. Zero nicotine, zero crash.

Caffeine, L-theanine, Dynamine and TeaCrine. Feel it in 5 to 10 minutes, then 6 to 8 hours of smooth focus.

## Five Caffeine Tolerance Reset Protocols

Here's the full menu. Pick the one that matches your life.

### Protocol 1: Cold Turkey (The Fast Reset)

Stop all caffeine immediately. Expect 2–5 days of discomfort, with the worst concentrated in the first 48 hours. Full receptor normalization typically occurs within 7–14 days.

**Best for:** People who want it over with quickly and can tolerate a rough few days. If you're scheduling a caffeine tolerance break, don't pick a week with major deadlines.

**The evidence:** The [StatPearls caffeine withdrawal review](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430790/) confirms that most symptoms resolve within 2–9 days, making cold turkey the fastest path to a clean reset.

### Protocol 2: The Gradual Taper (12–14 Days)

Reduce your daily caffeine intake by roughly **25% every 3–4 days**. If you're at 400 mg, drop to 300, then 200, then 100, then zero. This stretches the process to about two weeks but dramatically reduces withdrawal severity.

**Best for:** Heavy users (3+ cups daily) who can't afford cognitive downtime. The [American Psychiatric Association notes](https://www.coffeeandhealth.org/health/media-content/news-alerts/american-psychiatric-association-includes-caffeine-withdrawal-in-the-latest-edition-of-its-diagnostic-and-statistical-manual-of-mental-disorders-dsm-5) that withdrawal symptoms "can be avoided altogether if caffeine intake is decreased progressively."

### Protocol 3: Caffeine Cycling (Ongoing Tolerance Management)

Instead of a one-time reset, build regular breaks into your routine. The most common **caffeine cycling protocol**: 4 weeks on, 1 week off. Some people prefer 5 days on, 2 days off each week.

**Best for:** Athletes and gym-goers who rely on pre-workout caffeine for performance and want to preserve its ergogenic effects long-term. [Biology Insights recommends](https://biologyinsights.com/how-to-cycle-caffeine-and-reset-your-tolerance/) scheduling one caffeine-free day per week or taking a full week off every one to two months as a sustainable strategy.

### Protocol 4: Dose Reduction Without Quitting

You don't have to hit zero. Cutting your daily intake in half (say, from 400 mg to 200 mg) allows partial receptor normalization while keeping withdrawal symptoms minimal. After 2–3 weeks at the lower dose, caffeine's effects will feel stronger again.

**Best for:** People who genuinely enjoy coffee and don't want to give it up. This is stimulant tolerance management for realists.

### Protocol 5: The Caffeine Nap

This isn't a reset protocol per se, but a way to extract more from less caffeine. Drink a small dose of caffeine (100–150 mg), then immediately take a 20-minute nap. The nap clears adenosine from your receptors while the caffeine absorbs. When you wake up, both effects stack.

A [study published in Clinical Neurophysiology](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14652086/) found that a caffeine-plus-nap combination was the most effective intervention for reducing subjective sleepiness and improving performance, with effects lasting throughout the hour following the nap.

**Best for:** Afternoon slumps. Particularly useful during a caffeine tolerance break or taper when you're working with lower doses and need to maximize what you've got.

## Protocol Comparison

| Protocol | Duration to Reset | Withdrawal Severity | Best For |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cold Turkey | 7–14 days | High (peaks 20–51 hrs) | Fast, complete reset |
| Gradual Taper | 12–14 days | Low to moderate | Heavy users, busy schedules |
| Caffeine Cycling | Ongoing | Mild (periodic) | Athletes, pre-workout users |
| Dose Reduction | 2–3 weeks (partial) | Minimal | Coffee lovers, maintenance |
| Caffeine Nap | N/A (acute strategy) | None | Afternoon performance |

## The Asymmetric Solution: Compounds That Don't Build Tolerance

Every protocol above shares the same limitation: you're still working within caffeine's tolerance cycle. You reset, you reintroduce, tolerance rebuilds, and you reset again. It's a loop.

But what if part of your stack simply didn't trigger tolerance in the first place, opening the door to [alternatives to caffeine for energy](https://www.takeroon.com/blog/alternatives-to-caffeine-for-energy) that sidestep the cycle entirely?

### Theacrine (TeaCrine): 8 Weeks, Zero Habituation

Theacrine is a purine alkaloid structurally similar to caffeine, found naturally in kucha tea. It acts on both adenosine and dopamine receptors. But unlike caffeine, it doesn't cause the same receptor upregulation.

The key study: a [2016 placebo-controlled trial published in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4711067/) gave 60 healthy men either 200 mg or 300 mg of TeaCrine daily for **8 weeks**. The results showed no evidence of tachyphylaxis (the technical term for habituation) at either dose. The researchers concluded that theacrine's "non-habituating neuro-energetic effects" held steady across the entire study period. That's a stark contrast to caffeine, where tolerance can set in within days.

Why the difference? [Feduccia et al. (2012)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22579816/) demonstrated that theacrine activates both adenosinergic and dopaminergic systems but does not induce locomotor sensitization or tolerance after chronic exposure. The working theory: theacrine's additional methyl group changes its receptor binding profile enough to avoid triggering the compensatory upregulation that caffeine causes.

### Methylliberine (Dynamine): Fast Onset, No Habituation

Methylliberine is another caffeine relative with a shorter half-life and faster onset. [Safety data published in PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7146520/) confirms it does not produce the habituating effects seen with caffeine. It acts on similar neural pathways but, like theacrine, appears to avoid the receptor-level changes that drive tolerance.

When combined with caffeine and theacrine, the three compounds produced measurable cognitive benefits. A [2021 study published in Cureus](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35103121/) (Tartar et al.) found that a caffeine-theacrine-methylliberine combination improved cognitive performance and reaction time in adult male participants without negatively affecting mood.

### Why This Matters for Your Caffeine Strategy

The pharmacological asymmetry here is real. Caffeine builds tolerance. Theacrine and methylliberine, based on available clinical data, do not. This means a stack that uses a moderate caffeine dose alongside these compounds can deliver sustained cognitive effects without the same escalating-dose problem that pure caffeine creates.

This isn't theoretical. It's the design logic behind a new category of [caffeine alternatives worth trying](https://www.takeroon.com/blog/caffeine-alternatives-worth-trying-2026), and it directly addresses the trap that sends people searching for a caffeine tolerance reset every few months. Instead of cycling on and off caffeine forever, you reduce the caffeine load and let non-habituating compounds carry more of the cognitive weight, a principle at the heart of [natural energy without caffeine](https://www.takeroon.com/blog/natural-energy-boosters-without-caffeine) approaches.

# CAFFEINE TOLERANCE AND THE STRATEGIC RESET: A PERIODISED APPROACH FOR CYCLISTS

By anthony-walsh·

WHO THIS IS FOR

## IS THIS YOU?

* ▸A daily coffee drinker who has not felt the caffeine kick in months and wonders whether a reset would bring it back
* ▸A rider with one big target event who wants to time a caffeine washout to maximise race-day impact
* ▸Someone planning their off-season and looking for a logical window to reset caffeine tolerance
* ▸A cyclist who gets side effects from caffeine and suspects they might be a slow metaboliser who processes it differently

THE ROADMAN VIEW

## The Roadman View

* I used to drink four coffees a day and take a caffeine gel before every hard session. The effect had completely disappeared. A 10-day washout during an off-season recovery block brought the response back so sharply I could not believe the difference.
* Time the reset during a deload week or transition period. The withdrawal headaches and low motivation are real, and you do not want them landing in the middle of a build block.
* The counter-argument is legitimate though. If caffeine does not bother your sleep and you still feel it working, there is no obligation to periodise. Not everyone needs a reset, and the research supports both approaches.

Caffeine tolerance is not a binary switch. You do not go from "caffeine works" to "caffeine does nothing." What actually happens is slower, more insidious, and — for riders who care about racing performance — far more interesting than the simple story.

I have already covered [how to dose caffeine properly and when to take it](/blog/cycling-caffeine-performance-guide) in our [cycling nutrition](/topics/cycling-nutrition) guides. If you have not read that, start there. This article is about a different question entirely: what happens to the caffeine response over months and years of daily use, and whether you can strategically manipulate that response across a training season to get more out of the same substance.

The short answer is yes, you can. But the longer answer involves some honest trade-offs that most articles on this topic conveniently ignore.

## What Tolerance Actually Is — the Adenosine Story

Your brain runs on a neurotransmitter called adenosine. As you go through the day — and particularly during exercise — adenosine accumulates and binds to receptors that promote fatigue, drowsiness, and reduced neural drive. Caffeine works by physically blocking those receptors. The adenosine is still there, still building up, but your brain cannot register it. Perceived exertion drops. You feel sharper. You can push harder.

Here is where it gets really interesting. Your brain is not stupid. When caffeine keeps blocking adenosine receptors day after day, your central nervous system responds by growing more of them. This is called receptor upregulation, and it is your body's attempt to restore homeostasis despite the chemical interference. More receptors means more binding sites for adenosine, which means the same dose of caffeine cannot block them all. The original effect diminishes.

This process starts remarkably fast. Research published by Fredholm and colleagues in *Pharmacological Reviews* demonstrated that measurable receptor upregulation begins within 3-5 days of consistent caffeine intake. By day 20, the receptor density has largely plateaued at a new, higher baseline. That is three weeks. Three weeks of daily coffee and your brain has physically remodelled itself to compensate.

But — and this is the part people miss — the performance benefit does not vanish completely. Spriet's 2014 meta-analysis in *Sports Medicine*, which pooled data across dozens of studies, found that habitual caffeine users still showed a 1-3 per cent improvement in time trial performance from acute caffeine ingestion. The subjective experience changes dramatically — you stop feeling that sharp alertness, that clean energy — but the ergogenic effect persists at a reduced level. Your brain has adapted to the presence of caffeine, but it has not fully neutralised it.

This is the tension at the heart of the tolerance question. You are still getting something. But you could be getting more.

## The Full Washout Protocol

A caffeine washout is conceptually simple: stop consuming caffeine entirely and wait for your adenosine receptors to return to their original density. The practical execution is where it gets uncomfortable.

The research consensus puts the full reset window at 7-14 days. Most of the receptor downregulation — your brain dismantling the extra receptors it built — happens in the first week. By day 14, receptor density is essentially back to baseline in the vast majority of individuals.

Here is what those 14 days actually feel like, day by day:

**Days 1-2:** Surprisingly manageable for most people. You might feel a bit flat, slightly less focused. Nothing dramatic. Do not let this lull you into thinking withdrawal is easy.

**Days 2-4:** The headache window. This is real and it is physiological — not psychological, not imagined. The increased adenosine receptor density means adenosine is now binding more aggressively than it did before you ever started drinking coffee. Your blood vessels dilate (adenosine is a vasodilator), which causes a characteristic dull, persistent headache. Fatigue hits. Concentration fragments. Irritability spikes. Some riders describe a foggy, underwater feeling that makes even easy conversation feel effortful.

**Days 5-7:** The corner turns. Headaches ease. Energy starts to normalise, though you may still feel below your caffeinated baseline. Sleep often improves noticeably during this window — many riders report deeper, more restorative sleep once caffeine clears the system entirely.

**Days 8-14:** The new normal. Or rather, the old normal. By now, your receptor density is approaching pre-caffeine levels. When you reintroduce caffeine after this period, the effect is markedly stronger — both subjectively and physiologically.

Let me be really clear about the withdrawal symptoms: they are temporary and they are harmless. Nobody has ever been injured by a caffeine headache. Paracetamol takes the edge off. Staying hydrated helps. But the symptoms are real enough that you need to plan around them — which brings us to the question of when.

## Timing the Reset: Why Your Training Calendar Matters

This is where most advice on caffeine resets falls apart. People tell you to quit caffeine for two weeks, as if those two weeks exist in a vacuum. They do not. You are a cyclist. You train. You have sessions to hit, weeks to build, races to target. You cannot just carve out a fortnight of feeling terrible and pretend it will not affect your training.

The answer is to align the washout with a phase where the cost is lowest: a deload week, a recovery block, or the transition period between seasons.

During withdrawal, you can expect perceived exertion on the bike to increase by 10-15 per cent for the same power output. Your threshold intervals will feel harder. Your motivation will dip. Power may drop 2-5 per cent during the worst of it, days 2-4. None of this matters if your training prescription that week is three easy spins and a rest day.

The ideal timing windows:

**End-of-season transition (October-November for Northern Hemisphere riders).** You have just finished your race calendar. Training volume and intensity are at their lowest. You are doing unstructured rides, some gym work, maybe getting on the mountain bike. This is the single best time to reset — the withdrawal cost is absorbed by a period where productive training was never on the agenda.

**Mid-season recovery block.** If your season has two peak periods — spring classics and then a late-summer target — the recovery block between peaks is another natural window. You are deliberately backing off for 7-10 days anyway. Layer the caffeine reset on top and the training impact is negligible.

**Pre-build deload week.** For riders who are disciplined about periodisation, the deload week before a build phase is another option. You are already reducing load. The withdrawal aligns with the recovery, and you re-enter the build phase with a fresh caffeine response just as the intensity ramps up.

The one time you must never attempt a washout: during a build block or within three weeks of a target race. The combination of withdrawal fatigue and high training demands is a recipe for missed sessions, accumulated stress, and poor performance exactly when it counts.

## The Periodised Caffeine Model

Here is the framework that brings all of this together. It is not complicated, but it does require some forward planning.

**Off-season / base phase (typically 8-16 weeks):** Reduce caffeine to zero or near-zero. If you cannot face full elimination, drop to one small coffee per day — enough to prevent severe withdrawal but low enough that significant receptor downregulation occurs. During base phase, your training is predominantly Zone 2 endurance work. You do not need an ergogenic boost for a three-hour steady ride. The perceived exertion difference between caffeinated and uncaffeinated at these intensities is minimal.

**Build phase (typically 4-8 weeks):** Reintroduce caffeine at your performance dose — 3mg/kg, 60 minutes before key sessions. Your receptors have been partially or fully reset. The caffeine hits noticeably harder. Use it specifically for threshold intervals, VO2max work, race simulations — the sessions where the performance benefit is most valuable. On easy days and recovery rides, skip it.

**Race phase / peak (typically 2-6 weeks):** Use caffeine strategically for races and the key sessions that maintain race fitness. You now have 4-8 weeks of amplified caffeine response precisely when the stakes are highest. By the end of the race phase, tolerance will have rebuilt — but by then, the races are done and the cycle begins again.

**Transition (1-3 weeks):** Reset. Drop caffeine. Recover from the season. Allow receptor density to return to baseline. Repeat.

This model is not original to me. Versions of it have been discussed by sports nutrition researchers including Lawrence Spriet at the University of Guelph and Brendan Egan at Dublin City University. The principle mirrors how we periodise training load, nutrition, and recovery — applying the stimulus when it matters most and removing it when it matters least.

## Managing Withdrawal While Still Training

Here is where the practical rubber meets the theoretical road. You have decided to reset. You have timed it to a recovery week. You still have to ride your bike.

The first rule: do not try to be heroic. If day 3 of withdrawal falls on a day where you had an easy spin planned and you feel awful, take the rest day instead. The withdrawal passes. A missed recovery ride does not set your fitness back.

The second rule: hydrate aggressively. Caffeine is a mild diuretic, and your body has been compensating for that. When you remove it, fluid balance shifts. Drink more water than you think you need during the first week. This also helps with the headaches.

The third rule: manage the headaches proactively. Do not wait for them to build. If you know days 2-3 are the window, take paracetamol or ibuprofen at the first sign. The headaches are vascular — caused by adenosine-mediated vasodilation — and they respond well to standard analgesics.

The fourth rule: expect your RPE to lie to you. A ride that normally feels like a 5 out of 10 might feel like a 7 during withdrawal. That does not mean you are less fit. It means your perception of effort has temporarily recalibrated. Trust your power meter, not your legs.

Mark Beaumont, during his record-breaking around-the-world cycling attempt, reportedly managed caffeine intake carefully across the multi-week effort — using it specifically during the hardest segments and backing off during recovery periods to maintain its effectiveness. That is periodisation in real time, across a single event rather than a season. The principle is the same: deploy the tool when the demand is highest.

## Caffeine-Free Alternatives During the Reset

One of the hardest parts of a caffeine reset is not the headache. It is losing the ritual. The warm mug before a morning ride. The café stop halfway through the Sunday loop. The pre-race routine of holding a hot cup and getting your head right. These behavioural cues matter more than most people acknowledge.

The good news is that the ritual does not require caffeine. What it requires is the behaviour — the warm drink, the pause, the preparation.

**Decaffeinated coffee** is the obvious substitute and it is worth more credit than it gets. Swiss Water Process decaf retains the chlorogenic acids and polyphenols from the bean, the flavour is close enough to satisfy the ritual, and the residual caffeine content (2-5mg per cup) is too low to meaningfully affect receptor adaptation. If you are a coffee person, decaf is the path of least resistance.

**Rooibos tea** is naturally caffeine-free, has a robust flavour that works as a standalone or with milk, and contains antioxidant compounds. It is not coffee. It will not pretend to be. But as a warm pre-ride drink, it fills the gap.

**Hot water with lemon and a pinch of salt** sounds absurd until you try it. The salt provides sodium — useful before a ride. The lemon adds flavour. The warm water is the ritual. Some riders swear by it.

**Carbohydrate-based pre-ride drinks** — a bottle of diluted fruit juice, a commercial electrolyte mix, or even warm honey water — maintain the pre-ride routine while adding genuine fuel value. During base phase, this can serve double duty as the start of your ride nutrition without any stimulant component.

The point is not to find a caffeine replacement. There is no caffeine replacement. The point is to preserve the habits and routines that caffeine was embedded in so that the washout period does not feel like deprivation.

## The CYP1A2 Question: Does Your Genetics Change the Calculation?

Individual caffeine metabolism varies enormously, and the primary driver is the CYP1A2 gene. This gene encodes the liver enzyme responsible for breaking down caffeine, and the variant you carry determines whether you are a fast or slow metaboliser.

**Fast metabolisers (AA genotype)** clear caffeine from their system in 2-4 hours. They tend to experience the performance benefit cleanly, with fewer side effects and less sleep disruption. There is some evidence — though it is not conclusive — that fast metabolisers may build tolerance slightly more slowly because the caffeine clears before it can exert sustained receptor pressure. For these riders, periodisation still works but the tolerance problem may be less pronounced in the first place.

**Slow metabolisers (AC or CC genotype)** hold caffeine for 6-8 hours or longer. They accumulate more caffeine at any given dose, experience more side effects, and — critically — some research suggests they may not get the same magnitude of performance benefit. Womack and colleagues published a study in the *Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition* showing that slow metabolisers actually performed worse in a cycling time trial with caffeine compared to placebo. If you have never felt a clear benefit from caffeine despite dosing correctly, this might be why.

For slow metabolisers, the periodisation calculation changes. If caffeine is not reliably helping your performance even when you are sensitive to it, then periodising its use is less important. You might be better served by simply drinking coffee if you enjoy it and not worrying about the ergogenic angle at all. Asker Jeukendrup, whose work on sports nutrition is foundational, has noted that the individual response to caffeine is so variable that blanket protocols are inherently limited. Know your own response first. Then decide whether periodisation is worth the effort.

If you want to know your genotype, direct-to-consumer genetic tests from companies like DNAfit or 23andMe now include CYP1A2 analysis. It is not essential — your lived experience with caffeine is a reasonable proxy — but it removes the guesswork.

## The Case for Not Bothering

I would not be giving you the full picture if I did not say this: there is a perfectly reasonable argument for ignoring everything above and just drinking your coffee every day.

The 2022 British Journal of Sports Medicine meta-analysis — one of the largest pooled analyses on caffeine and exercise — confirmed that habitual caffeine users still derive a statistically significant performance improvement from acute caffeine ingestion. The effect is smaller than in caffeine-naive individuals, yes. But it is there. It is real. It is measurable.

Louise Burke's group at the Australian Institute of Sport has consistently recommended against pre-competition caffeine withdrawal for most athletes, on the grounds that the withdrawal costs — reduced training quality, headaches, irritability during taper — outweigh the marginal gain from resensitisation. Her position, and it is well-supported, is that the performance benefit of caffeine is robust enough to survive habitual use.

So who should actually bother with periodisation?

If you drink coffee daily, take a caffeine gel before every hard ride, and you have completely stopped noticing any effect — no sharpness, no RPE reduction, nothing — then a reset is worth trying. You have built substantial tolerance and the subjective response has flatlined. A 10-14 day washout timed to your off-season costs you almost nothing and may restore the response for your next block of serious training.

If you drink one coffee a day, still feel it working, sleep well, and race fine — you do not need to change anything. The evidence supports your approach. Periodisation is a tool for a specific problem. If you do not have the problem, you do not need the tool.

The riders I find this matters most for are the ones consuming 400-600mg per day — four to six coffees, pre-workout supplements, caffeinated gels stacked on top of their morning brew. At those levels, tolerance is aggressive, sleep is usually compromised whether they admit it or not, and the reset produces a dramatic difference in how caffeine feels when it comes back.

## Putting It Into Practice

If you have read this far and decided a periodised approach is worth trying, here is the condensed protocol:

1. **Identify your next natural low point** in the training calendar. Off-season transition is ideal. A deload week works if you cannot wait.
2. **Eliminate all caffeine sources** for 10-14 days. That includes tea, dark chocolate, pre-workout supplements, and caffeinated soft drinks. Go fully clean.
3. **Manage symptoms proactively.** Paracetamol for headaches. Extra hydration. Reduced training expectations for days 2-5. Easy spins only. No intensity.
4. **Substitute the ritual, not the substance.** Decaf coffee, rooibos, warm water with lemon. Keep your pre-ride routine intact.
5. **Reintroduce caffeine at the start of your next build phase** at your standard performance dose — 3mg/kg, 60 minutes before key sessions. Notice the difference.
6. **Use caffeine selectively through the build and race phases.** Key sessions and races only. Skip it on easy days. This extends the window of amplified response.
7. **When the race season ends, reset again.** One to two resets per year is sufficient for most riders.

This is not about demonising caffeine. It is about using it with the same intentionality you bring to your training plan, your nutrition periodisation, and your recovery strategy. Caffeine is a tool. Tools work best when you deploy them deliberately.

If you want to discuss your own caffeine strategy, compare notes with other riders who have tried the periodised approach, or just ask questions about any of this — the [Not Done Yet community on Skool](https://www.skool.com/roadmancycling) is where those conversations happen. Real riders working through this stuff in real time.

FAQ

## FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS

How long does it take to reset caffeine tolerance?+

Adenosine receptor density returns to baseline within 7-14 days of complete caffeine elimination. Most people experience the worst withdrawal symptoms on days 2-3, with symptoms largely resolving by day 5-7. A full 14-day washout provides the most complete reset, but even 7 days produces a noticeable resensitisation for most individuals.

Should I quit caffeine before a target race?+

Not necessarily. Recent research from Louise Burke's group at the Australian Institute of Sport shows that habitual users still gain a performance benefit on race day without withdrawal. If you do want to try a reset, time it 3-4 weeks before your target event so you have at least 7-10 days of full caffeine response before race day. Never attempt withdrawal in race week — the fatigue and irritability will hurt more than any marginal caffeine boost.

Can I just reduce caffeine instead of cutting it completely?+

Partial reduction slows receptor downregulation but does not produce the same resensitisation as complete elimination. Halving your intake will reduce withdrawal symptoms but will also produce a smaller reset effect. For the cleanest reset, eliminate all caffeine sources including tea, dark chocolate, and pre-workout supplements for the full washout period.

Will caffeine withdrawal hurt my training?+

Yes, temporarily. Expect 10-15 per cent higher perceived exertion on days 2-4 of withdrawal. Power output may drop by 2-5 per cent during this window. This is why timing the reset to a deload week or recovery phase is critical — the training prescription is already light, so the withdrawal cost is absorbed by planned rest rather than deducted from productive training.

How often should I reset caffeine tolerance?+

Once or twice per year is sufficient for most cyclists. The natural structure of a training season provides logical windows: the off-season transition and a mid-season recovery block. Riders with one A-race per year might do a single reset 4-6 weeks before their target event. Riders with two peak periods might reset before each build phase.
