Statistically significant and/or trend-level beneficial effects of L-theanine supplementation on sleep-related outcome measures were reported in 9 of the 13 included trials, including 9 of the 11 that used a dose ≥200 mg/day (see Table 1). Improvements were identified on both objective and participant-reported endpoints, though primarily on measures linked to sleep quality rather than total duration. Beneficial effects on sleep were noted in healthy adults as well as in individuals with psychiatric disorders, cancer and in boys with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), suggesting these results are not restricted to a particular group and appear to be broadly applicable across the general population. However, there were limited and mixed results with regards to the efficacy of L-theanine in improving sleep-related measures in those meeting criteria for clinical insomnia [[Citation 39](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 43](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)].

Where reported, dosing adherence was high and was supported by elevated serum L-theanine concentrations [[Citation 26](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 37](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 41](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 43](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. L-theanine was well tolerated by participants (including among those using it as an adjunct to common psychotropic medications), even at the highest dose (900 mg/day), and over an eight-week dosing period, with few adverse events reported across the included trials.

We performed an assessment of the methodological quality of each of the included trials using NIH Study Quality Assessment Tools [[Citation 33](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)] (Supplementary Table 1). These tools were originally developed to assess clinical intervention trials, but also offer a useful framework to assist in evaluating the design and reporting of other types of intervention studies. We rated most of the included studies as ‘Fair’ on the basis that these used a rigorous trial design and established outcome measures. However, details regarding intervention adherence, the specific method by which participants were randomised, and statistical power were not always explicitly listed.

## 4. Discussion

### 4.1. Overview of findings

Based on the current evidence, dietary supplementation with 200–450 mg/day of L-theanine appears to support healthy sleep. Specifically, results were most robust across markers of sleep quality, with benefits noted on associated measures linked to sleep latency, maintenance and efficiency, as well as greater perceived sleep satisfaction and feelings of refreshment and recovery on waking. Where reported, associated effect sizes were typically in the small-to-medium range. However, there was little evidence that L-theanine increases total sleep time. The positive effects identified in this review are consistent with previous pre-clinical studies that have noted beneficial effects of L-theanine on sleep measures in rodents [[Citation 28–31](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. These are also further supported by the results of recent randomised controlled trials that have reported beneficial effects of various supplements that include L-theanine, in combination with other potentially active ingredients, on sleep outcomes in largely healthy adult samples [[Citation 46–50](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. Though there are also some conflicting results in combination product trials, which have highlighted the methodological challenges facing trials in this area [[Citation 51](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)].

High compliance (where reported) and a lack of adverse events across the included studies, even following sustained use, suggests that L-theanine at the investigated doses was safe and well tolerated by users. Importantly, unlike many other products targeting sleep which have a sedative action, L-theanine does not appear to cause drowsiness or adversely impact cognitive function [[Citation 10](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 27](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. Tea is the most widely consumed beverage in the world after water and is the major source of L-theanine in the human diet [[Citation 52](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 53](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. However, a 200–450 mg dose of L-theanine is considerably higher than that found in a standard cup of commercially available green or black tea. The exact quantity varies depending on factors such as the type of tea, cultivation, manufacturing and preparation methods used, but is typically up to around 25 mg per 200 ml cup [[Citation 21](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 54](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. This suggests that while some benefits may be achieved through routine tea consumption, additional L-theanine would likely need to be consumed as a dietary supplement to achieve the optimal sleep benefit, particularly given that caffeine is also present in many forms of tea and acts as a stimulant which can adversely impact sleep (especially when consumed later in the day) [[Citation 36](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 55](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 56](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)].

Studies have reported that L-theanine crosses the blood-brain barrier and is transported into the brain in a dose-dependent manner [[Citation 24](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 25](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. However, the exact mechanism by which L-theanine produces its sleep-enhancing effects is unclear; it is likely that several potentially complimentary effects may facilitate this. In mice, intragastric administration of L-theanine over 30-days increased acetylcholine and GABA levels in brain tissue [[Citation 31](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. Both these neurotransmitters have proven roles in sleep; an increase in the release of acetylcholine is linked to rapid eye movement (REM) sleep and GABA is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain [[Citation 57](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. Additionally, L-theanine is structurally similar to glutamate, the major excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system, and has been shown to have micromolar affinities for glutamate receptors including the N-Methyl-D-Aspartate (NMDA) receptor [[Citation 58](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. It is likely that L-theanine’s mechanism is also linked to competition with glutamate at these receptors. At the behavioural level, studies have also demonstrated that L-theanine can enhance feelings of relaxation and associated alpha-waves in the brain [[Citation 27](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 59](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 60](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. It may be that it is easier to enter deep, restful sleep when in a relaxed state prior to going to bed [[Citation 10](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. In addition, both pre-clinical and human studies have suggested that L-theanine is able to mitigate some of the adverse effects that caffeine can have on sleep [[Citation 28–30](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 36](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. This may also have contributed to some of the observed beneficial effects given the ubiquitous use of caffeine-containing products globally, often throughout the day [[Citation 7](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 55](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)].

### 4.2. Strengths and limitations

While several narrative reviews have suggested that L-theanine may be able to support healthy sleep [[Citation 10](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 25](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 53](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)], this is among the first systematic reviews, to our knowledge, to evaluate the impact of L-theanine supplementation on sleep outcomes in humans (see also [[Citation 61](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]). It also builds on the findings of other recent reviews of participant-reported and physiological data which have highlighted L-theanine’s beneficial effects, at a similar dose, on measures of stress and anxiety [[Citation 27](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. A potential limitation of our review methodology was that it was not prospectively registered on an associated database (e.g. PROSPERO).

In order to examine all relevant research in this area, we used broad inclusion criteria and included all types of human intervention trials. While open-label, single-arm studies are known to suffer from various biases, the included trials noted beneficial effects on sleep that were consistent with those observed in the most rigorously designed randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials. Our quality assessment highlighted some methodological aspects that were often not explicitly detailed, particularly regarding sample size and associated power calculations, as well as formal evaluation and reporting of intervention adherence (see Supplementary Table 1), though these omissions were not deemed sufficient to invalidate the overall findings of this review. It is vital however, that future trials consider these limitations in their own design and reporting in order to provide further high-quality evidence on this topic. There is also a need for future trials to provide more complete reporting of outcome data in the associated publication. This would permit greater evaluation of the magnitude and meaningfulness of observed effects, as well as facilitating the ability to compare and combine data across studies for further quantitative review (e.g. via meta-analysis).

We found no evidence of publication bias based on our search of the ClinicalTrials.gov or WHO ICTRP databases (the latter aggregates trial registration data from many of the world’s largest national registers). However, we did identify several ongoing (‘Recruiting’) or recently completed trials (<12 months) that should add important additional data to the current evidence base following their publication. While we believe our search strategy represents a comprehensive and transparent approach to identifying both published and unpublished trials, it is possible that other relevant studies may have been conducted that we were unable to identify. Similarly, there may be additional trials that have not been listed or published in English that would otherwise meet our eligibility criteria for inclusion.

Though the majority of the included trials noted positive intervention effects, there were some studies that failed to report direct benefits on sleep measures [[Citation 36](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 41](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 44](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 45](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. This may be due to methodological limitations with those studies. For example, Tominaga et al. reported few notable differences between participants who received L-theanine or placebo [[Citation 44](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)], however the trial used a low dose of L-theanine (100 mg/day) and assessed participant-reported sleep quality using a single 3-point scale which may have lacked sensitivity to subtle but important changes in subjective sleep parameters. Issues with the use of their EEG-monitoring device were also experienced by some study participants, leading to their data being excluded from the analyses, suggesting this may not necessarily reliably reflect typical sleep patterns. Interestingly, though Baba et al. also did not report any benefits on EEG-derived measures of sleep latency, time or wake after sleep onset in a small sample (_n_ = 9) of healthy female university students following use of a single low-dose of L-theanine (50 mg) compared with placebo [[Citation 36](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)], they did note that using L-theanine in combination with caffeine significantly mitigated the adverse impact of caffeine on sleep quality that was observed when it was administered alone (over 60 minutes of additional time spent awake after sleep onset compared to when they received the placebo). This latter effect is also consistent with evidence from previous studies in rodents [[Citation 28–30](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)].

Moulin et al. reported a significant reduction in time spent asleep and in light sleep among those receiving L-theanine compared to placebo after 28 days of use [[Citation 41](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. However, this may be linked to the discrepancy between the two arms at baseline, where those randomised to receive L-theanine (_n_ = 15) already exhibited a significantly longer mean time asleep (∼38 minutes) compared to the placebo group (_n_ = 15). In addition, there were no significant changes in self-reported sleep measures over the course of the study, while significant improvements from baseline were also noted on measures of reaction time during an attention task at the day 14 and 28 assessments, leading the study authors to conclude that this may have actually indicated an improvement in sleep quality among those receiving L-theanine during the study [[Citation 41](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)].

The other trial that did not report a benefit was Unno et al. who only assessed total participant-reported sleep duration in their study of university students and did not examine any elements of perceived sleep quality [[Citation 45](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. Other trials included validated participant-reported sleep measures that provide a broad and detailed evaluation of perceptions of sleep. This included the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) [[Citation 62](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)] and the Oguri-Shirakawa-Azumi (OSA) sleep inventory [[Citation 63](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)], both of which have been used extensively as endpoints in previous intervention trials targeting sleep and detected beneficial effects among those receiving L-theanine on sleep parameters across studies included in the current review [[Citation 26](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 34](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 35](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 37](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 38](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 42](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. Similarly, actigraphy is a well-established and non-invasive approach that has long been used to objectively assess aspects of sleep-wake activity and sleep quality, providing complementary data to that acquired via participant-reported outcome measures [[Citation 64](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 65](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. This approach demonstrated sensitivity to subtle but significant changes in measures of sleep efficiency in favour of L-theanine among the included studies [[Citation 34](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#),[Citation 40](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)].

Several studies also reported only trend-level benefits on sleep measures in their analyses, however, given these results were consistent with the broader weight of evidence, it suggests that this was potentially due to a lack of power to detect statistically significant effects as a result of the relatively small sample sizes that were often used. Heterogeneity in sample demographics (such as age, sex and participant health status and medication use), study designs (e.g. parallel group and crossover trials), and dosing regimens may also have contributed to differences in the magnitude of effects observed across the various sleep-related outcome measures that were used in these trials. While the purpose of the current systematic review was to summarise all existing literature on this topic, we concluded that pooling the data into a meta-analysis was not appropriate based on the heterogeneity in study design, outcomes and reporting of associated data in these trials. Following the publication of further randomised controlled trials, future reviews could potentially conduct meta-analyses using specific outcome measures, subscales and populations to examine the effect of L-theanine supplementation on different aspects of sleep and to help identify potential moderators that might influence this relationship (where sufficient comparable study data would allow this to be done meaningfully).

### 4.3. Implications for future research

Though many of the included studies were conducted using healthy adults in Japan, beneficial effects of L-theanine on sleep related-measures were also reported in randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials involving various clinical and non-clinical populations across several distinct geographical regions, suggesting these results have broad applicability. However, this area would benefit from further large, high-quality trials and the use of objective measures, such as polysomnography, to provide a detailed evaluation of the impact of L-theanine on sleep architecture and associated physiological functions. This would help to establish the mechanisms by which L-theanine can enhance sleep quality and would complement the existing participant-reported and actigraphy-based data.

There is also a need for further evaluation into the effect of L-theanine in those with insomnia. One study reported that L-theanine supplementation showed no benefit among this population, despite it significantly improving various aspects of sleep quality among individuals without insomnia [[Citation 43](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. However, this subgroup analysis included only a small sample of patients with insomnia (_n_ = 18). In contrast, a larger trial in cancer patients with insomnia noted significantly greater improvement in sleep symptoms among those receiving L-theanine compared to placebo, though improvement in those receiving melatonin was superior to either of these groups [[Citation 39](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1028415X.2025.2556925#)]. This suggests that further investigation is warranted among those with insomnia before definitive conclusions can be drawn. This is relevant with regards to establishing the efficacy of L-theanine both as a standalone intervention, as well as its potential use as an adjunct to existing medicinal options given the severity, persistence and functional impact of sleep disturbances experienced by this population.

## 5. Conclusion

Based on the current evidence, dietary supplementation with 200–450 mg/day of L-theanine appears to be an effective way to support healthy sleep in adults. Results were most robust for markers of sleep quality, with associated beneficial effects noted on both objective and participant-reported outcome measures. These findings are consistent with previous pre-clinical studies and combination product trials that have also indicated that L-theanine supplementation may be an effective way to support sleep. Further high-quality trials using objective measures (including polysomnography) and into the mechanisms underlying L-theanine’s sleep supporting effects are warranted. There was also limited evaluation of the impact of L-theanine supplementation among individuals meeting clinical criteria for insomnia, therefore further studies are required before conclusions can be drawn on its efficacy in that specific population.

No new data were generated as part of this review.

args.summary:
This is a systematic review published in Nutritional Neuroscience (Volume 29, Issue 2, 2026) examining the effect of L-theanine dietary supplementation on sleep in humans. L-theanine is a naturally occurring non-protein amino acid found in Camellia sinensis (tea plant) leaves. The review included 13 eligible trials (n=550 participants) identified through database searches up to February 3, 2025, including 11 randomized controlled trials and 2 single-arm open-label trials. Doses ranged from 50–900 mg/day, with most studies using 200–450 mg/day.

Key findings: Supplementation with 200–450 mg/day of L-theanine appears safe and effective for supporting healthy sleep in adults. Beneficial effects were reported on both objective and participant-reported outcomes, particularly measures of sleep quality (sleep latency, maintenance, efficiency, perceived sleep satisfaction, and feelings of refreshment on waking). However, there was little evidence that L-theanine increases total sleep time. Effect sizes were typically small-to-medium. Benefits were noted in healthy adults, as well as in individuals with psychiatric disorders, cancer, and ADHD, suggesting broad applicability.

The review notes that L-theanine was well-tolerated with few adverse events, does not cause drowsiness or impair cognitive function (unlike many sleep aids), and a 200–450 mg dose is significantly higher than the ~25 mg found in a standard cup of tea. The mechanism is unclear but may involve increased GABA and acetylcholine levels, glutamate receptor competition, enhanced alpha-wave activity, relaxation promotion, and mitigation of caffeine's adverse effects on sleep. Mixed results were found for clinical insomnia populations, warranting further research. The authors are employees of British American Tobacco and The Water Street Collective.

## Abstract

In this randomised, placebo-controlled trial, adults with impaired sleep (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index ≥ 5) were randomly assigned using a minimization algorithm to receive a formulation containing l-theanine plus lemon balm, valerian, and saffron extracts, or placebo, during 6 weeks. Objective sleep quality parameters were measured using an actigraphy device. We enrolled and randomised 64 individuals, 31 from the active group and 27 from the placebo group completed the 6 week follow-up. Mean sleep efficiency remained unmodified in the active group, and increased by 3% in the placebo group, the between-group difference in the change was not statistically significant (p = 0.49). Total sleep time also improved more with placebo (13.0 vs. 1.33 min, p = 0.66). Time wake after sleep onset (WASO) decreased more in the active group (4.6% vs. 2.4%), but the difference was not significant (p = 0.33). Mean PSQI decreased by 3.11 points (32.3%) in the active group, and by 3.86 points (39.5%) in the placebo group (p = 0.41). SF-36 increased more with placebo (+ 18.3 in active, + 32.1 in placebo, p = 0.68). Salivary cortisol remained unchanged in both groups. No serious adverse events were reported. Among adults with impaired sleep, a nutraceutical combination did not improve objective or subjective sleep parameters more than a placebo infusion.

## Introduction

Sleep is a fundamental biological process for human health[1](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR1 "Grandner, M. & Fernandez, F. The translational neuroscience of sleep: A contextual framework. Science 374, 568–573 (2021)."). During sleep, the human organism saves energy, repairs tissues, restores energy sources and develops metabolic and immunologic adaptations[2](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR2 "Krueger, J. M., Frank, M. G., Wisor, J. P. & Roy, S. Sleep function: Toward elucidating an enigma. Sleep Med. Rev. 28, 46–54 (2016)."). Sleep also plays a fundamental role in memory consolidation[3](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR3 "Rash, B. & Born, J. About sleep’s role in memory. Physiol. Rev. 93, 381–766 (2013).") and in the clearance of beta-amyloid and other noxious metabolites[4](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR4 "Xie, L. et al. Sleep drives metabolite clearance from the adult brain. Science 342, 373–377 (2013).").

From an evolutionary perspective, sleep shows substantial variation among species, as it is determined largely by environmental conditions and feeding requirements[5](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR5 "Siegel, J. Sleep function: An evolutionary perspective. Lancet Neurol. 21, 937–946 (2022)."). In human beings, many additional elements may influence sleep, including social, environmental, and individual factors[6](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR6 "Grandner, M. Sleep, health, and society. Sleep Med. Clin. 15, 139–340 (2020)."). At the societal level, public policies, exposure to technology, and the 24/7 society characteristic of a globalized labour market, condition sleep habits. At the environmental level, factors like living conditions, work schedules, neighbourhood safety and prevailing cultural norms also impinge on sleep. Finally, the genetic makeup, beliefs, attitudes, and behaviours of each individual are key determinants of their sleep patterns[6](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR6 "Grandner, M. Sleep, health, and society. Sleep Med. Clin. 15, 139–340 (2020)."). All these features make sleep a complex and labile experience for humans.

Data from the 2021 Philips Global Sleep Survey show that sleep disturbances are an underdiagnosed and poorly controlled problem worldwide. Only 55% of adults were completely or somewhat satisfied with their sleep[7](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR7 "Koninklijke Philips NV. Seeking Solutions: How COVID-19 Changed Sleep Around the World. Philips Global Survey. 
                  https://www.philips.com/worldsleepday
                  
                . Accessed 04 Mar 2024 (2024)."). The majority of adults sleep on average 1.2 h less than recommended (6.8 h vs. 7–9 h), and eight out of ten want to improve their quality of sleep, but less than half of them (40%) have consulted a health professional for this. Data from an urban population in Colombia showed that almost 60% of adults had a sleep concern, of whom 45% might require medical management[8](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR8 "Ruiz, A. J. et al. Prevalence of sleep complaints in Colombia at different altitudes. Sleep Sci. 9, 100–1005 (2016).").

Given the multifactorial nature of sleep, and the fact that sleep disorders can be successfully managed when properly diagnosed[9](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR9 "Pavlova, M. & Latreille, V. Sleep disorders. Am. J. Med. 132, 292–299 (2019)."), multiple interventions have been tested to improve sleep quality. One such group of interventions is nutraceutical products, supplements derived from plants or plant extracts containing biological components that potentially improve different aspects of sleep quality[10](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR10 "Guadagna, S., Barattini, D. F., Rosu, S. & Ferini-Strambi, L. Plant extracts for sleep disturbances: A systematic review. Evid. Based Complement. Alternat. Med. 2020, 3792390 (2020)."). The public interest and exposure to advertising of nutraceutical products is growing rapidly[11](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR11 "Puri, V. et al. A comprehensive review on nutraceuticals: Therapy support and formulation challenges. Nutrients 14, 1–28 (2022)."), but there is a paucity of data from quality randomised trials assessing the efficacy and safety of nutraceutical products and their combinations among people with sleep problems[12](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR12 "Chan, V. & Lo, K. Efficacy of dietary supplements on improving sleep quality: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Postgrad. Med. J. 98, 285–293 (2022)."),[13](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR13 "Yurcheshen, M., Seehuus, M. & Pigeon, W. Updates on nutraceutical sleep therapeutics and investigational research. Evid. Based Complement. Alternat. Med. 2015, 105256 (2015)."). This scarcity of high-quality data on the combined efficacy of sleep supplements, and their large and increasing popularity, motivated us to undertake of this study.

l-theanine is an organic compound from tea, whose effects on sleep have been analyzed extensively. Different studies have found positive effects of l-theanine on relaxation, sleep quality, cognitive performance, and mood[14](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR14 "Nathan, P. J., Lu, K., Gray, M. & Oliver, C. The neuropharmacology of l-theanine (N-ethyl-L-glutamine): A possible neuroprotective and cognitive enhancing agent. J. Herb. Pharmacother. 6, 21–30 (2006)."). Lemon balm (*Melissa officinalis*) extract is postulated to increase bioavailability of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA, by reducing the activity of its degrading enzyme[15](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR15 "Flores-Ramos, M., Salinas, M., Carvajal-Lohr, A. & Rodríguez-Bores, L. El papel del ácido gamma-aminobutírico en la depresión de la mujer [The role of gamma-aminobutyric acid in female depression]. Gac. Med. Mex. 153, 486–495 (2017)."), potentially improving sleep quality among patients with insomnia and anxiety[16](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR16 "Cases, J., Ibarra, A., Feuillère, N., Roller, M. & Sukkar, S. G. Pilot trial of Melissa officinalis L. leaf extract in the treatment of volunteers suffering from mild-to-moderate anxiety disorders and sleep disturbances. Med. J. Nutr. Metab. 4, 211–218 (2011)."). Meanwhile, valerian (*Valeriana officinalis*), has been tested as a sleep aid in over 40 interventional studies, included in a recent meta-analysis[17](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR17 "Shinjyo, N., Waddell, G. & Green, J. Valerian root in treating sleep problems and associated disorders—A systematic review and meta-analysis. J. Evid. Based Integr. Med. 25, 2515690X20967323 (2020).") that found significant positive effects on sleep. Lastly, positive effects of saffron (*Crocus sativus*) on sleep have also been reported, with a meta-analysis of eight clinical trials in adults reporting improved sleep quality and minimal adverse effects[18](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR18 "Lian, J. et al. Effects of saffron supplementation on improving sleep quality: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Sleep Med. 92, 24–33 (2022).").

On this basis, we aimed to assess the impact of a nutraceutical formulation that combines extracts from plants for which positive impacts on sleep have been reported (green tea, lemon balm, valerian and saffron)[14](#ref-CR14 "Nathan, P. J., Lu, K., Gray, M. & Oliver, C. The neuropharmacology of l-theanine (N-ethyl-L-glutamine): A possible neuroprotective and cognitive enhancing agent. J. Herb. Pharmacother. 6, 21–30 (2006)."),[15](#ref-CR15 "Flores-Ramos, M., Salinas, M., Carvajal-Lohr, A. & Rodríguez-Bores, L. El papel del ácido gamma-aminobutírico en la depresión de la mujer [The role of gamma-aminobutyric acid in female depression]. Gac. Med. Mex. 153, 486–495 (2017)."),[16](#ref-CR16 "Cases, J., Ibarra, A., Feuillère, N., Roller, M. & Sukkar, S. G. Pilot trial of Melissa officinalis L. leaf extract in the treatment of volunteers suffering from mild-to-moderate anxiety disorders and sleep disturbances. Med. J. Nutr. Metab. 4, 211–218 (2011)."),[17](#ref-CR17 "Shinjyo, N., Waddell, G. & Green, J. Valerian root in treating sleep problems and associated disorders—A systematic review and meta-analysis. J. Evid. Based Integr. Med. 25, 2515690X20967323 (2020)."),[18](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR18 "Lian, J. et al. Effects of saffron supplementation on improving sleep quality: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Sleep Med. 92, 24–33 (2022)."), among adults with impaired sleep. The novelty of the study resides in that it formally tested the efficacy and safety of a combination of herbal supplements for sleep improvement, which are extensively used worldwide.

## Methods

### Study design

This was a randomised, double-blind, placebo controlled clinical trial conducted between December 2022 and June 2023 in Bogota, Colombia. The purpose of the study was to assess the efficacy and safety of a nutraceutical formulation aimed at improving sleep quality, among people with impaired sleep (see inclusion criteria). The study protocol was approved by the IRB Riesgo de Fractura S.A.*,* according to minute CEI-51 of December 15, 2022. The study was registered at <https://www.clinicaltrials.gov> under number NCT05609890 on 08/11/2022. All participants underwent an informed consent procedure and provided written informed consent before participation. All study procedures were executed in compliance with regulations for health research dictated by resolution 8430-1993 of the Colombian Ministry of Health and with the principles stated by the Helsinki Declaration of 1964 and its later amendments.

### Participants

Participants were men and women aged 18 or older with impaired sleep (defined as a Pittsburgh sleep quality score [PSQI] ≥ 5), not receiving any specific treatment for sleep improvement at the time of enrolment and not planning to take any for the next 2 months. The exclusion criteria were: history of a specific sleep disorder according to the diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders—fifth edition (DSM-5), history of an anxiety disorder, depression or other psychiatric or neurological condition, uncontrolled hypothyroidism [assessed by a measurement of basal thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)], history of cortisol deficit or excess, alcohol intake greater than two standard drinks (30 g of alcohol) per day, caffeine intake greater than 400 mg per day (3 cups of coffee or 1 energy drink per day), frequent sleep deprivation (shift work or need to skip sleep) over the last 2 months, smoking or use of tobacco products, use of recreational drugs, and childbearing desire among women. We did not set an upper PSQI cutoff as an exclusion criterion.

### Randomisation and masking

Eligible individuals who manifested their wish to take part in the study were contacted for screening by phone, filled a PSQI questionnaire to verify eligibility and provided their informed consent. Then, they underwent a 1 week run-in phase, in which all received the active nutraceutical formulation. Those with adherence ≥ 85% went on to a washout week, during which they wore a Fitbit Charge 5 actigraphy device, linked to a cloud-based server for collection of sleep variables, and kept a detailed sleep diary. Participants who completed the run-in and washout phases attended an in-person visit in which baseline vital signs, anthropometric variables and blood and saliva samples were collected. Weight was measured using a Tanita innerscan body composition monitor, and height was measured with a Seca portable stadiometer. Body-mass index (BMI) was calculated as the ratio of weight in kilograms to the square of the height in meters. Blood pressure was measured in the right arm after fifteen minutes of seating using a Welch Allyn DuraShock DS45 sphygmomanometer. Heart rate was recorded using a fully charged pulse oximeter. All measurements were conducted by trained staff members. Blood samples were used to analyse plasma glucose levels (biosystems cat 11803), HbA1c (NycoCard cat 1116083), lipid profile (biosystems total cholesterol cat11805, biosystems triglycerides cat 11828, biosystems HDL cholesterol cat 11523), liver enzymes (biosystems alanine aminotransferase cat 11832, biosystems aspartate aminotransferase cat 11830), creatinine (biosystems cat 11802), urea (biosystems cat 11536), bilirubin (biosystems cat 11515) and thyroid-stimulating hormone (by a fluorescent immunoassay in an Abbott ARCHITECT reader). Saliva samples were collected to measure cortisol (by an electrochemiluminescent assay in an Abbott ARCHITECT reader).

In the same visit, participants fulfilled a short form—36 questions (SF-36) quality of life questionnaire and were randomised using a minimization algorithm to the active intervention or placebo group with minimization by age (< 40 or ≥ 40), sex, and basal PSQI (< 8 or ≥ 8). Minimization is a randomization technique in which each new enrolled participant is assigned to one intervention group in a way that minimizes the overall differences between groups in a set of variables (in our case, age, sex, and basal PQI)[19](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR19 "Altman, D. G. & Bland, J. M. Treatment allocation by minimisation. BMJ 330, 843 (2005)."). Participants, data collectors and researchers who performed statistical analysis were unaware of the group allocation codes. The nutraceutical formulation and placebo were both powdered and contained in sealed opaque envelopes. Even though the appearance and taste of the two interventions were not identical, participants and researchers who provided the envelopes and assessed the results were unaware of which colour or taste corresponded to which intervention.

### Procedures

The nutraceutical formulation was a powder mixture of green tea (*Camellia sinensis*) extract, equivalent to 200 mg of l-theanine, lemon balm (*Melissa officinalis*) leaf extract (400 mg), valerian (*Valeriana officinalis*) extract (500 mg), saffron extract (Lepticrosalides®) (14 mg), and excipients. The placebo group received a powder mixture of the excipients that was contained lemongrass, peppermint, and mint flavourings, but not their active components.

Participants were instructed to pour the full content of each envelope into 200 ml of warm water and drink it 1 h before going to bed. They were also advised not to add anything else to this beverage, and to store all empty envelopes in order to return them to the study staff for assessment of adherence. In the randomization visit, each participant received enough envelopes of their allocated intervention for the study duration (6 weeks). Participants received a diary book to keep track of their taken doses of the intervention and were asked to record any new symptom in this book, and to communicate it immediately to the study staff. All participants received a phone call at week 3 of the intervention phase, in which they were inquired about adverse events and adherence. At the end of week 5 for each participant, we delivered the actigraphy device at their home in order to collect the final values of actigraphy measures during week 6. At the end of week 6, participants attended a final in-person visit in which they returned the unused intervention doses (which were used to calculate adherence), returned the actigraphy device, fulfilled again the PSQI and SF-36 questionnaires, and provided final blood and saliva samples. Figure [1](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#Fig1) summarizes the study timeline.

### Outcomes

Our primary outcome was the between-group difference in the change in sleep efficiency (final-basal) over 6 weeks. Sleep efficiency is defined as the ratio of total time asleep to total time in bed (expressed as a percentage). Total time in bed was calculated by subtracting the go-to-sleep time from the time when the participant was no longer trying to sleep (rise time), both reported in the sleep diary. Patients were instructed to be as accurate as possible in registering the exact time they attempted to fall asleep, and the exact time they woke up and no longer intended to sleep[20](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR20 "Ancoli-Israel, S. et al. The SBSM guide to actigraphy monitoring: Clinical and research applications. Behav. Sleep Med. 13(Suppl 1), S4–S38 (2015)."). Total time asleep was extracted from actigraphy data registered by the Fitbit Charge 5. We selected the Fitbit Charge 5, as this actigraphy device has shown comparable recordings of sleep–wake states and sleep stage composition relative to the gold standard (polysomnography)[21](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR21 "de Zambotti, M., Goldstone, A., Claudatos, S., Colrain, I. M. & Baker, F. C. A validation study of Fitbit Charge 2™ compared with polysomnography in adults. Chronobiol. Int. 35, 465–476 (2018)."),[22](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR22 "Menghini, L., Yuksel, D., Goldstone, A., Baker, F. C. & de Zambotti, M. Performance of Fitbit Charge 3 against polysomnography in measuring sleep in adolescent boys and girls. Chronobiol. Int. 38, 1010–1022 (2021).").

One secondary outcome was the group difference in change in PSQI, collected from participants at the screening contact and at the final visit. The PSQI[23](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR23 "Buysse, D. J., Reynolds, C. F. 3rd., Monk, T. H., Berman, S. R. & Kupfer, D. J. The Pittsburgh sleep quality index: A new instrument for psychiatric practice and research. Psychiatr. Res. 28, 193–213 (1989)."),[24](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR24 "Escobar-Córdoba, F. & Eslava-Schmalbach, J. Validación colombiana del índice de calidad de sueño de Pittsburgh [Colombian validation of the Pittsburgh sleep quality index]. Rev. Neurol. 40, 150–155 (2005).") is an 18-item, ten-section instrument that assesses seven domains related to sleep quality, namely subjective sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep duration, habitual sleep efficiency, sleep disturbances, use of sleep medications, and daytime dysfunction; all of them over the last month. PSQI scores range from 0 to 21, with higher scores indicating worse sleep quality. Another secondary outcome was the group difference in change in wake after sleep onset (WASO), defined as the total number of minutes that the participant was awake after having initially fallen asleep[25](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR25 "Shrivastava, D., Jung, S., Saadat, M., Sirohi, R. & Crewson, K. How to interpret the results of a sleep study. J. Community Hosp. Intern. Med. Perspect. 4, 24983 (2014)."). WASO was obtained directly from actigraphy data. We also analysed as secondary outcomes the group difference in salivary cortisol (measured at the exact same time of the day for each participant), and the change in the 36-item short form survey score (SF-36). SF-36[26](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR26 "Ware, J. E. Jr. & Sherbourne, C. D. The MOS 36-item short-form health survey (SF-36): I. conceptual framework and item selection. Med. Care 30, 473–483 (1992)."),[27](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR27 "Luz, L. A., Helena, G. G., Iván, H. & Carlos, G. R. Confiabilidad del cuestionario de calidad de vida en salud SF-36 en Medellín. Colomb. Rev. Fac. Nac. Salud Pública 24, 37–50 (2006).") is a questionnaire that assesses health-related quality of life reflected in eight domains: physical functioning, physical role, bodily pain, general health, vitality, social functioning, emotional role, and mental health[28](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR28 "Hooker, S. A. SF-36. In Encyclopedia of Behavioral Medicine (eds Gellman, M. D. & Turner, J. R.) 1784–1786 (Springer, New York, 2013)."). Higher SF-36 scores represent better health and functioning. Safety was monitored by inquiring in detail about adverse events in all study visits, and by assessing changes in liver and kidney function tests. All measurements were undertaken in a centralized laboratory.

### Statistical analyses

Sample size was calculated using the expression for two-arm trials with a continuous outcome[29](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR29 "Wittes, J. Sample size calculations for randomized controlled trials. Epidemiol. Rev. 24, 39–53 (2002)."). For an assumed variability in sleep efficiency of 2.3%[30](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR30 "Ong, J. L. et al. COVID-19-related mobility reduction: Heterogenous effects on sleep and physical activity rhythms. Sleep 44, zsaa179 (2021)."), a sample size of 60 participants would provide us with 95% power to detect a true difference of 2.18% in our primary outcome, at a two-sided type I error rate (alpha) of 0.05. Expecting a 10% dropout rate, we aimed to recruit a total of 66 participants.

The intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis population consisted of all participants who were randomised and received at least one dose of the assigned study intervention. The normality of continuous variables was tested using the Shapiro–Wilk and Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests. Within-group comparisons of study outcomes were made using a Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Between-group comparisons in changes in study outcomes were made using an ANCOVA linear model, with intervention group as fixed factor, and basal value of each outcome as covariate. Statistical analyses were performed in IBM SPSS statistics 23. For all analyses we used a significance level of 5% (0.05).

### Role of the funding source

The funding source of this study had no role in study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation or writing of the report. All authors had full access to the data in the study and had final responsibility for the decision to submit for publication.

Both groups experienced a noticeable improvement in the PSQI, a decrease of 3.86 points (39.1%) in the placebo group, and of 3.11 points (32.3%) in the active group (between-groups p-value 0.41) (Fig. [3](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#Fig3)B). In actigraphy variables, the mean WASO also decreased in both groups, by 2.4% in the placebo arm, and by 4.6% in the active treatment arm (Fig. [3](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#Fig3)C). Nonetheless, the between-group difference was not significant (p = 0.68) (Fig. [3](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#Fig3)E). There were no serious adverse events during the trial. The frequency of reported adverse events is displayed in Table [3](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#Tab3). The most frequently reported adverse events were gastrointestinal in both groups: 22.9% of the participants in the active and 10.3% in the placebo group referred heartburn, while bloating was reported by 14.3% and 3.4%, respectively. Daytime sleepiness was more frequent in the active (17.1%) than in the placebo group (10.3%). One participant from the placebo group reported a poorer quality of sleep. All adverse events improved after the first week of intervention and had resolved by the end of the follow-up period. At the end of week 6, the mean adherence rate was 80.9% in the active group and 79.4% in the placebo group.

## Discussion

Nutraceutical products have been proposed as a treatment alternative for sleep disturbances. This study assessed the effect of a nutraceutical combination on objective and subjective sleep parameters during 6 weeks of intervention among adults with impaired sleep. Our primary outcome, sleep efficiency, remained unchanged in the intervention group and improved in the placebo group, but the difference between groups was not statistically significant. For patient-reported outcomes like sleep quality (measured by PSQI) and health-related quality of life (measured by SF-36), there were improvements regardless of intervention group. On the other hand, other objective variables measured by actigraphy showed a slightly different result according to the intervention. In the active group the reduction in WASO was larger than in the placebo group, while total sleep time improved markedly in the placebo group. Salivary cortisol levels remained relatively stable in both groups.

In concordance with our results, a prior clinical trial of valerian extract among older women with insomnia found no significant effect on sleep efficiency, but a trend towards a benefit in WASO with the supplementary intervention[31](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR31 "Taibi, D. M. et al. A randomized clinical trial of valerian fails to improve self-reported, polysomnographic, and actigraphic sleep in older women with insomnia. Sleep Med. 10, 319–328 (2009)."). Likewise, a randomised study of saffron against placebo in adults with mild to moderate sleep disorders and anxiety, found no between-groups difference in the change in sleep efficiency[32](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR32 "Pachikian, B. D., Copine, S., Suchareau, M. & Deldicque, L. Effects of saffron extract on sleep quality: A randomized double-blind controlled clinical trial. Nutrients 13, 1473 (2021)."). Concerning other components of the study intervention, there was a host of prior evidence suggesting a positive impact of lemon balm and green tea on sleep quality, but these studies had derived sleep efficiency from PSQI component 4, rather than directly measuring it[33](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR33 "Taavoni, S., Nazem Ekbatani, N. & Haghani, H. Valerian/lemon balm use for sleep disorders during menopause. Complement. Ther. Clin. Pract. 19, 193–196 (2013)."),[34](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR34 "Hidese, S. et al. Effects of l-theanine administration on stress-related symptoms and cognitive functions in healthy adults: A randomized controlled trial. Nutrients 11, 2362 (2019)."). Interestingly, the small 3% increase in sleep efficiency in the placebo group reached within-group significance. This finding highlights the potential relevance of the placebo effect even on objective sleep measurements[35](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR35 "Winkler, A. & Rief, W. Effect of placebo conditions on polysomnographic parameters in primary insomnia: A meta-analysis. Sleep 38, 925–931 (2015)."),[36](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR36 "Yeung, V., Sharpe, L., Geers, A. & Colagiuri, B. Choice, expectations, and the placebo effect for sleep difficulty. Ann. Behav. Med. 54, 94–107 (2020).").

One of the outcomes most related to sleep quality is WASO, the amount of time spent in the wake state after initially having fallen asleep. In our study, WASO decreased in both groups, but the change was not significant. Moreover, total sleep time increased in the placebo group by 13 min, but this change was also not statistically significant. A clinical trial in healthy young woman assessed the acute effect of green tea extract on sleep and polysomnographic variables, registering no difference in WASO and total sleep time between green tea extract and placebo[37](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR37 "Baba, Y., Takihara, T. & Okamura, N. Theanine maintains sleep quality in healthy young women by suppressing the increase in caffeine-induced wakefulness after sleep onset. Food. Funct. 14, 7109–7116 (2023).").

PSQI summarizes in a single score the perceived quality of sleep and represents a true measure of the burden imposed by sleep disturbances. Participants in the active and placebo group started with a comparable PSQI, after 6 weeks of intervention both groups had a notable 3 point-improvement in their mean total score. A study of green tea extract among healthy Japanese adults found a substantial improvement in PSQI with the intervention, but like in our study, it was not significantly different from placebo[34](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR34 "Hidese, S. et al. Effects of l-theanine administration on stress-related symptoms and cognitive functions in healthy adults: A randomized controlled trial. Nutrients 11, 2362 (2019)."). Moreover, when the presumed active component of tea extract (L-theanine) was combined with magnesium, B-vitamins and Rhodiola in a single nutraceutical supplement, its effect on the PSQI among adults who scored high on a stress questionnaire was comparable to placebo[38](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR38 "Noah, L. et al. Effect of a combination of magnesium, B vitamins, Rhodiola, and green tea (L-theanine) on chronically stressed healthy individuals—A randomized, placebo-controlled study. Nutrients 14, 1863 (2022)."). Despite initially encouraging results among post-menopausal women[33](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR33 "Taavoni, S., Nazem Ekbatani, N. & Haghani, H. Valerian/lemon balm use for sleep disorders during menopause. Complement. Ther. Clin. Pract. 19, 193–196 (2013)."), the evidence on the efficacy of lemon balm for sleep quality has yielded heterogeneous results. Haybar H et al., assessed the effect of lemon balm or placebo on the PSQI among patients with chronic stable angina, both groups had equally significant reductions in the PSQI[39](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR39 "Haybar, H. et al. The effects of Melissa officinalis supplementation on depression, anxiety, stress, and sleep disorder in patients with chronic stable angina. Clin. Nutr. ESPEN 26, 47–52 (2018)."). Contrastingly, a study in patients with type 2 diabetes plus depression or anxiety symptoms found no significant modification in the PSQI after 4 weeks of lemon balm supplementation[40](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR40 "Safari, M. et al. The effects of Melissa officinalis on depression and anxiety in type 2 diabetes patients with depression: A randomized double-blinded placebo-controlled clinical trial. BMC Complement. Med. Ther. 23, 140 (2023)."). In patients with insomnia, a 4 week study of a combination of lemon balm with the plant *Nepeta menthoides* evidenced a PSQI improvement significantly different from placebo[41](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR41 "Ranjbar, M. et al. Efficacy of a combination of Melissa officinalis L. and Nepeta menthoides Boiss. & Buhse on insomnia: A triple-Blind, randomized placebo-controlled clinical trial. J. Altern. Complement. Med. 24, 1197–1203 (2018)."). A host of prior evidence suggested an effect of valerian on sleep quality. A meta-analysis of six studies comparing valerian mono-preparations to placebo indicated statistically significant placebo-subtracted reductions in the PSQI[42](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR42 "Zhang, X., Lu, Y., Lv, F. & Hu, Y. Valerian for insomnia on subjective and objective sleep parameters: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Curr. Sleep Med. Rep. 9, 211–224 (2023)."), albeit with a large between-trial heterogeneity (I2 = 93%). Unfortunately, such results were not replicated in our study.

We observed a very large improvement in the PSQI, regardless of intervention group. The magnitude of the placebo effect can be unusually high for sleep-related outcomes: a meta-analysis of 82 treatment groups from 32 clinical trials reported a mean placebo effect of 61% on subjective sleep parameters[35](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR35 "Winkler, A. & Rief, W. Effect of placebo conditions on polysomnographic parameters in primary insomnia: A meta-analysis. Sleep 38, 925–931 (2015)."). Hence, the inclusion of a placebo control is of utmost importance in studies that assess the efficacy of any intervention for sleep, nutraceuticals included. In parallel to the improvements in PSQI, participants from both groups increased their SF-36 scores. This is an anticipated result, as quality of sleep greatly influences health-related quality of life [43](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR43 "Lee, S., Kim, J. H. & Chung, J. H. The association between sleep quality and quality of life: A population-based study. Sleep Med. 84, 121–126 (2021)."),[44](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR44 "Matsui, K. et al. Association of subjective quality and quantity of sleep with quality of life among a general population. Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 18, 12835 (2021).").

Multiple factors can explain the results of our study, in which the intervention and placebo group experienced similar improvements in key sleep outcomes. Many effective interventions for sleep disturbances are behavioural in nature, including relaxation training, stimulus control therapy, sleep restriction therapy, sleep hygiene, paradoxical intention therapy, cognitive restructuring, and many others[45](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR45 "Sharma, M. P. & Andrade, C. Behavioral interventions for insomnia: Theory and practice. Indian J. Psychiatr. 54, 359–366 (2012)."). In our study, participants had to follow a pre-bed routine that included tasks like warming and drinking a beverage, which may have induced a particular disposition, more favourable to sleep. This implicit behavioural and cognitive influence may partially explain the positive effect in both groups, without evidence of an added benefit from the composition of the tested intervention. Some of the favourable changes may also reflect a plausible Hawthorne effect from feeling observed while wearing the actigraphy device[46](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR46 "McCarney, R. et al. The Hawthorne effect: A randomised, controlled trial. BMC Med. Res. Methodol. 7, 30 (2007).").

The proportion of adverse events was low and very similar between groups, and we found no evidence of renal or hepatic impairment.

Strengths of our study include its randomised design, careful collection and control of study variables, provision of the study intervention and close monitoring of adherence. Also, the combination of objective and subjective outcome measures of sleep quality provided a more holistic assessment of sleep. We assessed not only sleep itself, but variables closely related to it and with clinical or biological relevance, such as health-related quality of life or salivary cortisol, information that is not always collected in studies of non-pharmacological interventions for sleep. Concerning the intervention, the simultaneous assessment of various nutraceutical products with prior indications of positive effects on sleep, increased the probability of evidencing a beneficial effect, if it was present. The central limitations of our study are its duration of only 6 weeks, although most evidence shows that sleep-related variables can be substantially modified in such timespan[47](/articles/s41598-024-58661-z#ref-CR47 "Zheng, X. et al. Quantitative analysis of the placebo response in pharmacotherapy of insomnia and its application in clinical trials. Sleep 43, zsz286 (2020)."), and its relatively modest sample size. Also, we performed thyroid function tests only before inclusion in the trial. Another phenomenon that we cannot rule out is the existence of antagonism among the components of the nutraceutical intervention, so that one component may partially antagonize the effects of another, we had no mechanism for testing this hypothesis. Moreover, it is also possible that participants communicated among them leading to some degree of unmasking, but there was no way for the participants to tell the particular organoleptic characteristics of each intervention. Lastly, we could not rule out that some participants might have sleep disorders without a formal diagnosis or treatment. However, any potential influence from such individuals would exist in both groups due to randomization including minimization by a sleep-quality parameter (PSQI). Importantly, our results pertain to the general population with impaired sleep, not necessarily to individuals with a formal diagnosis of insomnia.

Future research efforts should focus on the use of nutraceuticals as part of a broader behavioural strategy aimed at patients with sleep disturbances. In this context, the inclusion of an appropriate comparator will be of extreme relevance. Larger studies of the efficacy and safety of nutraceuticals (including excessive daytime sleepiness) are needed, in order to inform evidence-based recommendations about products from this growing market.

In conclusion, in this clinical trial among adults with impaired sleep, a nutraceutical combination did not improve sleep compared to a placebo infusion. This result may be explained by the influence of behavioural and cognitive factors.

This is a peer-reviewed, open-access scientific article published in *Scientific Reports* (volume 14, article 8062, 2024) reporting on a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial conducted in Bogota, Colombia (December 2022–June 2023) to assess the effect of a nutraceutical combination on sleep quality among adults with impaired sleep.

**Study Design:** 64 adults with impaired sleep (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index ≥5) were randomised via minimisation algorithm to receive either an active nutraceutical formulation (containing l-theanine 200mg from green tea, lemon balm extract 400mg, valerian extract 500mg, and saffron extract 14mg) or a placebo infusion, taken nightly for 6 weeks. Objective sleep quality was measured using a Fitbit Charge 5 actigraphy device, and subjective measures included PSQI and SF-36 questionnaires.

**Key Results:**
- **Primary outcome (sleep efficiency):** No significant between-group difference (p=0.49). Sleep efficiency remained unchanged in the active group and increased by 3% in the placebo group.
- **Total sleep time:** Improved more with placebo (13.0 min vs. 1.33 min, p=0.66).
- **Wake After Sleep Onset (WASO):** Decreased more in the active group (4.6% vs. 2.4%), but not significant (p=0.33).
- **PSQI:** Decreased 3.11 points (32.3%) in active group and 3.86 points (39.5%) in placebo group (p=0.41).
- **SF-36 quality of life:** Increased more with placebo (+18.3 active vs. +32.1 placebo, p=0.68).
- **Salivary cortisol:** Remained unchanged in both groups.
- **Safety:** No serious adverse events; most common side effects were gastrointestinal (heartburn, bloating) and daytime sleepiness, more frequent in the active group.

**Conclusion:** The nutraceutical combination did not improve objective or subjective sleep parameters more than placebo. The authors attribute results to possible behavioural/cognitive influences (pre-bed ritual, Hawthorne effect) and the well-known high placebo effect in sleep studies. The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05609890).

Key Takeaways

L-theanine is a natural ingredient found in tea. Tea is the second-most widely consumed beverage in the world after water. L-theanine is also sold as a dietary supplement in liquid, pill, and ointment forms. Although research into the health benefits of L-theanine is ongoing, studies suggest that L-theanine may reduce anxiety and promote the level of relaxation in the brain needed for high quality, restful sleep.

[![Commercial CTA](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/In-conent-ad-Large-Desktop.png)![Commercial CTA](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/In-conent-ad-Large-Mobile.png)](https://sleepdoctor.com/products/nightly-sleep-stack?utm_campaign=sf&utm_cta_location=display_ad)

## What Is L-Theanine?

L-theanine is an amino acid that occurs naturally in tea leaves and dissolves readily in water. It also supplies green and black teas with their savory, umami flavor and balances the bitter taste of caffeine in teas.

Amino acids form proteins in the body that serve a variety of vital functions. Unlike other amino acids though, L-theanine does not build proteins. Instead, L-theanine affects neurotransmitters, which are the body’s chemical messengers.

Scientific evidence about L-theanine is still emerging, but researchers believe its role in the body may be to have a soothing effect on the central nervous system, reducing stress [Trusted Source](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/about-us/editorial-policy) National Library of Medicine, Biotech InformationThe National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information.[View Source](#references-118208) and [promoting relaxation](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/sleep-hygiene/relaxation-exercises-to-help-fall-asleep).

### Where L-Theanine Is Found

L-theanine is found in tea brewed from the leaves of the Camellia sinensis plant, more commonly known as green, black, white, or oolong teas. Although L-theanine has also been identified in some mushrooms, tea is the primary naturally occurring source of L-theanine.

One serving of tea contains about 25 to 60 milligrams of L-theanine. The level of L-theanine in an individual cup depends in part on the amount of tea leaves used and the length of time the tea is steeped. The level of L-theanine is highly variable [Trusted Source](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/about-us/editorial-policy) National Library of Medicine, Biotech InformationThe National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information.[View Source](#references-118211) across different tea brands and preparations, but on average green teas contain slightly more L-theanine than black teas.

L-theanine is also available in the U.S. as a dietary supplement. Green tea extracts containing L-theanine and other ingredients are available in liquid, pill, and ointment form.

## How Does L-Theanine Affect Sleep?

Research suggests that L-theanine may affect sleep by influencing several neurotransmitters and promoting relaxing brain activity. L-theanine crosses the blood-brain barrier, allowing it to rapidly affect neurotransmitters within the central nervous system. It has a similar structure to glutamate, a neurotransmitter that may play a role in promoting wakefulness.

Animal studies have found that L-theanine blocks glutamate from binding to cells in the brain. L-theanine also affects other neurotransmitters, increasing gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), dopamine, and serotonin levels while decreasing levels of norepinephrine. These combined chemical changes may slow brain activity [Trusted Source](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/about-us/editorial-policy) Medline PlusMedlinePlus is an online health information resource for patients and their families and friends.[View Source](#references-79931) , promote positive feelings [Trusted Source](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/about-us/editorial-policy) National Center for Biotechnology InformationThe National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information.[View Source](#references-118214) , and reduce both alertness [Trusted Source](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/about-us/editorial-policy) National Center for Biotechnology InformationThe National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information.[View Source](#references-118215) and [anxiety](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/mental-health/anxiety-and-sleep).

L-theanine may also facilitate sleep through its effects on brain waves. Several studies of the effects of L-theanine on brain activity have found that L-theanine at doses ranging from 50 to 200 milligrams increases alpha brain waves compared to a placebo. [Alpha brain waves](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/how-sleep-works/alpha-waves-and-sleep) are the most prevalent brain waves in people who are relaxed or drowsy.

### The Relationship Between L-Theanine and GABA

L-theanine and [GABA](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/sleep-aids/gaba-for-sleep) have all been reported to play roles in sleep. While GABA are both made in the human body, L-theanine only comes from outside sources such as [tea](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/sleep-aids/best-tea-for-sleep) or dietary supplements.

L-theanine increases the concentration of GABA in the brain. A 2017 study found that mice and rats given a mixture of L-theanine and GABA fell asleep faster and slept longer [Trusted Source](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/about-us/editorial-policy) National Library of Medicine, Biotech InformationThe National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information.[View Source](#references-81635) compared with those that were given either L-theanine or GABA alone. However, no published human studies are currently available on the safety or effectiveness of taking L-theanine and GABA supplements together. People considering taking both supplements should speak with their doctors before starting them.

## Side Effects of L-Theanine

The side effects of L-theanine are not well understood, and there is limited data available on L-theanine taken on its own. However, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) classifies L-theanine as a food ingredient that is generally recognized as safe [Trusted Source](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/about-us/editorial-policy) U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)The FDA is responsible for protecting the public health by ensuring the safety, efficacy, and security of human and veterinary drugs, biological products, and medical devices; and by ensuring the safety of our nation's food supply, cosmetics, and products that emit radiation.[View Source](#references-183290) up to 250 milligrams per serving.

Additionally, rare cases of liver problems [Trusted Source](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/about-us/editorial-policy) UpToDateMore than 2 million healthcare providers around the world choose UpToDate to help make appropriate care decisions and drive better health outcomes. UpToDate delivers evidence-based clinical decision support that is clear, actionable, and rich with real-world insights.[View Source](#references-118223) have been reported in people taking green tea extract.

It is important to keep in mind that both green and black teas contain [caffeine](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/nutrition/caffeine-and-sleep). Caffeine is a powerful stimulant that can cause anxiety, irritability, and [insomnia](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/insomnia). Therefore, caffeinated teas may counteract the sleep-promoting and stress-reducing effects of L-theanine. People drinking green tea for sleep or relaxation may consider decaffeinated or low-caffeine options.

Health experts have not yet established the safety of L-theanine for people who are pregnant or breastfeeding. However, people who consume more than 300 milligrams of caffeine per day during pregnancy have a higher risk of poor pregnancy outcomes [Trusted Source](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/about-us/editorial-policy) UpToDateMore than 2 million healthcare providers around the world choose UpToDate to help make appropriate care decisions and drive better health outcomes. UpToDate delivers evidence-based clinical decision support that is clear, actionable, and rich with real-world insights.[View Source](#references-183292) . People who are pregnant or breastfeeding should talk to their doctors before taking L-theanine or green tea extract, or increasing their tea consumption.

### Interactions Between L-Theanine and Other Medications

Interactions between L-theanine and other medications, supplements, or stimulants are not yet known. However, caffeinated teas should not be taken with other stimulant medications, as the combined effects may cause serious side effects including heart problems.

Tea may also cause interactions with:

* Asthma medications
* Antidepressants

## Recommended L-Theanine Dosage for Sleep

Experts do not yet know the best dosage of L-theanine as a [natural sleep aid](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/sleep-aids/natural-sleep-aids). However, published studies suggest that taking 200 milligrams of L-theanine before bed may promote restful sleep. People considering taking L-theanine supplements should discuss the dosage with a doctor.

Tea drinkers should follow dietary guidelines for tea and caffeine consumption. Caffeine content varies across different tea preparations, so tea drinkers should check nutrition labels. args.summary:
This article from the Sleep Foundation explains L-Theanine, a natural amino acid found in tea leaves (Camellia sinensis plant), and its potential benefits for sleep and relaxation.

**What is L-Theanine?** L-theanine is a non-protein-building amino acid found in green, black, white, and oolong teas, as well as some mushrooms. One serving of tea contains about 25-60 mg of L-theanine. It is also available as a dietary supplement in liquid, pill, and ointment forms.

**How It Affects Sleep:** L-theanine crosses the blood-brain barrier and influences neurotransmitters by blocking glutamate, increasing GABA, dopamine, and serotonin, and decreasing norepinephrine. Studies show that doses of 50-200 mg increase alpha brain waves associated with relaxation and drowsiness. A 2017 animal study found that a combination of L-theanine and GABA helped mice fall asleep faster and sleep longer, though no human studies on this combination are available.

**Safety and Side Effects:** The FDA classifies L-theanine as generally recognized as safe (GRAS) up to 250 mg per serving. Side effects are not well understood. Tea contains caffeine, which can counteract L-theanine's sleep-promoting effects. Rare cases of liver problems have been reported with green tea extract. Pregnant or breastfeeding individuals should consult a doctor. Potential interactions exist with anti-seizure medications, asthma medications, antidepressants, blood pressure medicine, and anti-clotting medications.

**Recommended Dosage:** Published studies suggest taking 200 mg of L-theanine before bed may promote restful sleep. The FDA states most adults can safely consume up to 400 mg of caffeine daily. Individuals should consult a healthcare professional before starting L-theanine supplements.
