## Introduction

In dealing with daily activities, organisms need to reach an appropriate level of arousal (activation) to perform efficiently, which varies according to the famous Yerkes–Dodson’s inverted-U shaped law[1](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR1 "Yerkes, R. M. & Dodson, J. D. The relation of strength of stimulus to rapidity of habit-formation. J. Comp. Neurol. Psychol. 18, 459–482 (1908)."). According to this law, the optimal level of arousal very much depends on task difficulty, so that performance on rather easy tasks profits from high levels of arousal whereas low levels of arousal are beneficial for rather difficult tasks. In other words, depending on its difficulty, each task requires an optimal level of arousal, with important decrements in performance when such level deviates, below or beyond, from the optimal one.

In Posner and Petersen’s[2](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR2 "Posner, M. I. & Petersen, S. E. The attention system of the human brain. Annu. Rev. Neurosci. 13, 25–42 (1990).") theory, such arousal state is linked to the alerting network of the attention system, which is involved both in achieving and maintaining an optimal level of activation, and in preparing the person to perceive and/or respond to a forthcoming target. The alerting network involves both cortical and subcortical areas, which share norepinephrine modulation rooted in the locus coeruleus[2](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR2 "Posner, M. I. & Petersen, S. E. The attention system of the human brain. Annu. Rev. Neurosci. 13, 25–42 (1990)."),[3](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR3 "Beane, M. & Marrocco, R. T. Norepinephrine and acetylcholine mediation of the components of reflexive attention: Implications for attention deficit disorders. Prog. Neurobiol. 74, 167–181 (2004)."). The alertness state can be reached either exogenously (phasic alertness) or endogenously (tonic alertness). The former refers to a rather transient and nonspecific activation state that increases response readiness and that is triggered automatically by the presence of external warning signals (e.g., a white noise). This phasic alerting component depends on ascending thalamic projections to the right parietal lobe, which are also involved in orienting visual attention[4](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR4 "Robertson, I. H. Cognitive rehabilitation: Attention and neglect. Trends Cogn. Sci. 3, 385–393 (1999)."). Tonic alertness develops slower and refers to the ability to maintain attention for rather long periods of time-on-task, sometimes at the scale of hours. This endogenous component is activated when the task is rather monotonous and tedious, usually because it does not require strong perceptual, cognitive, or motoric demands to be performed (examples of laboratory tasks with these characteristics are the psychomotor visual test, PVT; the continuous performance test, CPT; and the sustained attention to response task, SART). During this kind of tedious tasks, a vigilant attention network is recruited to maintain the attentional state endogenously in a top-down manner[5](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR5 "Robertson, I. H., Manly, T., Andrade, J., Baddeley, B. T. & Yiend, J. “Oops!”: Performance correlates of everyday attentional failures in traumatic brain injured and normal subjects. Neuropsychologia 35, 747–758 (1997)."). Vigilant attention involves a right lateralized cortical network including the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), two brain areas that are also involved in executive control[6](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR6 "MacDonald, A. W., Cohen, J. D., Stenger, V. A. & Carter, C. S. Dissociating the role of the dorsolateral prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortex in cognitive control. Science 288, 1835–1838 (2000)."), as well as the right inferior parietal lobe[7](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR7 "Sturm, W. & Willmes, K. On the functional neuroanatomy of intrinsic and phasic alertness. Neuroimage 14, S76–S84 (2001)."),[8](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR8 "Robertson, I. H. & O’Connell, R. Vigilant attention. In Attention and Time (eds Nobre, A. C. & Coull, J. T.) 79–88 (Oxford University Press, Oxford, 2010).").

Beside time-on-task, vigilant attention seems to be also affected by circadian rhythm, our endogenous biological clock that determines our physiological and behavioral processes, usually in synchrony with external time. Vigilance levels stabilize along daytime when the circadian rhythm system offsets the sleep-regulation homeostatic system, which accumulates pression to sleep as a function of time spent awake[9](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR9 "Schmidt, C., Collette, F., Cajochen, C. & Peigneux, P. A time to think: Circadian rhythms in human cognition. Cogn. Neuropsychol. 24, 755–789 (2007)."). However, some people undergo shifts in circadian phase. As a consequence, individuals may differ in neurobiological functioning, such as in their peak times of day (periods of high alertness[10](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR10 "Di Milia, L. & Bohle, P. Morningness or morning affect? A short composite scale of morningness. Chronobiol. Int. 26, 494–509 (2009)."),[11](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR11 "Lehnkering, H. & Siegmund, R. Influence of chronotype, season, and sex of subject on sleep behavior of young adults. Chronobiol. Int. 24, 875–888 (2007).") or vigilance[9](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR9 "Schmidt, C., Collette, F., Cajochen, C. & Peigneux, P. A time to think: Circadian rhythms in human cognition. Cogn. Neuropsychol. 24, 755–789 (2007)."),[12](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR12 "Valdez, P., Ramírez, C. & García, A. Circadian rhythms in cognitive performance: Implications for neuropsychological assessment. Chrono Physiol. Therapy 2, 81–92 (2012).")), in their sleep times, bedtime, wake up time and daytime sleepiness[13](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR13 "Taillard, J., Philip, P., Coste, O., Sagaspe, P. & Bioulac, B. The circadian and homeostatic modulation of sleep pressure during wakefulness differs between morning and evening chronotypes. J. Sleep Res. 12, 275–282 (2003)."), in their melatonin levels[14](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR14 "Duffy, J. F., Rimmer, D. W. & Czeisler, C. A. Association of intrinsic circadian period with morningness–eveningness, usual wake time, and circadian phase. Behav. Neurosci. 115, 895–899 (2001)."), cortisol levels[15](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR15 "Oginska, H. et al. Chronotype, sleep loss, and diurnal pattern pf salivary cortisol in a simulated daylong driving. Chronobiol. Int. 27, 959–974 (2010)."), and in their body temperature rhythm[16](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR16 "Sarabia, J. A., Rol, M. A., Mendiola, P. & Madrid, J. A. Circadian rhythm of wrist temperature in normal-living subjects: A candidate of new index of the circadian system. Physiol. Behav. 95, 570–580 (2008).") and peaks[17](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR17 "Kerkhof, G. A. & Van Dongen, H. P. A. Morning-type and evening-type individuals differ in the phase position of their endogenous circadian oscillator. Neurosci. Lett. 218, 153–156 (1996)."). All these variations are based on one’s innate circadian rhythm. In fact, people display preferences for activity at certain time of day, leading to a circadian phenotype that may be classified with the concept of chronotype. Thus, chronotype can be defined as the time of day preferred by individuals to perform daily activities or to sleep[9](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR9 "Schmidt, C., Collette, F., Cajochen, C. & Peigneux, P. A time to think: Circadian rhythms in human cognition. Cogn. Neuropsychol. 24, 755–789 (2007)."),[18](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR18 "Levandovski, R., Sasso, E. & Hidalgo, M. P. Chronotype: A review of the advances, limits and applicability of the main instruments used in the literature to assess human phenotype. Trends Psychiatry Psychotherapy 35, 3–11 (2013).").

Chronotype is derived from genetic factors since it depends on clock genes that interact among them determining specific circadian patterns[19](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR19 "Montaruli, A. et al. The circadian typology: The role of physical activity and melatonin. Sport Sci. Health 13, 469–476 (2017)."). The central coordination of circadian rhythms at an endogenous level takes place through the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, which in turn integrates external inputs such as natural and artificial light[20](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR20 "Bonaconsa, M. et al. Differential modulation of clock gene expression in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, liver and heart of aged mice. Exp. Gerontol. 55, 70–79 (2014)."),[21](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR21 "Correa, A., Alguacil, S., Ciria, L. F., Jiménez, A. & Ruz, M. Circadian rhythms and decision-making: A review and new evidence from electroencephalography. Chronobiol. Int. 37, 520–541 (2020)."). Despite endogenous regulation, it is important to note that humans can voluntarily modify circadian rhythms through some activities such as physical exercise, food intake or time spent resting and being awake. Such practices become inputs that modulate the circadian pattern[19](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR19 "Montaruli, A. et al. The circadian typology: The role of physical activity and melatonin. Sport Sci. Health 13, 469–476 (2017)."). In this sense, the efficiency of the circadian system always depends on the conjunction of physiology and behavior of the organism[20](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR20 "Bonaconsa, M. et al. Differential modulation of clock gene expression in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, liver and heart of aged mice. Exp. Gerontol. 55, 70–79 (2014).").

These preferences for performing daily activities and resting are often determined through the use of questionnaires[22](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR22 "Horne, J. A. & Östberg, O. A self-assessment questionnaire to determine Morningness–Eveningness in human circadian rhythms. Int. J. Chronobiol. 4, 97–110 (1976)."), but also thorough some physiological indices such as body temperature or melatonin secretion, both deemed as the best markers of circadian rhythm[19](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR19 "Montaruli, A. et al. The circadian typology: The role of physical activity and melatonin. Sport Sci. Health 13, 469–476 (2017)."). Accordingly, three different chronotypes can be described: Morning-types (referred to as “larks”), characterized by circadian rhythmicity that occurs earlier with their optimal functioning early in the morning, Evening-types (referred to as “owls”), characterized by circadian rhythmicity that occurs later with their optimal functioning late in the evening, the two representing the two extreme typologies. The delay of Evening-types with respect to Morning-types oscillates between 2 and 4 h in the circadian rhythmicity of all variables described above[23](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR23 "Mongrain, V., Noujaim, J., Blais, H. & Dumont, M. Daytime vigilance in chronotypes: Diurnal variations and effects of behavioral Sleep fragmentation. Behav. Brain Res. 190, 105–111 (2008)."). Finally, a third chronotype has been referred to as the Neither-types (or intermediate), that is, those without a pronounced circadian preference[9](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR9 "Schmidt, C., Collette, F., Cajochen, C. & Peigneux, P. A time to think: Circadian rhythms in human cognition. Cogn. Neuropsychol. 24, 755–789 (2007)."). Synchrony effects are frequently reported in a variety of tasks[24](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR24 "Adan, A. et al. Circadian typology: A comprehensive review. Chronobiol. Int. 29, 1153–1175 (2012)."), so it is possible to reach the best performance during the optimal time of day (in the morning for Morning-types, in the evening for Evening-types) compared to the non-optimal time of day (in the morning for Evening-types, in the evening for Morning-types), following the circadian typology.

As circadian variability differentially affects endogenous alertness at different times of day, it is expected that performance in tasks that require vigilant attention differs in people with extreme chronotypes depending on time of testing. Previous studies have found chronotype and time of day interactions (synchrony effect) in tasks requiring vigilant attention (e.g., the PVT)[23](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR23 "Mongrain, V., Noujaim, J., Blais, H. & Dumont, M. Daytime vigilance in chronotypes: Diurnal variations and effects of behavioral Sleep fragmentation. Behav. Brain Res. 190, 105–111 (2008)."),[25](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR25 "Lara, T., Madrid, J. A. & Correa, A. The vigilance decrement in executive function is attenuated when individual chronotypes perform at their optimal time of day. PLoS ONE 9, e88820 (2014)."). Besides vigilant attention tasks, synchrony effects are also expected in cognitive demanding tasks that require sustained attention to maintain an accurate level of performance, such as those involving attentional control (e.g., Stroop or flanker interference tasks), or inhibitory control (e.g., some versions of the SART[25](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR25 "Lara, T., Madrid, J. A. & Correa, A. The vigilance decrement in executive function is attenuated when individual chronotypes perform at their optimal time of day. PLoS ONE 9, e88820 (2014).")).

Important interactions between the two components of the alerting system have also been widely documented. For instance, top-down vigilant attention seems to compensate for the lack of sufficient arousal that monotonous and tedious tasks convey. On the other hand, the phasic component of alerting compensates for the decrement on vigilant attention as time-on-task increases. For instance, when clonidine is administered to inhibit the release of norepinephrine from the locus coeruleus, lapses of vigilant attention are observed, but they are attenuated when white noise, activating the exogenous component of the alerting network (phasic alert), is supplied while performing the task[8](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR8 "Robertson, I. H. & O’Connell, R. Vigilant attention. In Attention and Time (eds Nobre, A. C. & Coull, J. T.) 79–88 (Oxford University Press, Oxford, 2010)."),[26](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR26 "Smith, A. & Nutt, D. Noradrenaline and attention lapses. Nature 380, 291 (1996).").

The objective of the present study is threefold. As a first objective, we aimed to determine whether the high level of endogenous alert, that we assume to occur in the optimal time of day according to the individual’s chronotype, improves performance in both a rather monotonous task that is supposed to activate the vigilant attentional network (the PVT), and in a conflict demanding task that requires sustained attention throughout the task (the flanker task). Additionally, as attention is thought to be biased to novel stimulus and/or locations[27](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR27 "Chen, Q., Fuentes, L. J. & Zhou, X. Biasing the organism for novelty: A pervasive property of the attention system. Hum. Brain Mapp. 31, 1146–1156 (2010)."),[28](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR28 "Horstmann, G. & Herwig, A. Novelty biases attention and gaze in a surprise trial. Attent. Percep. Psychophys. 78, 69–77 (2016)."), we assessed whether synchrony effects in the two aforementioned tasks can be modulated by task-related novelty, that is, first-experience-with-task occurring in the first session. It might be that first-experience-with-task increases alerting levels, compensating the low endogenous alertness when participants complete the tasks for the first time at their non-optimal time. If that were the case, we expect synchrony effects in this situation to be reduced in comparison with when the first session takes place at the optimal time of day and the second at the non-optimal time of day.

As a second objective, we aimed to determine whether the exogenous component of the alerting system modulates also people’s performance according to their chronotypes. Given the interactive relationship between the exogenous and endogenous components of alerting, we expect that warning auditory signals that are usually used to assess the effect of phasic alerting (e.g., in the interactive version of the Attention Network Test, ANT-I[29](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR29 "Callejas, A., Lupiáñez, J. & Tudela, P. The three attentional networks: On their independence and interactions. Brain Cogn. 54, 225–227 (2004).")), compensates for the low level of endogenous alertness when people perform the task at their non-optimal time of day.

Finally, as a third objective, we aimed to assess the impact of the two different components of the alerting system on executive control as a function of chronotype. Phasic alerting seems to have a negative impact in some measures of cognitive control[30](#ref-CR30 "Asanowicz, D. & Marzecová, A. Differential effects of phasic and tonic alerting on the efficiency of executive attention. Acta Physiol. (Oxf) 176, 58–70 (2017)."),[31](#ref-CR31 "Callejas, A., Lupiánez, J., Funes, M. J. & Tudela, P. Modulations among the alerting, orienting and executive control networks. Exp. Brain Res. 167, 27–37 (2005)."),[32](#ref-CR32 "McConnell, M. M. & Shore, D. I. Mixing measures: Testing an assumption of the attention network test. Attent. Percep. Psychophys. 73, 1096–1107 (2011)."),[33](#ref-CR33 "Weinbach, N. & Henik, A. Phasic alertness can modulate executive control by enhancing global processing of visual stimuli. Cognition 121, 454–458 (2011)."),[34](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR34 "Weinbach, N. & Henik, A. The relationship between alertness and executive control. J. Exp. Psychol. Hum. Percept. Perform. 38, 1530–1540 (2012)."). For instance, conflict based on stimulus–response interference, like in the Simon task[35](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR35 "Simon, J. R. & Rudell, A. P. Auditory S-R compatibility: The effect of an irrelevant cue on information processing. J. Appl. Psychol. 51, 300–304 (1967).") is increased when targets are preceded by an auditory signal[36](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR36 "Fischer, R., Plessow, F. & Kiesel, A. The effects of alerting signals in action control: Activation of S-R associations or inhibition of executive control processes?. Psychol. Res. 76, 317–328 (2012)."), but conflict based on stimulus-stimulus interference, like in the Stroop task is not[34](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR34 "Weinbach, N. & Henik, A. The relationship between alertness and executive control. J. Exp. Psychol. Hum. Percept. Perform. 38, 1530–1540 (2012)."). These results suggest that alerting improves the translation of the visual code into the correspondent motor code[36](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR36 "Fischer, R., Plessow, F. & Kiesel, A. The effects of alerting signals in action control: Activation of S-R associations or inhibition of executive control processes?. Psychol. Res. 76, 317–328 (2012)."), rather than the alerting tone producing a general state of readiness to respond.

However, of greatest relevance for the present study is the negative effect of phasic alerting on flanker interference. With this task, two main accounts have been proposed. The deactivation account[29](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR29 "Callejas, A., Lupiáñez, J. & Tudela, P. The three attentional networks: On their independence and interactions. Brain Cogn. 54, 225–227 (2004)."),[31](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR31 "Callejas, A., Lupiánez, J., Funes, M. J. & Tudela, P. Modulations among the alerting, orienting and executive control networks. Exp. Brain Res. 167, 27–37 (2005)."),[37](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR37 "Fuentes, L. J. & Campoy, G. The time course of alerting effect over orienting in the attention network test. Exp. Brain Res. 185, 667–672 (2008).") suggests that the alerting tone would inhibit the attentional control network involved in conflict resolution[38](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR38 "Cohen, R. M. et al. Functional localization of sustained attention. Neuropsychiatry Neuropsychol. Behav. Neurol. 1, 17–30 (1988)."), producing a subjective feeling of clearing of consciousness, and rendering the individual more prone to react to forthcoming external stimuli than to current thoughts or internal states[39](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR39 "Posner, M. I. Attention: the mechanisms of consciousness. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 91, 7398–7403 (1994)."),[40](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR40 "Posner, M. I. & Raichle, M. E. Images of Mind (Scientific American Library/Scientific American Books, New York, 1994)."). Alternatively, phasic alerting might prioritize spatial processing of stimuli in the visual field, being them task-relevant or task-irrelevant, and consequently enhancing the processing of to-be-ignored distracters when they are presented separated from the target, as it happens in the flanker task[34](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR34 "Weinbach, N. & Henik, A. The relationship between alertness and executive control. J. Exp. Psychol. Hum. Percept. Perform. 38, 1530–1540 (2012)."). Thus, the increased conflict effect with alerting warning tones would be the indirect consequence of higher accessibility of spatially presented flankers.

All these results suggest that the interaction between phasic alerting and conflict may depend on the type of interference involved. Thus, when interference is based on stimulus–response mapping, alerting may facilitate translation between visual and motor codes, whereas when interference is based on spatial processing of target and distracters, like in the present study, alerting may either inhibit the executive network or facilitate spatial processing of task-irrelevant flankers.

To elucidate which is the best explanation for the alerting and conflict network interaction is beyond the aim of the present study. However, data from synchrony effects on the conflict effect can help assess the pertinence of the two aforementioned accounts in the flanker task. According to the former explanation (clearing of consciousness), conducting the flanker task in the optimal time of day could compensate for the reduced activity of the executive control network produced by the alerting tone, as the vigilant attention network and the executive attention network share common brain areas, such as the DLPFC and the ACC[8](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR8 "Robertson, I. H. & O’Connell, R. Vigilant attention. In Attention and Time (eds Nobre, A. C. & Coull, J. T.) 79–88 (Oxford University Press, Oxford, 2010)."). Therefore, such increment in the conflict effect with the alerting tone should not be observed when participants perform the task in the optimal time of day. However, if the alerting tone increases spatial attention to distracters in the flanker task, such increment in conflict effect should be observed irrespective of the moment of day. Importantly, tonic alertness has been found to enhance spatial processing in orienting tasks[41](#ref-CR41 "Heber, I. A., Valvoda, J. T., Kuhlen, T. & Fimm, B. Low arousal modulates visuospatial attention in three-dimensional virtual space. J. Int. Neuropsychol. Soc. 14, 309–317 (2008)."),[42](#ref-CR42 "Schock, L., Schwenzer, M., Sturm, W. & Mathiak, K. Alertness and visuospatial attention in clinical depression. BMC Psychiatry 11, 78 (2011)."),[43](#ref-CR43 "Sturm, W. et al. Spatial attention: More than intrinsic alerting?. Exp. Brain Res. 171, 16–25 (2006)."),[44](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR44 "Thimm, M., Fink, G. R., Küst, J., Karbe, H. & Sturm, W. Impact of alertness training on spatial neglect: A behavioural and fMRI study. Neuropsychologia 44, 1230–1246 (2006)."), like the phasic component does[37](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR37 "Fuentes, L. J. & Campoy, G. The time course of alerting effect over orienting in the attention network test. Exp. Brain Res. 185, 667–672 (2008)."),[45](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR45 "Robertson, I. H., Tegnér, R., Tham, K., Lo, A. & Nimmo-Smith, I. Sustained attention training for unilateral neglect: Theoretical and rehabilitation implications. J. Clin. Exp. Neuropsychol. 17, 416–430 (1995)."). Therefore, according to the spatial processing account, the endogenous component of the alerting network should have similar effects on conflict effects as the alerting tone has been found to have. If that were the case, we should observe increased conflict effects when testing occurs in the optimal time of day compared with when testing occurs in the non-optimal time of day with the alerting tone absent. However, previous findings have reported no differences in flanker interference due to the endogenous component of the alerting network either when tonic alerting is promoted throughout the whole task[46](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR46 "Weinbach, N. & Henik, A. The interaction between alerting and executive control: Dissociating phasic arousal and temporal expectancy. Attent. Percep. Psychophys. 75, 1374–1381 (2013).") or as a function of chronotype and time of testing[47](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR47 "Knight, M. & Mather, M. Look out—it’s your off-peak time of day! Time of day matters more for alerting than for orienting or executive attention. Exp. Aging Res. 39, 305–321 (2013)."),[48](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR48 "Matchock, R. L. & Mordkoff, J. T. Chronotype and time-of-day influences on the alerting, orienting, and executive components of attention. Exp. Brain Res. 192, 189–198 (2009)."). These results suggest that the endogenous component of the alerting network has influence in spatial orientation but not in how people deal with cognitive conflict in the flanker task.

## Method

Morning-types and Evening-types participants were tested in two different sessions separated by 1 week. One session took place in the morning and the other in the evening. In each session, all participants completed two computer-based reaction-time tasks. First, the PVT, a rather monotonous task that measures vigilant attention[49](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR49 "Dinges, D. F. & Powell, J. W. Microcomputer analyses of performance on a portable, simple visual RT task during sustained operations. Behav. Res. Methods Instrum. Comput. 17, 652–655 (1985)."). Second, a flanker task, preceded or not by alerting tones, in which target and distracters were located in the center of the screen to avoid uncertainty about target location.

### Participants

Details of the study were announced through the distribution list existing in the Faculty of Psychology (University of Murcia) to recruit participants in exchange of course credit. Thirty-four undergraduate students (27 females; M age = 21.0 years, SD age = 2.3) were selected from a total of 132 students who agreed to participate and complete a reduced Spanish version of the Horne and Östberg’s Morningness–Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ)[22](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR22 "Horne, J. A. & Östberg, O. A self-assessment questionnaire to determine Morningness–Eveningness in human circadian rhythms. Int. J. Chronobiol. 4, 97–110 (1976)."). On the basis of MEQ scores, we selected 16 students (14 females; M age = 21.6, SD age = 3.0) for the Morning-types group, and 18 students (13 females; M age = 20.4, SD age = 1.5) for the Evening-types group. We excluded participants with intermediate chronotype to maximize differences in vigilant attention between extreme chronotypes. We did not explore the influence of sex because only 7 participants were males. All participants reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no chronic medical conditions.

### Procedure

Participants first signed the written informed consent, and then completed the reduced Spanish version of the reduced Morningness–Eveningness Questionnaire (rMEQ) develop by Adan and Almirall[50](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR50 "Adan, A. & Almirall, H. Horne and Östberg Morningness–Eveningness questionnaire: A reduced scale. Person. Individ. Differ. 12, 241–253 (1991)."). The rMEQ consisted of five items with scores ranging from 4 (definitively Evening-types) to 25 (definitively Morning-types). Participants who scored between 17 and 25 (M = 19.4) formed the Morning-types group, and participants who scored between 4 and 11 (M = 8.6) formed the Evening-types group.

Participants were tested individually in sound-attenuated booths. All tasks were programmed in E-Prime 3 (Psychology Software Tools)[51](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR51 "Schneider, W., Eschman, A. & Zuccolotto, A. E-Prime Reference Guide (Psychology Software Tools, Inc., Pittsburgh, 2012)."). Visual stimuli were presented on a 22′′ TFT monitor with a screen resolution of 1920 by 1,080 pixels. A Chronos device (Psychology Software Tools) with five buttons was used to collect responses and present auditory stimuli (via headphones).

All participants came to the laboratory twice, with an interval of seven days between the two sessions. One of the sessions was scheduled to begin at 8:00 AM (the morning session), and the other at 20:30 PM (the evening session), both lasting by 30 min of duration, approximately. This allowed us to evaluate participants in both their optimal and their non-optimal time of day according to their chronotype (when we expected their vigilant attention to be maximum and minimum, respectively). Testing was carried out during the week days, and the order of the sessions was counterbalanced across participants within each chronotype group, so that half of the participants from each group completed the first session in their optimal time and the second session in their non-optimal, with the reverse order for the other half.

Both sessions had the same structure. We began with a 5-min interview by asking participants whether they had consumed coffee during the previous two hours or other stimulants during the previous 24 h (all reported no consumption) and whether they had slept at least 5 h the night before (all reported having slept between 7 and 9 h). Then, participants performed a ten-min version of the PVT. Each PVT trial began with a random interval ranging from 2 to 10 s in which the computer screen remained black. Then, a red circle (50 pixels in diameter) appeared in the center of the screen and participants had to press, as quickly as possible, the central bottom of the response box with the index finger of their dominant hand. When the response was made, the screen went blank and a new trial began.

Immediately after the PVT, participants completed the flanker task for 15 min, approximately. The task consisted of five arrows (pointing left or right) as stimuli and alerting tones preceding half of the trials in each congruency condition. Each trial began with a fixation point (a plus sign) presented in the center of the screen for 2,500 ms. Then, a row of five arrows appeared in the center of the screen and participants indicated, as quickly and accurately as possible, whether the arrow in the middle (the target) pointed left or right by pressing the leftmost or rightmost button of the response box, respectively. The five arrows remained visible until a response was made or for 3,000 ms. In half of the trials, the four flanking arrows pointed in the opposite direction as the target (incongruent condition), whereas, in the other half, flankers and target pointed to the same direction (congruent condition). In each congruence condition, an alerting tone (a 50 ms beep of 2000 Hz) was presented prior to the target in half the trials, with a tone-target interval of 500 ms (from onset to onset). Participants completed three blocks of 72 trials with a short break between blocks. Experimental trials were preceded by 16 practice trials.

### Ethical approval

This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Murcia and was conducted conformed with the ethical standards laid down in the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki.

## Results

Data were preprocessed with R[52](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR52 "R Core Team. R: A language and environment for statistical computing. R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria (2017) 
                  https://www.R-project.org/
                  
                ."), and analyzed by analysis of variance (ANOVA) with JASP 0.9.2[53](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR53 "JASP Team. JASP (Version 0.9.1) [Computer software] (2019)."). We adopted a significance level of 0.05 for all analyses.

### Psychomotor vigilance task (PVT)

The first trial of each session was considered as practice and discarded. Besides, we considered extreme outliers and discarded reaction times (RTs) shorter than 150 ms or longer than 1,200 ms (0,11% of the data), in addition to those separated by more than six interquartile ranges from the median value of each participant in each session (an additional 0.22% of the data). We employed this lenient trimming procedure because, in order to exploit the additional information that emerges from RT distributions, and taking advantage of the relatively large number of trials per condition, we planned to perform a bin-means analysis[54](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR54 "Houghton, G. & Grange, J. A. CDF-XL: Computing cumulative distribution functions of reaction time data in Excel. Behav. Res. Methods 43, 1023–1032 (2011)."),[55](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR55 "Ratcliff, R. Group reaction time distributions and an analysis of distribution statistics. Psychol. Bull. 86, 446–461 (1979)."). Note that, with this kind of analysis, the presence of moderate outliers (as those that could result from fluctuations in alertness during a session) turns out to provide valuable information, rather than compromise data analysis and interpretation.

RTs for each participant in each session were rank ordered and divided into ten bins as equally sized as possible (the number of data per bin ranged from 8 to 11; M = 9.4). Mean RTs were calculated for each bin and submitted to a mixed analysis of variance (ANOVA) with the within-participants factors test time (optimal, non-optimal) and RT bin (1–10), and the between-participants factors chronotype (Morning-types, Evening-types) and order (optimal session first, optimal session second). Main statistical results are presented in Table [1](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#Tab1) (rightmost column, bottom row). Neither the main effect of chronotype nor the main effect of order reached statistical significance (both *F*s < 1). However, there was a main effect of test time (the synchrony effect), revealing shorter RTs at the optimal time (M = 300 ms) than at the non-optimal time (M = 319 ms; synchrony effect = 19 ms). There was also an interaction between test time and RT bin, showing that the synchrony effect varied across bins. As illustrated in Fig. [1](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#Fig1), the effect increased towards the slower end of the distribution (for bins 1 to 10, synchrony effect = 10, 14, 13, 14, 16, 17, 18, 21, 28, and 41 ms). Finally, there was an interaction between test time, RT bin, and chronotype; and also, between test time, RT bin, and order. To disentangle these interactions and further understand the pattern of results, we performed separate analyses for each chronotype and for each order (see Table [1](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#Tab1)). Evening-types participants showed synchrony effects that increased at the slower end of the RT distribution and that did not significantly differ as a function of session order (when the optimal session was completed first, synchrony effect for bins 1 to 10 = 8, 13, 12, 14, 19, 23, 25, 33, 50, and 73 ms; M = 27 ms; when the optimal session took place second, synchrony effect = 18, 18, 18, 17, 18, 19, 21, 22, 27, and 42 ms; M = 22 ms). This is the same pattern that was observed for Morning-types participants when the optimal session was completed first (synchrony effect = 9, 19, 20, 22, 23, 24, 26, 34, 40, 68 ms; M = 29 ms). However, the synchrony effect was completely abolished for Morning-types participants when the non-optimal session took place first (synchrony effect = 6, 4, 3, 3, 2, 0, − 1, − 6, − 7, − 24 ms; M = − 2 ms).

The PVT allowed us to evaluate the tonic alert that resulted from the synchrony between participants' chronotype and the time of day in which the task was performed. In addition to this form of tonic alert, the flanker task allowed us to also evaluate the phasic alert generated by the presentation of alerting tones. We also evaluated the interaction between tonic and phasic alert and the modulation of the congruency effect by these two kinds of alerting.

### Flanker task

We excluded from the RT analysis trials with incorrect responses (2.78% of the data) and trials with RTs separated by more than three interquartile ranges from the median value of each participant in each condition (1.95% of the data). Mean RTs were submitted to a mixed ANOVA with test time (optimal, non-optimal), alerting tone (tone, no tone), and congruency (congruent, incongruent) as within-participant factors; and chronotype (Morning-types, Evening-types) and order (optimal session first, optimal session second) as between-participants factors.

There was a main effect of test time, *F*(1, 30) = 8.212, *p* = 0.008, η2 = 0.169, revealing that RTs were shorter at the optimal time (M = 394 ms) than at the non-optimal time (M = 412; synchrony effect = 18 ms). However, this effect was not equivalent for Morning-types and Evening-types participants, as revealed by the interaction between test time and chronotype, *F*(1, 30) = 9.864, *p* = 0.004, η2 = 0.203. In fact, only the Evening-types participants showed a significant effect of test time (synchrony effect = 35 ms), whereas this effect was completely abolished in the Morning-types group (synchrony effect = − 1.6 ms). As illustrated in Fig. [2](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#Fig2)A, the synchrony effect was numerically greater when the optimal session took place second than when the optimal session was completed first, in contrast to what was observed with the PVT. However, this tendency was not statistically significant (for both the test time × order interaction and the test time × chronotype × order interaction, *F* < 1).

**Figure 2**

![Figure 2](//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41598-020-68755-z/MediaObjects/41598_2020_68755_Fig2_HTML.png)

[Full size image](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z/figures/2)

(**A**) Synchrony effect (RT at the non-optimal time minus RT at the optimal time) as a function of chronotype and order. (**B**) Synchrony effect as a function of chronotype and alerting tone. (**C**) Congruency effect (RT in the incongruent condition minus RT in the congruent condition) as a function of alerting tone and test time.

In addition, we found a statistically significant interaction between test time and alerting tone, *F*(1, 30) = 4.653, *p* = 0.039, η2 = 0.119, revealing greater synchrony effect in the no-tone condition than in the tone condition (synchrony effect = 24 and 12 ms, respectively). An inspection of Fig. [2](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#Fig2)B suggests that this interaction was mainly consequence of Evening-types participants' performance. In fact, for Morning-types participants just a main effect of alerting tone was observed, *F*(1, 14) = 31.399, *p* < 0.001, η2 = 0.684, that is, RTs were shorter with the tone than when the tone was not presented. However, for Evening-types participants we also observed a main effect of alerting tone, *F*(1, 16) = 23.093, *p* < 0.001, η2 = 0.586 but test of time and alerting tone interacted in this group of participants. Although admittedly the interaction was only marginally significant, *F*(1, 16) = 4.111, *p* = 0.060, η2 = 0.195 it is worth noting that the alerting tone reduced the differences between the optimal and non-optimal time of day by almost half (synchrony effect = 25 ms) in comparison to when the alerting tone was absent (synchrony effect = 44 ms).

Finally, there was statistically significant main effects of congruency, *F*(1, 30) = 233.828, *p* < 0.001, η2 = 0.884 and alerting tone, *F*(1, 30) = 49.415, *p* < 0.001, η2 = 0.614. RTs were shorter in the congruent condition (M = 377 ms) than in the incongruent condition (M = 418 ms; congruency effect = 51 ms); and RTs were also shorter in trials with alerting tone (M = 387 ms) than in trials with no tone (M = 418; alerting tone effect = 31 ms). However, the congruency × alerting tone interaction was statistically significant, *F*(1, 30) = 33.400, *p* < 0.001, η2 = 0.515 because the congruency effect was greater in the tone condition (congruency effect = 61 ms) than in the no tone condition (congruency effect = 42 ms). Importantly, however, the congruency × test time interaction did not reach statistical significance, *F*(1, 30) = 1.934, *p* = 0.175, η2 = 0.055 suggesting equivalent congruency effect at the optimal time (congruency effect = 49 ms) than at the non-optimal time (congruency effect = 54 ms; Fig. [2](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#Fig2)C).

## Discussion

Three main objectives were addressed in the present study regarding the role of chronotype in attention-related tasks. We first asked whether synchrony effects, that is, the difference in performance between the optimal and non-optimal time of day as a function of chronotype, are observed in two tasks that differently involve the endogenous component of the alerting network, the PVT and the flanker tasks. The second objective was to explore the role of phasic alerting as a function of chronotype and time of testing when participants performed the flanker task. In the final objective we assessed the role of the two components of the alerting network in executive attention-dependent conflict resolution, and whether chronotype and time of testing had any modulatory effect.

### The role of chronotype in attention tasks

The first task, the PVT, requires vigilant attention that is activated when rather monotonous tasks are performed during long periods of time. Our results showed that when participants performed the PVT at the non-optimal time of day reaction times to targets were longer than when participants performed the task at the optimal time of day[25](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR25 "Lara, T., Madrid, J. A. & Correa, A. The vigilance decrement in executive function is attenuated when individual chronotypes perform at their optimal time of day. PLoS ONE 9, e88820 (2014)."),[56](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR56 "Doran, S. M., Van Dongen, H. P. A. & Dinges, D. F. Sustained attention performance during sleep deprivation: Evidence of state instability. Arch. Ital. Biol. 139, 253–267 (2001)."). This synchrony effect increased towards the slower end of the RT distribution, which suggests that the effect largely emerged from more frequent or extreme fluctuations of attention at the non-optimal time of day. Besides, the synchrony effect was modulated by the first-experience-with-task, but very especially for the Morning-types participants. Specifically, whereas Evening-types participants showed synchrony effects irrespective of whether the task was performed first at either the non-optimal or optimal time of day, Morning-types participants showed synchrony effects only when they performed the task first at the optimal time of day. When they performed the task first at the non-optimal time of day, the synchrony effect vanished away, being performance at their non-optimal time of day similar to that observed at their optimal time of day. This novel result suggests that novelty of the task produced an increment in the level of alerting that overcame the deleterious effect of poor vigilant attention characteristic of the non-optimal time of day, but that this novelty effect only occurred or was much more pronounced for Morning-types chronotype. Consequently, the novelty effect fully compensated the fact of being at the non-optimal time of day for Morning-types participants, but not for Evening-types participants. These results extend what is usually observed when novel objects or locations are presented along task performance[27](/articles/s41598-020-68755-z#ref-CR27 "Chen, Q., Fuentes, L. J. & Zhou, X. Biasing the organism for novelty: A pervasive property of the attention system. Hum. Brain Mapp. 31, 1146–1156 (2010).") to the task as a whole when it is presented for the first time under low vigilant attention conditions.

As in the PVT, Evening-types participants showed reliable synchrony effects in the flanker task irrespective of whether first-experience-with-task took place at the non-optimal or at the optimal time of day. Morning-types participants, however, did not show any synchrony effect in the two session, and first-experience-with-task did not have any modulation effect like that observed with the PVT. This unexpected pattern of results showed by Morning-types participants across tasks deserves further discussion. One possible explanation for these results is that Morning-types individuals are, in general, more sensitive than Evening-types individuals to certain factors potentially capable of increasing alerting levels at their non-optimal time of day. args.summary:
This scientific article published in Scientific Reports (2020) investigates how chronotype (morningness-eveningness preference) affects the interaction between alerting and executive control networks in attention. The study involved 34 participants (18 Evening-types, 16 Morning-types) selected from 132 students using the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ). Participants completed two tasks - the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT) and a flanker task - in both morning (8:00 AM) and evening (20:30 PM) sessions, separated by one week.

**Key findings:**
1. **PVT results**: Evening-types showed synchrony effects (better performance at optimal time of day) regardless of session order. Morning-types showed synchrony effects only when the optimal session came first; when the non-optimal session was first, the synchrony effect was abolished, suggesting task novelty compensated for low alertness at their non-optimal time.

2. **Flanker task results**: Evening-types showed significant synchrony effects (35ms difference), while Morning-types showed no synchrony effect. Alerting tones reduced the synchrony effect for Evening-types by nearly half (from 44ms to 25ms).

3. **Alerting-executive interaction**: Phasic alerting (warning tones) increased the congruency effect (conflict score) in the flanker task (61ms with tone vs. 42ms without), consistent with prior research. However, time of day did not modulate the congruency effect, suggesting endogenous alertness does not influence flanker interference.

4. **Chronotype differences**: Evening-types showed more consistent synchrony effects across both tasks. Morning-types appeared more sensitive to factors that increase alertness (task novelty, cognitive demands) at their non-optimal time, potentially compensating for low vigilant attention.

The study concludes that chronotype determines vigilant attention more decisively in Evening-types than Morning-types, and that exogenous (phasic) but not endogenous alerting exerts a deleterious effect on conflict resolution.

# Caffeine Tolerance Reset: How Long It Takes And How To Brew During A Reset

![Drip coffee maker brewing into a glass carafe beside a red mug, coffee beans, and an alarm clock on a kitchen counter.](//rockcreekcoffee.com/cdn/shop/articles/Caffeine_Tolerance_Reset_How_Long_It_Takes_And_How_To_Brew_During_A_Reset.png?v=1773107684&width=2000)

Caffeine is one of the most widely consumed psychoactive compounds in the world. It fuels productivity, supports endurance, enhances focus, and anchors morning rituals. Yet many regular coffee drinkers eventually ask the same question: why does caffeine stop working the way it used to?

If your morning cup no longer delivers the same clarity, energy, or motivation, you are not imagining it. This is not a problem of bean quality or roast level. It is neurobiology. It is receptor adaptation. It is caffeine tolerance.

This guide explores how caffeine tolerance develops, how long it takes to reset, whether the 3 day reset myth is accurate, how to taper strategically, and how to brew during a reset without sacrificing the ritual of coffee.

## Why Caffeine Eventually “Stops Working”

Caffeine works primarily by blocking adenosine receptors in the brain. Adenosine is a neurotransmitter that promotes sleep pressure and relaxation. Throughout the day, adenosine accumulates and binds to receptors, signaling fatigue.

Caffeine resembles adenosine structurally. When consumed, it competes for those receptors and blocks adenosine from binding. The result is alertness, reduced perceived fatigue, and enhanced cognitive performance.

However, the brain adapts.

### Adenosine Receptor Upregulation

When caffeine blocks adenosine receptors consistently, the brain compensates by creating more receptors. This process is called receptor upregulation.

More receptors mean more places for adenosine to bind. Over time, the same caffeine dose blocks a smaller percentage of total receptors. This reduces perceived stimulation.

This is why caffeine tolerance develops.

The coffee did not weaken. Your nervous system adapted.

## Does Caffeine Tolerance Go Away?

Yes. Caffeine tolerance is reversible.

When caffeine intake decreases, the brain gradually downregulates excess adenosine receptors. As receptor density normalizes, smaller caffeine doses produce stronger perceived effects.

The key question becomes: how long does that take?

## How Long Does It Take To Reset Caffeine Tolerance?

Research suggests receptor normalization begins within a few days but may take 7 to 14 days for full perceptual reset in regular daily users.

The popular 3 day caffeine reset myth likely reflects early receptor adjustment. Many people feel sharper caffeine sensitivity after 72 hours. However, deeper receptor adaptation may require a longer reduction period.

Factors influencing reset speed include:

* Total daily caffeine intake
* Duration of habitual use
* Genetic metabolism rate
* Sleep patterns
* Stress levels

Heavy users consuming 400 mg or more daily may require closer to 10 to 14 days for full recalibration.

## Withdrawal Symptoms During A Reset

Reducing caffeine abruptly can cause temporary withdrawal symptoms:

* Headaches
* Fatigue
* Brain fog
* Irritability
* Mild flu-like sensations

These symptoms occur because adenosine activity increases temporarily while receptor density remains elevated.

This is why strategic tapering is often more effective than abrupt cessation.

## How To Lower Caffeine Without Headaches

The most effective approach is gradual reduction using brew ratio control and half-caf blending.

### Step 1: Adjust Brew Ratio

If you typically brew at a 1:15 ratio, adjust to 1:17 or 1:18 while keeping grind consistent. This reduces caffeine per cup without eliminating ritual.

Precision grinders like the [Baratza Encore Grinder](https://rockcreekcoffee.com/products/encore) allow consistent grind control while adjusting extraction variables carefully.

### Step 2: Introduce Half-Caf

Blend 50 percent regular coffee with 50 percent decaf for several days.

The [Swiss Water Decaf Medium Roast](https://rockcreekcoffee.com/products/swiss-water-decaf-medium-roast) is ideal for strategic blending because it preserves flavor complexity without chemical processing.

### Step 3: Reduce Total Cups

Maintain ritual but reduce frequency. Replace afternoon cup with decaf or herbal tea.

## Is Decaf Good For A Caffeine Reset?

Yes. Decaf allows behavioral continuity while reducing caffeine intake.

Psychological ritual plays a significant role in coffee dependence. Aroma, warmth, and routine reinforce habit loops beyond caffeine itself.

Using decaf during a reset maintains ritual stability while allowing neurological recalibration.

## 3 Day Vs 7 Day Reset: What Is Realistic?

Three days may reduce withdrawal intensity. Seven to fourteen days produce more complete receptor adjustment.

A 7 day structured taper is often more sustainable than a sudden 72 hour elimination.

## How To Brew During A Reset Without Sacrificing Quality

You do not need to drink inferior coffee during a reset.

Continue sourcing from the [Coffee Collection](https://rockcreekcoffee.com/collections/coffee) and explore lighter brew ratios or half-caf blends.

Use gear from the [Coffee Gear Collection](https://rockcreekcoffee.com/collections/coffee-gear) to control extraction precisely.

The reset is neurological. Quality standards remain unchanged.

## The Neurobiology Of Caffeine Tolerance In Greater Detail

To truly understand a caffeine tolerance reset, we must go beyond adenosine receptor upregulation and explore the broader neurochemical adaptation process.

Caffeine primarily blocks A1 and A2A adenosine receptors. These receptors influence sleep pressure, dopamine regulation, and cerebral blood flow. When caffeine consistently blocks these receptors, the nervous system adapts in three primary ways:

* Increased receptor density
* Increased receptor sensitivity
* Altered neurotransmitter signaling balance

Over time, this means the same 200 milligram dose produces a diminished subjective effect. The brain is remarkably adaptive. It seeks equilibrium.

This is why caffeine tolerance is not a failure of willpower. It is neuroplasticity in action.

## Dopamine, Motivation, And Perceived Energy

Many people associate caffeine with dopamine. While caffeine does not directly release dopamine like certain stimulants, it indirectly enhances dopaminergic signaling by blocking adenosine’s inhibitory effects.

When tolerance develops, dopamine signaling becomes less noticeably enhanced. This is why caffeine can begin to feel less motivating even if it still reduces sleepiness.

A tolerance reset restores the contrast between baseline and stimulated state. When receptor density normalizes, smaller caffeine doses once again feel effective.

This is one reason many individuals report that after a reset, even a single cup from the [Best Sellers Collection](https://rockcreekcoffee.com/collections/best-sellers) feels stronger than multiple cups before the reset.

## Metabolism And Genetic Variability

Not all caffeine tolerance develops at the same speed. Genetic differences in CYP1A2 liver enzyme activity influence how quickly caffeine is metabolized.

Fast metabolizers clear caffeine quickly and may consume more throughout the day, potentially accelerating tolerance.

Slow metabolizers experience longer plasma caffeine elevation, sometimes reducing total daily consumption but increasing sleep disruption risk.

Understanding your own response pattern helps tailor a reset strategy.

## The 7 Day Structured Caffeine Taper Plan

Rather than abruptly eliminating caffeine, a structured taper reduces withdrawal symptoms while allowing receptor downregulation.

### Day 1 To Day 2: Ratio Adjustment

Maintain normal number of cups but reduce brew ratio by increasing water relative to coffee. Move from 1:15 to 1:17.

This reduces caffeine exposure while preserving flavor clarity when using quality beans from the [Whole Bean Coffee Collection](https://rockcreekcoffee.com/collections/whole-bean-coffee).

### Day 3 To Day 4: Introduce Half-Caf

Blend 50 percent regular coffee with 50 percent decaf. Continue morning ritual.

The Swiss Water Decaf Medium Roast maintains sweetness and body, preventing flavor sacrifice.

### Day 5 To Day 6: Reduce Volume

Limit caffeine to one morning serving. Replace afternoon coffee with decaf or herbal tea.

### Day 7: Decaf Only Or Very Light Dose

Transition to decaf or extremely light brew for one to two additional days if desired.

At this point, adenosine receptor density is trending downward. Sensitivity to caffeine is beginning to return.

## Behavioral Habit Loops And Ritual Preservation

Caffeine tolerance is partly physiological and partly behavioral.

The ritual of grinding beans, hearing water bloom through grounds, inhaling aroma, and holding a warm mug reinforces habit loops in the basal ganglia.

Removing caffeine abruptly can feel disruptive not just chemically but emotionally.

This is why brewing decaf during a reset is powerful. It maintains identity and continuity.

Using gear from the Coffee Gear Collection allows precise extraction control whether brewing full caffeine or decaf.

## Half-Caf Strategy For Long Term Moderation

After a reset, many individuals choose not to return to previous caffeine levels.

A long term half-caf approach provides moderate stimulation without rapidly rebuilding tolerance.

Combining beans from the Coffee Collection with Swiss Water decaf offers control without sacrificing quality.

## Does Caffeine Tolerance Fully Reset?

Yes, but baseline sensitivity depends on genetics and lifestyle.

After a 7 to 14 day reset, most individuals experience noticeably stronger response to lower doses.

However, consistent high intake will rebuild tolerance over time.

## How Often Should You Reset?

There is no universal rule.

Some individuals reset every few months. Others manage tolerance through dose cycling.

A practical approach is monitoring perceived effectiveness. If caffeine no longer enhances alertness, consider tapering.

## Caffeine Reset And Sleep Quality

Many individuals report improved sleep depth during resets. Reduced caffeine lowers evening adenosine suppression, allowing natural sleep pressure to accumulate.

Improved sleep quality can enhance morning alertness even before caffeine is reintroduced.

## Performance Optimization After A Reset

Once tolerance resets, smaller doses become more effective.

Instead of 300 milligrams daily, 100 to 150 milligrams may produce comparable stimulation.

This reduces total receptor stress and prolongs effectiveness.

## Strategic Coffee Selection During And After Reset

During tapering, lighter roasts often feel more stimulating due to perceived acidity and brightness.

Medium roasts offer balanced transition.

Rotating selections through the [Roasters Choice Collection](https://rockcreekcoffee.com/collections/roasters-choice) supports mindful consumption and prevents monotony.

## Common Myths About Caffeine Reset

* You must quit completely for weeks
* Decaf ruins tolerance reset
* Three days always fully resets receptors
* Tolerance means caffeine is unhealthy

These myths oversimplify receptor adaptation science.

## Why This Topic Matters For Coffee Drinkers

This discussion is not anti-caffeine. It is pro-awareness.

Coffee is a powerful tool when used intentionally.

Understanding tolerance allows you to maintain performance without escalation.

Quality beans, controlled brewing, and intelligent tapering protect both flavor enjoyment and neurological responsiveness.

## Caffeine Tolerance Reset As A Performance Strategy

A reset is not deprivation. It is recalibration.

When you return to regular coffee after structured reduction, even a single cup from the Best Sellers Collection may feel vibrant again.

That contrast restores appreciation.

And appreciation is part of the coffee experience.

## Reset Intentionally. Brew Intentionally.

A caffeine tolerance reset is not about abandoning coffee. It is about restoring sensitivity and reclaiming intentional enjoyment.

Whether you taper using half-caf blends, explore decaf options, or adjust brew ratios, you can maintain quality while recalibrating your nervous system.

## Frequently Asked Questions

How Long Does It Take To Reset Caffeine Tolerance?+

Most people begin to regain caffeine sensitivity within three to seven days of reducing intake. However, a more complete reset of adenosine receptor density may take seven to fourteen days depending on total daily intake, genetics, and sleep patterns.

Does Caffeine Tolerance Go Away Completely?+

Yes. Caffeine tolerance is reversible. When intake is reduced, the brain gradually downregulates excess adenosine receptors, restoring sensitivity to lower doses of caffeine.

How Do You Lower Caffeine Without Headaches?+

The most effective strategy is gradual tapering. Adjust brew ratios to reduce caffeine concentration, introduce half-caf blends, and replace later servings with decaf to minimize withdrawal symptoms such as headaches and fatigue.

Is Decaf Good For A Caffeine Reset?+

Yes. Decaf supports a caffeine reset by maintaining the ritual of coffee while significantly lowering caffeine intake. Swiss Water Process decaf preserves flavor complexity without chemical processing.

Is A Three Day Caffeine Reset Enough?+

Three days may reduce withdrawal intensity and begin receptor adjustment, but many individuals require seven to fourteen days for more complete tolerance recalibration.

Will Caffeine Feel Stronger After A Reset?+

Yes. After receptor density normalizes, smaller doses of caffeine often produce noticeably stronger perceived alertness and focus compared to pre-reset levels.

How Often Should You Do A Caffeine Reset?+

There is no fixed schedule. Some individuals reset every few months, while others manage tolerance by moderating intake through half-caf blending and controlled brew ratios.

Can You Drink Coffee During A Caffeine Reset?+

Yes. You can continue drinking coffee by reducing brew strength, switching to half-caf, or using high quality decaf. This maintains ritual consistency while allowing neurological recalibration.

This article from Rock Creek Coffee Roasters explains caffeine tolerance, how it develops, and how to reset it effectively. Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors in the brain, but consistent use causes the brain to create more receptors (receptor upregulation), reducing caffeine's effects over time. Tolerance is reversible through a structured reset.

**Key Timeline:** The popular "3-day reset" myth reflects early receptor adjustment, but full recalibration of adenosine receptor density typically requires 7 to 14 days, especially for heavy users (400mg+ daily).

**Withdrawal Symptoms:** Headaches, fatigue, brain fog, irritability, and mild flu-like sensations can occur when reducing abruptly.

**Strategic Tapering Plan (7-Day):**
- Days 1-2: Adjust brew ratio (e.g., 1:15 to 1:17)
- Days 3-4: Introduce half-caf blends (50% regular, 50% decaf)
- Days 5-6: Limit to one morning serving; replace afternoon coffee with decaf
- Day 7: Decaf only or very light dose

**Decaf Role:** Decaf allows behavioral continuity and ritual preservation during reset. Swiss Water Process decaf is recommended for flavor quality.

**After Reset:** Smaller doses (100-150mg) can produce comparable stimulation to previous higher doses. There is no universal rule for reset frequency; some reset every few months, others manage through dose cycling. The article emphasizes that a reset is about restoring sensitivity and intentional enjoyment, not abandoning coffee.

# How Long Does It Take for Caffeine Tolerance to Occur?

* Medical Reviewer: [Jabeen Begum, MD](/bio/jabeen_begum_md)

* [Is Caffeine Tolerance Real](#is_caffeine_tolerance_real)

### Is caffeine tolerance real?

![Caffeine tolerance is the body's ability to adapt to regular caffeine intake, causing you to need more coffee to feel the same effects. Caffeine tolerance can take up to a month to fully develop.](https://images.medicinenet.com/images/article/main_image/coffee-beans-happy-mug-drink-caffeine-morning.jpg?output-quality=75)

Caffeine tolerance is the body's ability to adapt to regular caffeine intake, causing you to need more coffee to feel the same effects. Caffeine tolerance can take up to a month to fully develop.

[Caffeine](https://www.medicinenet.com/caffeine/article.htm) tolerance is the body's ability to adapt to regular caffeine intake, causing you to need more coffee to feel the same effects. It can occur in conjunction with any amount of regular caffeine intake, including [caffeinated](https://www.medicinenet.com/caffeine/article.htm) beverages like coffee, tea, and energy drinks, and it is thought to be caused by changes in brain chemistry.

Caffeine tolerance can take up to a month to fully develop, and while it affects physical performance, it does not affect cognitive performance. Here’s what you need to know.

Most caffeine users have heard about caffeine tolerance, which causes you to gradually need more coffee to feel the same effects. While many people disregard it, research has shown that **caffeine tolerance is real** — even if you can’t directly feel it. Several studies have proven that, over time, all regular caffeine users will experience lesser effects from their usual caffeine dose.

Although caffeine tolerance mainly affects people who drink coffee, it’s also possible to develop it by drinking other beverages. For example, tea and energy drinks are two of the most popular drinks that contain caffeine. If you regularly use those to improve your performance or to keep you awake and energized, you’ll eventually start to feel less and less affected.

Another common belief is that caffeine tolerance only affects heavy coffee users. However, this is also incorrect — tolerance will develop no matter the dose. The only factor that’s crucial for developing a tolerance is the frequency at which you drink coffee. For instance, a person who takes less than 50 milligrams of caffeine (about half a cup of coffee) will still develop a tolerance if they take it every day.

**Why does caffeine tolerance happen?**

In simple terms, caffeine tolerance occurs when the body starts getting used to taking caffeine every day. As such, it starts changing parts of its brain to accommodate the daily dose and function normally even after you take it. Specifically, your body can create more adenosine receptors, which play a crucial part in the impact of caffeine on your body.

Experts have also theorized that caffeine tolerance may also stem from genetic changes in the striatum — a part of your brain responsible for voluntary movement. The exact mechanism behind caffeine tolerance isn’t fully understood, but experts have nonetheless been able to confirm that it is a real phenomenon.

### How long does it take to develop a caffeine tolerance?

The timeline for developing a caffeine tolerance will depend on several factors — most notably, whether you’re looking for changes in the physical or mental effects. Research shows that **caffeine tolerance only seems to affect the physical effects, while cognitive performance doesn’t diminish after caffeine tolerance has developed.**

A 2019 study compared the athletic performance of several participants who were divided into a caffeine group and a placebo group. After a month of testing, researchers found that participants who received coffee performed better, reaching their peak during the first day of testing.

However, they also found that this effect decreased as the days passed. After about 15 days, the performance increase was nearing the participants’ normal levels, although there were still small-to-moderate improvements. This suggests that **even though tolerance is noticeable after about two weeks of daily caffeine, the effects are still present for a bit longer.**

A similar but longer 2017 trial showed the same results — caffeine increases performance even after some level of tolerance has developed. Yet, experts found that **these effects completely disappeared after a month of daily caffeine intake.**

Considering the two trials, it’s possible to establish an approximate timeline for caffeine tolerance regarding physical performance. However, it’s important to remember that each person is different, so your experience may vary. Here’s how caffeine tolerance develops:

* Days 1 – 15 — Your athletic and physical performance will increase considerably, although this effect will become less noticeable as the days go by.
* Days 15 – 30 — The performance benefits become moderate at best and won’t be far away from your usual, non-caffeinated performance.
* After day 30 — The physical benefits of caffeine will disappear, and your performance will be the same as before starting the daily caffeine intake.

 [![](https://images.medicinenet.com/images/quiz/diet-and-nutrition/diet-and-nutrition-s1.jpg)

#### QUESTION

According to the USDA, there is no difference between a “portion” and a “serving.” See Answer](https://www.medicinenet.com/diet_and_nutrition_quiz/quiz.htm)

### How do I restore my caffeine tolerance?

Unfortunately, there aren’t any clear guidelines on how to restore your caffeine tolerance. Naturally, it’s assumed that you must either significantly reduce or completely abstain from drinking coffee to remove tolerance. However, experts haven’t yet determined how long you need to limit your caffeine intake.

A 2011 study tested the behavior of caffeine tolerance after a four-day withdrawal period among trained athletes. Surprisingly, they found that caffeine could significantly improve their performance regardless of whether or not the four-day period was imposed.

A similar study measured caffeine withdrawal regarding cognitive performance. While researchers found that mood and reaction time were improved among those who had undergone a 30-hour withdrawal period, all the other factors showed no change in those who were in a state of withdrawal.

If you want to fully break your caffeine tolerance, you may want to abstain or severely limit your caffeine intake for some time. If you’re unsure how to best go about this, check with a doctor or licensed dietitian. They can give you precise advice considering the effects you’re looking for and your usual daily intake.

**Preventing caffeine tolerance**

If you don’t take caffeine regularly, you may wonder how to prevent caffeine tolerance. While there aren’t any specific guidelines regarding how often you should take it, some experts recommend four days of caffeine intake followed by some days of not taking it. This is particularly useful if you want to increase your athletic performance temporarily or you’re going through intense study or work sessions.

### What can I expect when withdrawing from caffeine?

If you’re a frequent user of caffeine, you will probably have developed dependence and tolerance. This means that your body isn’t just used to caffeine — it also needs it to function as usual. You can expect some of the following symptoms if you're withdrawing from caffeine after a long time of using it daily:

* [Headaches](https://www.medicinenet.com/headache/article.htm)
* [Anxiety](https://www.medicinenet.com/anxiety/article.htm) and irritability
* Muscular [pain](https://www.medicinenet.com/pain_management/article.htm)
* [Fatigue](https://www.medicinenet.com/fatigue/article.htm) and lethargy
* [Nausea](https://www.medicinenet.com/nausea_and_vomiting/article.htm)
* Difficulty concentrating

These symptoms will usually appear during the first day of withdrawal. However, it’s important to remember that they won’t last forever — most symptoms disappear after a week. If you want to avoid these side effects, gradually reducing your daily caffeine intake might be a good idea instead of going [cold](https://www.medicinenet.com/common_cold/article.htm) turkey.

This is a PubMed record for a randomized controlled trial published in the European Journal of Nutrition (2024 Dec; 63(8): 3025-3035) titled "Effects of different doses of caffeine on cognitive performance in healthy physically active individuals." The study, led by María Ramírez-delaCruz and colleagues from Spanish universities, aimed to determine the dose-response effects of caffeine on sport-related cognitive performance.

Twenty-nine healthy physically active young adults completed three trials under placebo, 3 mg/kg, and 6 mg/kg body mass of caffeine conditions. Cognitive abilities were assessed using reaction time (Dynavision™ D2), anticipation (Bassin Anticipation Timer), sustained attention (Go/No-Go and Eriksen Flanker Test), and memory tests. Side effects were recorded 24 hours post-test.

Key findings: Only the 6 mg/kg dose improved reaction time (Physical reaction time: -0.04 s, 95% CI -0.08 to -0.01 s, P = 0.036, d = 0.5; Motor reaction time: -0.04 s, 95% CI -0.07 to -0.01 s, P = 0.008, d = 0.6) compared to placebo. Anticipation, sustained attention, and memory were not affected by either dose. The 6 mg/kg dose increased side effects of activeness (P = 0.046) and nervousness (P = 0.001). The study concluded that acute intake of 6 mg/kg caffeine effectively improves reaction time despite increased side effects in healthy physically active young adults. <summary>
This integrative review article (published December 7, 2018, in Risk Management and Healthcare Policy) examines the complex relationship between caffeine consumption, sleep quality, and daytime functioning. Caffeine is one of the most widely consumed stimulants globally, with 90% of American adults consuming it almost daily, averaging 200 mg/day. The review addresses a key question: can caffeine reverse the performance deficits caused by the sleep disruption it may itself induce?

Key findings include:
- Caffeine is an adenosine-receptor antagonist, efficiently absorbed with peak plasma levels in 30 minutes and a half-life of 2-10 hours.
- Caffeine consumption (even 400 mg taken 6 hours before bedtime) significantly disturbs sleep, reducing total sleep time and sleep efficiency.
- Sleep deprivation (even 90 minutes less sleep for one night) reduces daytime alertness by one-third and impairs cognition, attention, vigilance, and higher-order processes.
- The "withdrawal reversal" hypothesis suggests that caffeine's apparent benefits may simply be the reversal of withdrawal effects rather than a net gain, since overnight abstinence occurs naturally for regular users.
- Animal studies and well-controlled human studies comparing high and low habitual users tend to confirm a "net benefit" for caffeine use, particularly for psychomotor performance.
- One predictive model suggests 200 mg of caffeine can provide equivalent performance benefits to 3 hours of additional sleep.
- The convenience of caffeine compared to ensuring adequate restorative sleep means its use as a performance "enhancing" substance is likely to persist.

The authors conclude that while caffeine has measurable positive impacts on physical and cognitive functioning, further research with caffeine-naive populations is needed to fully elucidate the complexities of the relationship between caffeine, sleep, and daytime functioning.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article published in *Annals of Neurosciences* (2021) investigates the neuro-cognitive profiles of morning versus evening chronotypes at different times of day. The study included 28 healthy adult male subjects (15 morning chronotypes "M" and 13 evening chronotypes "E"), aged 18-25, from All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Raipur, India. Chronotypes were assessed using the Horne & Östberg Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ). Cognitive status was measured objectively through event-related potentials (ERP) via a visual oddball paradigm test (P300 latency and amplitude) and subjectively via the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) questionnaire. Resting EEG (20-30 min) was also recorded for alpha and beta power at FZ and PZ cortical sites. Key results: (1) Evening chronotypes showed significantly higher alpha and beta power at the PZ site during the evening session compared to morning types, indicating better attention and alertness in the evening. (3) Evening types showed reduced latency and amplitude for rare stimuli during the evening session, indicating faster and more efficient cognitive processing during their preferred time. (4) A significant negative correlation was found between latency of rare stimuli and alpha/beta power at the FZ site during the evening session in evening chronotypes only. --- SOURCE 18: Chronotype - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/chronotype

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This ScienceDirect topic page on "Chronotype" provides a comprehensive overview of the concept and its measurement in psychology. Chronotype refers to an individual's preference for morning or evening hours for optimal intellectual and physical performance, influenced by their endogenous circadian clock. It is associated with various lifestyle and personality traits, including substance use tendencies and emotional stability.

**Key Definitions and Models:**
Chronotype is described as a multimodal construct reflecting circadian rhythms in body temperature, cortisol, cognitive functions, eating, and sleeping patterns. It is influenced by internal (genetics) and external (light exposure) factors. The 2023 article by Chauhan et al. proposes a multidimensional model integrating individual, environmental, and social factors, arguing that existing models focus too narrowly on the sleep dimension.

**Measurement Instruments:**
- **Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ):** First validated measure (1976), 19 items assessing phase preference. Scores 16-86; lower=evening type, higher=morning type. Reliable (α=0.77-0.86) but criticized for using student-based cut-offs, not considering work schedules, and ignoring socio-cultural factors.
- **Reduced MEQ (rMEQ):** 5-item version; quick but poor inter-item correlations.
- **Composite Scale of Morningness (CSM):** 13 items from MEQ and Circadian Type Questionnaire. Scores 13-55; reliable (α=0.87) but factor structure inconsistent.
- **Munich Chronotype Questionnaire (MCTQ):** Differentiates sleep on work vs. free days; uses sleep midpoint corrected for sleep deficit. Correlates with melatonin and cortisol markers. Limitations include reliance on structured work schedules and not incorporating other temporal behaviors.

**Key Findings:**
- Evening chronotype is associated with higher BMI, obesity risk, poorer diet quality (more fast food, less fruits/vegetables), higher energy intake at night, and night eating syndrome.
- Eveningness is linked to addictive behaviors (substance use, internet addiction, online gaming disorder).
- Morningness is associated with healthier lifestyles and emotional stability.
- Chronotype changes with age: children and older adults have earlier chronotypes; adolescents and young adults lean toward eveningness.
- Evening types face circadian misalignment due to conflicts with typical work/social schedules.

**Future Directions:**
The 2023 review calls for (1) more comprehensive standardized measures incorporating sleep and non-sleep aspects, (2) longitudinal studies on age-dependent chronotype changes predicting health outcomes, and (3) greater attention to sex, hormonal status, and personality traits in chronotype research.
</summary>
