--- SOURCE 8: Optimising the caffeine nap for counteracting driver sleepiness in ... ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42894-1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study, published in Scientific Reports (volume 16, article 14380, 2026), investigates the optimal "caffeine nap" composition for counteracting driver sleepiness in CPAP-treated obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) patients. Driver sleepiness contributes to a substantial proportion of road crashes, and drivers are typically advised to consume caffeine followed by a short nap, but this guidance was developed based on healthy individuals and had not been tested in OSA patients.

The research comprised three studies involving 21 CPAP-treated OSA participants (mean age 59 years, 6 female, 15 male) who completed six laboratory visits: one after a normal night's CPAP-treated sleep and five after sleep restriction (4 hours CPAP-treated sleep), driving a monotonous simulated scenario before and after each countermeasure.

Key findings:
- Study 1 (caffeine dose): Two cans of iced coffee (255 mg caffeine) mitigated driver sleepiness more effectively than one can (127.5 mg). C2 significantly reduced minor out-of-lane events and lowered Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS) scores compared to C1. One can was insufficient to counteract sleep loss in OSA patients despite positive findings at lower doses (80-200 mg) in healthy adults.
- Study 2 (nap duration): A 30-minute nap opportunity provided no significant additional benefit compared to a 15-minute nap opportunity on driving performance or subjective sleepiness.
- Study 3 (caffeine nap): An optimised caffeine nap (two coffees + 15-minute nap) provided some temporary benefit to subjective alertness and driving performance but offered little practical improvement compared to two coffees alone for OSA drivers. The nap component appeared to provide minimal additional benefit and may have introduced some disbenefit.

The authors recommend that if a treated OSA driver experiences sleepiness, stopping to drink two cans of coffee (255 mg caffeine) is the course of action with the greatest evidence of temporary effectiveness. All countermeasures were temporary, with benefits often dissipating after 15 minutes, and none can replace a good night's sleep before driving. The findings suggest that official guidance recommending caffeine naps (e.g., NHTSA) may not be appropriate for OSA drivers, and future research should systematically compare caffeine alone with caffeine naps in this population. Participants rated the caffeine nap as more effective than other countermeasures but not more likely to be used in real life, suggesting perceived barriers to implementation.
</summary>

"An optimised caffeine nap of two coffees followed by a 15 min nap opportunity provides some temporary benefit, but for OSA drivers a caffeine nap offers little practical improvement compared to two coffees alone. All countermeasures are temporary and cannot replace a good night of sleep before driving."

SUMMARY:

This is an educational blog article from Mattress Miracle, a family-owned mattress store in Brantford, Ontario (441½ West Street, phone 519-770-0001), that explains the science behind "coffee naps" — drinking a cup of coffee (~200 mg of caffeine) immediately before a 20-minute nap.

The article explains that coffee naps work through the interplay of adenosine (a neurotransmitter that builds up with wakefulness and causes sleepiness) and caffeine (which blocks adenosine receptors rather than eliminating adenosine). Sleep actively clears adenosine from the brain, so a short 15–20 minute nap reduces adenosine levels, allowing caffeine to work more effectively with less competition. Caffeine takes 15–30 minutes to absorb, so it arrives at the brain's receptors just as the napper wakes — perfectly timed.

Key research findings cited include: Reyner & Horne (1997) found caffeine naps improved driving simulator performance better than caffeine or nap alone; Hayashi et al. (2003) found 200 mg caffeine before a short nap improved alertness scores; Horne & Reyner (1996) found caffeine-nap drivers made significantly fewer tracking errors; Mednick et al. (2002) found naps outperformed caffeine on certain memory tasks. A 2020 pilot study found caffeine naps reduced fatigue and improved cognitive performance in simulated night shift work, with participants reporting 91% less subjective sleepiness when driving. Research limitations include small sample sizes (12–20 participants) and lab settings.

The step-by-step protocol: (1) drink coffee quickly (avoid large amounts of milk/cream which slow absorption); (2) set an alarm for 20 minutes to avoid deep sleep and sleep inertia; (3) lie down in a quiet, dark environment (even without full sleep onset, light rest provides adenosine-clearing benefit); (4) give it 10–15 minutes after waking for the full alerting effect.

Best candidates for coffee naps include shift workers, long-distance drivers, people with significant sleep debt, and afternoon slump sufferers (1–3 p.m. circadian dip). The coffee nap is a mitigation tool, not a solution — no combination of caffeine and naps restores full overnight sleep function.

Optimal nap environment: cool room (17–19°C), eye mask/blackout curtains for light, earplugs or white noise for sound, and any comfortable surface (recliner, couch, or bed with appropriate firmness).

Those who should avoid coffee naps: caffeine-sensitive individuals, people with anxiety or heart arrhythmias (should consult a physician), and insomniacs (daytime napping reduces overnight sleep pressure and can perpetuate the insomnia cycle). Timing: take the coffee nap more than 6 hours before bedtime since caffeine's half-life is 5–7 hours — a 3 p.m. nap is appropriate, 7 p.m. is not.

FAQs clarify: optimal nap length is 15–20 minutes (over 30 minutes risks sleep inertia); ~200 mg caffeine is needed (a single espresso at 60–80 mg is insufficient; caffeine pills offer precision); even a wakeful rest provides partial benefit; and coffee naps cannot replace full overnight sleep. Any comfortable flat surface works, though a supportive mattress that helps quick relaxation is beneficial for regular nappers.

The article includes a quote from Talia (Showroom Specialist) about adjustable bases in a zero-gravity position making daytime naps more comfortable for shift workers.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 10: Comparing the benefits of Caffeine, Naps and Placebo on Verbal, Motor and Perceptual Memory - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2603066

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article published on November 3, 2008, by Sara C. Mednick and colleagues from the University of California, San Diego, comparing the effects of caffeine (200mg), napping (60–90 minutes), and placebo on three distinct memory processes: declarative verbal memory, procedural motor skills, and perceptual learning.

**Methods:** 61 adults (ages 18–39, low-to-moderate caffeine users) were randomly assigned to nap, caffeine, or placebo groups. The study examined:
- **Verbal Memory:** Recall and recognition for unrelated word lists tested after 7-hour retention (with intervention) and 20-minute retention (post-intervention).
- **Motor Task:** Finger tapping task (FTT) trained before and tested after intervention.
- **Perceptual Task:** Texture discrimination task (TDT) trained before and tested after intervention.

**Key Findings:**
- **Verbal Memory:** Naps significantly enhanced recall after both 7-hour and 20-minute retention intervals compared to caffeine and placebo. For 7-hour recall, nap performed significantly better than caffeine (p=.003) and marginally better than placebo (p=.06). For recognition after 7 hours, nap performed significantly better than both caffeine (p=.008) and placebo (p=.03).
- **Motor Learning:** Caffeine significantly impaired motor learning compared to both placebo (p=.003) and naps (p=.03). The caffeine group showed no improvement across sessions, while nappers and placebo groups showed significant learning.
- **Perceptual Learning:** Napping produced robust perceptual learning compared to placebo (p=.02), while caffeine was intermediate and not significantly different from either group.
- **Subjective Sleepiness:** Caffeine increased subjective alertness, but this did not translate to memory benefits.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Frontiers in Neuroscience review article (published October 2, 2025) examines the relationship between sleep chronotype (morningness-eveningness preference), cognitive function, and perioperative changes. The review defines chronotype as individual preference for sleep-wake timing, classified into morning, evening, and intermediate types. Key factors influencing chronotype include age, gender, melatonin and other hormones, clock genes, ion channels, social jetlag, and anesthesia/surgery. Regarding cognitive function, the review presents mixed findings: some studies show evening chronotypes perform better on cognitive tasks, while others find morning types have lower risk of cognitive decline. Neural mechanisms include differences in white matter microstructure (lower fractional anisotropy in evening types), gray matter volumes, and functional connectivity of default mode and frontoparietal networks. Cognitive performance is enhanced at circadian-preferred times due to increased cortical excitability and neuroplasticity. In the perioperative period, surgery and anesthesia (particularly NMDA antagonists and GABA agonists) can cause phase shifts in sleep midpoint—patients with later chronotypes experience larger phase advances (30-40 minutes) post-surgery. The review highlights that most anesthetic drugs share pathways with chronotype-cognition mechanisms but whether they affect postoperative cognitive dysfunction (POCD) through chronotype changes remains unclear. The authors call for future multicenter studies exploring the relationship between chronotype and POCD.

Chronotype exerts regulatory effects on cognitive function via circadian rhythm modulation, neuroinflammatory cascades, and metabolic homeostasis. The sleep midpoint, serving as a critical metric for assessing circadian phase alignment, frequently represents a concrete manifestation of altered sleep patterns. Most anesthetic drugs are NMDA receptor antagonists or GABAergic agonists, which share many similar pathways with the mechanism of sleep chronotype on cognitive function.

--- SOURCE 12: Time of day and chronotype in the assessment of cognitive functions ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10683050

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This narrative review article published in Advances in Psychiatry and Neurology (2023) by Wiłkość-Dębczyńska and Liberacka-Dwojak from Kazimierz Wielki University, Bydgoszcz, Poland, examines the relationship between time of day, chronotype, and cognitive functioning. The review covers how circadian rhythms, synchronized through the endogenous biological clock with the 24-hour cycle, influence cognitive performance. Key findings include:

- **Purpose**: Circadian rhythms are associated with daily fluctuations in cognitive performance due to interacting homeostatic and circadian processes. Chronotype is defined as a phenotype of circadian cycles determined by an endogenous biological clock, with individuals classified as morning/early, evening/late, or neutral/intermediate.

- **Impact of Time of Day**: Attention components show homeostatic and circadian fluctuations, improving during the day with higher levels in afternoon/evening hours. The strength of the time-of-day effect on cognitive performance increases with age, with older adults performing significantly worse at non-optimal times.

- **Chronotype Effects by Cognitive Domain**:
  - **Mental Activity Variables**: Morning types show maximum activation ~3 hours earlier than evening types. Extreme evening chronotypes rate mental activity lowest at 8am, while extreme morning chronotypes rate it highest at that time, with inverse findings at 11pm.
  - **Receptive Functions**: Simple visual recognition task speed reflects body temperature rhythm, with peak performance in late afternoon and decreasing accuracy throughout the day.
  - **Memory and Learning**: Declarative (explicit) memory shows synchrony effect—better at optimal times according to chronotype. Older adults (60-75) with morning chronotype perform as well as younger adults (18-24) in the morning, but younger adults perform 35% better in the afternoon. Non-declarative (implicit) memory performs better at suboptimal times for both chronotypes and age groups.
  - **Expressive Functions**: Language processing shows chronotype-specific neuronal mechanisms. Morning chronotypes exhibit attenuated fMRI BOLD responses in language-related brain areas and slower reaction times than evening chronotypes.

- **Conclusions**: The review emphasizes the dominant effect of synchrony between chronotype and time of cognitive testing, with large differences between younger and older age groups. Failure to account for these variables may lead to erroneous conclusions.

--- SOURCE 13: Chronotype - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/chronotype

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This ScienceDirect topic page on "Chronotype" provides a comprehensive overview of the concept and its measurement in psychology. Chronotype refers to an individual's preference for morning or evening hours for optimal intellectual and physical performance, influenced by their endogenous circadian clock. It is associated with various lifestyle and personality traits, including substance use tendencies and emotional stability.

**Key Definitions and Models:**
Chronotype is described as a multimodal construct reflecting circadian rhythms in body temperature, cortisol, cognitive functions, eating, and sleeping patterns. It is influenced by internal (genetics) and external (light exposure) factors. The 2023 article by Chauhan et al. proposes a multidimensional model integrating individual, environmental, and social factors, arguing that existing models focus too narrowly on the sleep dimension.

**Measurement Instruments:**
- **Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ):** First validated measure (1976), 19 items assessing phase preference. Scores 16-86; lower=evening type, higher=morning type. Reliable (α=0.77-0.86) but criticized for using student-based cut-offs, not considering work schedules, and ignoring socio-cultural factors.
- **Reduced MEQ (rMEQ):** 5-item version; quick but poor inter-item correlations.
- **Composite Scale of Morningness (CSM):** 13 items from MEQ and Circadian Type Questionnaire. Scores 13-55; reliable (α=0.87) but factor structure inconsistent.
- **Munich Chronotype Questionnaire (MCTQ):** Differentiates sleep on work vs. free days; uses sleep midpoint corrected for sleep deficit. Correlates with melatonin and cortisol markers. Limitations include reliance on structured work schedules and not incorporating other temporal behaviors.

**Key Findings:**
- Evening chronotype is associated with higher BMI, obesity risk, poorer diet quality (more fast food, less fruits/vegetables), higher energy intake at night, and night eating syndrome.
- Eveningness is linked to addictive behaviors (substance use, internet addiction, online gaming disorder).
- Morningness is associated with healthier lifestyles and emotional stability.
- Chronotype changes with age: children and older adults have earlier chronotypes; adolescents and young adults lean toward eveningness.
- Evening types face circadian misalignment due to conflicts with typical work/social schedules.

**Future Directions:**
The 2023 review calls for (1) more comprehensive standardized measures incorporating sleep and non-sleep aspects, (2) longitudinal studies on age-dependent chronotype changes predicting health outcomes, and (3) greater attention to sex, hormonal status, and personality traits in chronotype research.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article published in Scientific Reports (2020) investigates how chronotype (morningness-eveningness preference) affects the interaction between alerting and executive control networks in attention. The study involved 34 participants (18 Evening-types, 16 Morning-types) selected from 132 students using the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ). **Key findings:**
1. **PVT results**: Evening-types showed synchrony effects (better performance at optimal time of day) regardless of session order. Morning-types showed synchrony effects only when the optimal session came first; when the non-optimal session was first, the synchrony effect was abolished, suggesting task novelty compensated for low alertness at their non-optimal time.

2. **Flanker task results**: Evening-types showed significant synchrony effects (35ms difference), while Morning-types showed no synchrony effect. Alerting tones reduced the synchrony effect for Evening-types by nearly half (from 44ms to 25ms).

3. **Alerting-executive interaction**: Phasic alerting (warning tones) increased the congruency effect (conflict score) in the flanker task (61ms with tone vs. 42ms without), consistent with prior research. 4. **Chronotype differences**: Evening-types showed more consistent synchrony effects across both tasks. Morning-types appeared more sensitive to factors that increase alertness (task novelty, cognitive demands) at their non-optimal time, potentially compensating for low vigilant attention.

The study concludes that chronotype determines vigilant attention more decisively in Evening-types than Morning-types, and that exogenous (phasic) but not endogenous alerting exerts a deleterious effect on conflict resolution.

--- SOURCE 1: Effects of different doses of caffeine on cognitive performance in healthy physically active individuals - PubMed ---
URL: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39231871

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a PubMed record for a randomized controlled trial published in the European Journal of Nutrition (2024 Dec; 63(8): 3025-3035) titled "Effects of different doses of caffeine on cognitive performance in healthy physically active individuals." The study, led by María Ramírez-delaCruz and colleagues from Spanish universities, aimed to determine the dose-response effects of caffeine on sport-related cognitive performance.

Twenty-nine healthy physically active young adults completed three trials under placebo, 3 mg/kg, and 6 mg/kg body mass of caffeine conditions. Cognitive abilities were assessed using reaction time (Dynavision™ D2), anticipation (Bassin Anticipation Timer), sustained attention (Go/No-Go and Eriksen Flanker Test), and memory tests. Caffeine is one of the most widely consumed stimulants globally, with 90% of American adults consuming it almost daily, averaging 200 mg/day. The review addresses a key question: can caffeine reverse the performance deficits caused by the sleep disruption it may itself induce?

Key findings include:
- Caffeine is an adenosine-receptor antagonist, efficiently absorbed with peak plasma levels in 30 minutes and a half-life of 2-10 hours.
- Caffeine consumption (even 400 mg taken 6 hours before bedtime) significantly disturbs sleep, reducing total sleep time and sleep efficiency.
- Sleep deprivation (even 90 minutes less sleep for one night) reduces daytime alertness by one-third and impairs cognition, attention, vigilance, and higher-order processes.
- The "withdrawal reversal" hypothesis suggests that caffeine's apparent benefits may simply be the reversal of withdrawal effects rather than a net gain, since overnight abstinence occurs naturally for regular users.
- Animal studies and well-controlled human studies comparing high and low habitual users tend to confirm a "net benefit" for caffeine use, particularly for psychomotor performance.
- One predictive model suggests 200 mg of caffeine can provide equivalent performance benefits to 3 hours of additional sleep.
- The convenience of caffeine compared to ensuring adequate restorative sleep means its use as a performance "enhancing" substance is likely to persist.

The authors conclude that while caffeine has measurable positive impacts on physical and cognitive functioning, further research with caffeine-naive populations is needed to fully elucidate the complexities of the relationship between caffeine, sleep, and daytime functioning.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This ScienceDirect topic page on "Chronotype" provides a comprehensive overview of the concept and its measurement in psychology. Chronotype refers to an individual's preference for morning or evening hours for optimal intellectual and physical performance, influenced by their endogenous circadian clock. It is associated with various lifestyle and personality traits, including substance use tendencies and emotional stability.

**Key Definitions and Models:**
Chronotype is described as a multimodal construct reflecting circadian rhythms in body temperature, cortisol, cognitive functions, eating, and sleeping patterns. It is influenced by internal (genetics) and external (light exposure) factors. The 2023 article by Chauhan et al. proposes a multidimensional model integrating individual, environmental, and social factors, arguing that existing models focus too narrowly on the sleep dimension.

**Measurement Instruments:**
- **Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ):** First validated measure (1976), 19 items assessing phase preference. Scores 16-86; lower=evening type, higher=morning type. Reliable (α=0.77-0.86) but criticized for using student-based cut-offs, not considering work schedules, and ignoring socio-cultural factors.
- **Reduced MEQ (rMEQ):** 5-item version; quick but poor inter-item correlations.
- **Composite Scale of Morningness (CSM):** 13 items from MEQ and Circadian Type Questionnaire. Scores 13-55; reliable (α=0.87) but factor structure inconsistent.
- **Munich Chronotype Questionnaire (MCTQ):** Differentiates sleep on work vs. free days; uses sleep midpoint corrected for sleep deficit. Correlates with melatonin and cortisol markers. Limitations include reliance on structured work schedules and not incorporating other temporal behaviors.

**Key Findings:**
- Evening chronotype is associated with higher BMI, obesity risk, poorer diet quality (more fast food, less fruits/vegetables), higher energy intake at night, and night eating syndrome.
- Eveningness is linked to addictive behaviors (substance use, internet addiction, online gaming disorder).
- Morningness is associated with healthier lifestyles and emotional stability.
- Chronotype changes with age: children and older adults have earlier chronotypes; adolescents and young adults lean toward eveningness.
- Evening types face circadian misalignment due to conflicts with typical work/social schedules.

**Future Directions:**
The 2023 review calls for (1) more comprehensive standardized measures incorporating sleep and non-sleep aspects, (2) longitudinal studies on age-dependent chronotype changes predicting health outcomes, and (3) greater attention to sex, hormonal status, and personality traits in chronotype research.

--- SOURCE 2: Caffeine Stimulation of Cortisol Secretion Across the Waking ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2257922

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a scientific research article published in the National Library of Medicine (PMC) titled "Caffeine Stimulation of Cortisol Secretion Across the Waking Hours in Relation to Caffeine Intake Levels" by William R. Lovallo, PhD, and colleagues. The study investigated whether tolerance develops to caffeine's cortisol-elevating effects with regular daily intake.

**Methods:** 96 healthy adults (48 men, 48 women) completed a double-blind, crossover trial over 4 weeks. Each week, subjects abstained from dietary caffeine for 5 days and instead took capsules totaling 0 mg, 300 mg, or 600 mg/day in 3 divided doses. On day 6, they took capsules with either 0 mg or 250 mg at 9:00 AM, 1:00 PM, and 6:00 PM, with cortisol sampled from saliva 8 times from 7:30 AM to 7:00 PM.

**Results:** After 5 days of caffeine abstinence, caffeine challenge doses caused a robust increase in cortisol across the test day (p < .0001). After 5 days of caffeine intake at 300 mg/day and 600 mg/day, the cortisol response to the initial 9:00 AM caffeine dose was abolished, but cortisol levels were again elevated between 1:00 PM and 7:00 PM (p = .02 to .002) after the second caffeine dose at 1:00 PM. Cortisol levels declined to control levels during the evening. Men and women did not differ in their patterns of tolerance formation.

**Conclusion:** Cortisol responses to caffeine are reduced, but not eliminated, in healthy young men and women who consume caffeine on a daily basis. The study suggests that at moderate consumption levels (300 mg/day, ~3 cups of coffee), tolerance is incomplete, and cortisol elevations may occur in the afternoon hours with repeated caffeine dosing throughout the day. At higher doses (600 mg/day), tolerance was more complete. The findings may have implications for health, particularly in persons at risk for hypertension, who may show greater cortisol responses to caffeine.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: A novel bedtime pulsatile-release caffeine formula ameliorates sleep inertia symptoms immediately upon awakening | Scientific Reports ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-021-98376-z

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Scientific Reports article (published 2021) describes a novel delayed, pulsatile-release caffeine formulation designed to alleviate sleep inertia symptoms immediately upon awakening. Sleep inertia is a state of grogginess and impaired vigilance right after waking, and reactive caffeine intake (e.g., coffee) takes 20-30 minutes to work, missing the most severe early symptoms. The researchers engineered a chronotherapeutic caffeine formula intended to be taken at bedtime (22:30) that releases an efficacious dose (160 mg) approximately 7 hours later, targeting planned awakening.

The study was conducted in two parts: (1) an in vivo validation study of the release profile in 10 healthy young men, and (2) a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover pharmacodynamic study in 22 sleep-restricted healthy young men. Participants were kept awake until 03:00, then given a 4-hour sleep opportunity, and awakened at 07:00. Upon awakening, researchers measured psychomotor vigilance (PVT), mood (PANAS), sleep inertia ratings (ASIQ), caffeine-related effects (CAQ), working memory (n-back), sustained attention (d2 task), cortisol awakening response (CAR), and polysomnography during both nocturnal sleep and a 1-hour nap opportunity at 08:00.

Key results: Compared to placebo, the caffeine formula significantly improved vigilance (PVT median reaction time improved by ~10 ms within 15 minutes), increased positive affect and reduced negative affect scores, improved sleep inertia ratings across all subscales, prolonged the cortisol awakening response (significantly higher cortisol at 60 min post-awakening), and delayed nap sleep latency (indicating reduced physiological sleep pressure) one hour after awakening. The caffeine did not significantly affect working memory or sustained attention tasks. Notably, the caffeine condition slightly reduced deep sleep (N3) compared to placebo, though overall nocturnal sleep architecture was largely preserved.

The in vivo validation study confirmed the intended delayed-release profile (efficacious plasma levels >5 μM after 7 hours). However, in the pharmacodynamic study, release occurred earlier (efficacious levels by 5 hours), likely triggered by a standardized meal served 3.5 hours post-administration. The authors conclude this pulsatile-release caffeine formulation facilitates the sleep-to-wake transition and may benefit individuals suffering from disabling sleep inertia.
</summary>

**2. Timing relative to circadian cortisol peak:**
- Lovallo et al. (PMC2257922): At 300 mg/day, tolerance to cortisol response is incomplete - morning dose blunted but afternoon cortisol still elevated. At 600 mg/day, more complete tolerance.
- CAR (cortisol awakening response): Peaks 30-60 min after waking, 50-75% increase from baseline
- The "60-90 min delay" recommendation is widely cited but largely based on theoretical reasoning (not wanting to stack caffeine on top of natural cortisol peak) rather than direct RCT evidence. Blog sources (Oura, Ratio, BodySpec, Neuro Injury Care) all recommend this.
- Key nuance from Oura: Evening chronotypes have naturally lower morning cortisol, so delaying may not be beneficial for them.

**3. Caffeine curfew / sleep disruption:**
- CRITICAL 2024 RCT (Sleep journal): 100 mg can be consumed up to 4 hours before bed without significant effect; 400 mg should be avoided within 12 hours of bedtime
- 2023 meta-analysis (Gardiner et al., Sleep Medicine Reviews): Coffee (107 mg/250 mL) should be consumed ≥8.8 hours before bed; preworkout (217.5 mg) ≥13.2 hours before bed
- 2013 Drake/AASM study: 400 mg 6 hours before bed reduced sleep time by >1 hour
- 2018 review (PMC6292246): Half-life 2-10 hours; caffeine (even 400 mg at 6h) disturbs sleep
- 2025 meta-analysis (Kocak et al.): 3-6 mg/kg after 16:00 reduced sleep efficiency by ~4.87%, TST by ~32 min (non-significant)
- CYP1A2 genetics: ~50% of population are slow metabolizers (half-life up to 10 hours), ~50% fast (half-life 2-4 hours)

**4. Chronotype-based optimization:**
- 2025 systematic review (Chauhan et al., Chronobiology International): >80% of studies found no main effect of chronotype on cognition; synchrony effect in ~45% of studies of young adults, 83% in older adults
- 2021 Annals of Neurosciences study: Morning types perform better in morning, evening types in evening (synchrony effect on P300 ERP)
- 2025 Kose et al. (Chronobiology International): 3 mg/kg caffeine improved physical performance regardless of chronotype; morning types had stronger gains from caffeine in morning, evening types in evening
- Oura article: Evening chronotypes have naturally lower morning cortisol, so delaying caffeine may not be beneficial for them

# L-Theanine for Anxiety: How Doctors Use It, Dose It, and Combine It with Caffeine

[![Yoshinori Abe](/_next/image?url=%2Fportrait%2Fave.png&w=96&q=90)

Reviewed by Yoshinori Abe, MD

Internal Medicine](/doctors/yoshinori-abe)

L-theanine, an amino acid found in green tea, is commonly recommended by doctors as a complement to therapy or medication for mild-to-moderate anxiety. Typical doses range from 100 to 400 mg per day. When combined with caffeine in a 2:1 ratio, L-theanine can sharpen focus and reduce jitters.

Below, you'll find detailed dosing guidelines, safety considerations, potential drug interactions, and tips for pairing L-theanine with caffeine effectively. Always review these details with your healthcare provider before adjusting your regimen.

If you're considering L-theanine because of ongoing anxiety, focus issues, or other symptoms, it's worth understanding the root cause first. ## Explanation

# L-Theanine for Anxiety: How Doctors Use It, Dose It, and Combine It with Caffeine

Anxiety affects millions of people worldwide. As interest in natural remedies grows, L-theanine—an amino acid found in green tea—has gained attention for its potential to promote relaxation without drowsiness. Below, we explore how doctors integrate L-theanine into anxiety management, typical dosing strategies, its combination with caffeine, safety considerations, and next steps you might take.

## What Is L-Theanine?

L-theanine is an amino acid primarily found in Camellia sinensis (tea plants). It:

* Crosses the blood–brain barrier
* Promotes alpha brain waves, associated with a relaxed but alert state
* May increase levels of GABA, serotonin, and dopamine
* Counters the stimulating effects of caffeine, smoothing out any jitters

## Evidence for Anxiety Relief

Clinical studies suggest L-theanine may help reduce symptoms of stress and anxiety:

* A 2019 randomized trial found 200 mg of L-theanine daily lowered perceived stress and improved sleep quality in healthy adults.
* In another controlled study, 100 mg of L-theanine taken before an anxiety-inducing task led to lower heart rate and salivary cortisol (a stress hormone) compared to placebo.
* Reviews indicate that 200–400 mg per day can produce significant calming effects, especially when taken consistently over 4–6 weeks.

While not a standalone cure for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) or panic disorder, L-theanine can be a valuable adjunct to therapy, lifestyle changes, or prescription medications under a doctor's supervision.

## How Doctors Use L-Theanine

Integrative and primary care physicians may recommend L-theanine as part of a broader anxiety-management plan. Key points:

* **Adjunctive therapy**: Used alongside cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), mindfulness, or prescription anxiolytics to potentially enhance overall relief.
* **Preventive use**: For patients who experience mild, situational anxiety (e.g., public speaking or work stress), a single dose may be taken 30–60 minutes before the event.
* **Maintenance regimen**: For ongoing mild-to-moderate anxiety, a daily dose spread out over the day may provide sustained support.

## Typical Dosing Guidelines

There's no one-size-fits-all dose, but evidence-based guidelines include:

* **Acute relief**: 100–200 mg taken once, 30–60 minutes before a stressor.
* **Daily support**: 200–400 mg per day, split into two doses (e.g., 100–200 mg in the morning and early afternoon).
* **Maximum range**: Up to 600 mg per day in divided doses—but higher doses should only be used under medical supervision.

Always start with the lowest effective dose to assess tolerance and response.

## Combining L-Theanine with Caffeine

L-theanine and caffeine naturally co-occur in tea leaves. When paired, they can offer synergistic benefits:

* **Enhanced focus**: Caffeine's alertness boost combined with L-theanine's calming effect can improve attention and cognitive performance.
* **Reduced jitters**: L-theanine may blunt the anxious side effects of caffeine, such as racing heart or nervous energy.
* **Recommended ratio**: A common ratio is 2:1 (L-theanine to caffeine). For example, 200 mg L-theanine with 100 mg caffeine (roughly one strong cup of coffee).

Studies show this combination can improve reaction time and working memory more than caffeine alone, without the crash or overstimulation.

## Safety and Side Effects

L-theanine is generally well tolerated. Reported side effects are rare and mild:

* Headache
* Gastrointestinal upset
* Dizziness (uncommon)

Key safety considerations:

* **Pregnancy and breastfeeding**: Limited data—consult your doctor before use.
* **Medication interactions**: May interact with sedatives, antihypertensives, or stimulants. Always review all supplements and medications with your healthcare provider.
* **Underlying conditions**: People with severe anxiety, depression, or cardiovascular issues should seek medical guidance before self-dosing.

## Potential Interactions

* **Sedatives/benzodiazepines**: L-theanine might enhance sedative effects; dosage adjustments may be needed.
* **Stimulants (e.g., ADHD medications)**: Combination could alter stimulant impact—monitor heart rate and blood pressure.
* **Antihypertensives**: L-theanine can lower blood pressure; watch for signs of hypotension (dizziness, lightheadedness).

## Who Might Benefit?

Good candidates for L-theanine supplementation include:

* Those with mild to moderate, situational anxiety
* Individuals seeking cognitive enhancement without a stimulant crash
* People looking for a natural, low-risk adjunct to therapy or other treatments

However, it is not a substitute for professional care in the case of severe, disabling, or life-threatening mental health conditions.

## Next Steps: Monitoring and Professional Guidance

If you're considering L-theanine for anxiety:

1. Talk with your healthcare provider about your mental health history, current medications, and any concerns.
2. Start with a low dose (e.g., 100 mg) and track your response in a journal.
3. Adjust dose gradually under medical supervision to find your optimal level.
4. Maintain lifestyle habits that support stress management: regular exercise, balanced diet, good sleep hygiene, and mindfulness practices.

If you're experiencing concerning symptoms and aren't sure whether professional care is needed, try Ubie's free [AI symptom checker](https://ubiehealth.com/symptom-checker) to get personalized guidance on your next steps based on what you're feeling.

## When to Seek Immediate Help

Never ignore serious or life-threatening symptoms. Seek urgent medical attention if you experience:

* Thoughts of self-harm or suicide
* Severe chest pain or shortness of breath
* Uncontrolled panic attacks or inability to function in daily life

Always speak to a doctor about any concerns that feel overwhelming or potentially dangerous.

## Conclusion

L-theanine offers a promising, well-tolerated option for people seeking relief from mild to moderate anxiety or looking to smooth out the effects of caffeine. Doctors often use it as an adjunct to conventional therapies, with doses ranging from 100 to 400 mg per day. When combined with caffeine, it can enhance focus while reducing jitteriness. As with any supplement, professional guidance is crucial—discuss your specific situation with a healthcare provider and if you need help determining whether your symptoms warrant a medical visit, use Ubie's [free symptom checker](https://ubiehealth.com/symptom-checker) for personalized recommendations. Always address potentially serious or life-threatening issues directly with a medical professional.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422)Abstract

### Introduction

Stress is a complex life occurrence essential for survival and goal achievement but can be damaging in excess. Because of the high prevalence of stress in North America, a safe supplement that effectively reduces stress is in demand. The objective of this study was to investigate the efficacy and safety of AlphaWave®l-Theanine on whole-scalp and frontal alpha power, midline theta power, and salivary cortisol in healthy, moderately stressed adults.

### Methods

This was a randomized, triple-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover study that consisted of two study periods with a 7-day washout. A single dose of AlphaWave®l-Theanine (200 mg) or placebo was administered. To induce stress, a mental arithmetic test (MAT) was administered before and after the dose. Electroencephalogram, salivary cortisol, blood pressure, heart rate, self-reported stress, adverse events, clinical chemistry, and hematology were assessed to evaluate efficacy and safety.

### Results

Increases in heart rate, blood pressure, and self-reported stress and state anxiety indicated that participants experienced stress during the MAT. AlphaWave®l-Theanine led to a greater increase in frontal region and whole-scalp alpha power 3 h post-dose compared to placebo (_p_ ≤ 0.050). Within groups, there were increases in alpha power, at 3 h with AlphaWave®l-Theanine, over the whole recording and during the eyes-open portions (_p_ ≤ 0.048) of the alpha task. The changes in alpha wave activity are supported by greater decreases in salivary cortisol 1 h post-dose (_p_< 0.001) with AlphaWave®l-Theanine compared to placebo.

### Conclusion

This study was conducted during the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, which has had a rapid and significant effect on both physical and mental health around the world. A single dose of AlphaWave®l-Theanine significantly increased frontal region alpha power compared to placebo in response to an acute stress challenge. These changes are indicative of relaxation in the brain and suggest a calming response. AlphaWave®l-Theanine was found to be safe and well tolerated by participants.

### Trial Registration

ClinicalTrials.gov identifier [NCT04706494](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/NCT04706494).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422)Abstract

Stress is a complex part of life that is essential for survival and achieving goals. Too much stress, however, can be damaging. There is a high prevalence of stress in North America, creating a demand for a safe and effective supplement to reduce it. This study investigated the effectiveness and safety of AlphaWave®l-Theanine on brainwaves and salivary cortisol in healthy, moderately stressed adults facing an acute stressor. This was a randomized, triple-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover study that consisted of two study periods with a 7-day washout. A single dose of 200 mg of AlphaWave®l-Theanine or placebo was administered before and after a mental arithmetic test to elicit acute stress. Electroencephalogram, salivary cortisol, blood pressure, heart rate, self-reported stress, and safety were assessed to evaluate efficacy and safety. This study was conducted during the coronavirus pandemic, which has had a rapid and significant effect on both physical and mental health around the world. A single dose of AlphaWave®l-Theanine had significant positive effects on brainwaves, salivary cortisol, and self-reported state anxiety compared to the placebo in response to an acute stress challenge. These changes are indicative of relaxation in the brain and suggest a calming response in a moderately stressed but otherwise healthy population. AlphaWave®l-Theanine was found to be safe and well tolerated by participants.

**Keywords:**AlphaWave®l-Theanine, Electroencephalogram, l-Theanine, Stress, Alpha power

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422)Key Summary Points

Adults facing acute and chronic stressors account for up to three quarters of Americans and can cost the workforce ~ $300 billion annually in lost productivity.The objective of this study was to determine the safety and efficacy of AlphaWave®l-Theanine in whole-scalp and frontal alpha power (indicators of relaxation) in moderately stressed adults using an acute stress model.We found that a single dose of AlphaWave®l-Theanine led to a greater increase in alpha power 3 h post-dose compared to placebo.These data suggest that AlphaWave®l-Theanine reduced stress when moderately stressed but otherwise healthy adults were facing an acute stressor.Future work should investigate the safety and efficacy of prolonged l-theanine supplementation in healthy populations to provide insight into application to vulnerable populations diagnosed with stress-related disorders, such as general anxiety disorder.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422)Introduction

Seventy-five percent of Americans report having experienced a stress-related outcome such as irritability, changes in appetite or sleep patterns, restlessness, or general negative thoughts within the past month [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR1), [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR2)]. Common sources of stress include finances, the economy, familial responsibilities, health concerns, and work [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR1), [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR2)]. Job-related stress alone costs American industries an estimated $300 billion a year due to diminished productivity, job accidents, absenteeism, and turnover. Additionally, health care expenditures are nearly 50% greater for workers experiencing high levels of stress [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR3)]. Prolonged stress exposure increases the risk for various health problems and concerns such as mental health issues, substance abuse, and cardiovascular issues, and can even dampen the immune system, increasing susceptibility to both colds and common infections [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR4), [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR5)]. Indeed, when healthy young adults are exposed to acute mental (mental arithmetic) or physiological (cold pressor test) stress, there are increases in arterial stiffness that are independent of the increases in heart rate and blood pressure [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR6)]. Additionally, a direct relationship has been demonstrated between the physiological response to acute mental stress and future adverse cardiovascular events [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR4)].

Stress is a complex part of life that is necessary for survival and goal achievement but can be damaging in excess. It was first defined clinically by Hans Selye as the nonspecific response of the body to any demand for change [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR7)]. More recently, stress has been described as a response to an intrinsic or extrinsic stimulus that causes a deviation from homeostasis [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR5), [8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR8)]. Stressful events lead to a series of responses which are an intricate interaction between the central and peripheral nervous systems and the rest of the body [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR9)]. Further, there are individual differences in stress response due to sex differences, genetic uniqueness, age, and environmental factors like urbanicity [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR9), [10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR10)].

The currently available drug treatments for managing the signs and symptoms of stress can result in side effects, prompting the need for a more suitable approach for pursuing a healthy lifestyle. Treatment and management of stress is a complex process involving interactions between individuals and environmental factors [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR11)]. Lifestyle changes, such as exercise and socialization, are commonly encouraged to deal with stress [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR9)]. Adopting new lifestyle routines is challenging and requires time and compliance to be effective. As a result, a safe supplement that effectively reduces stress levels is in high demand. This is especially applicable for otherwise healthy populations, experiencing moderate levels of stress, who may not require pharmacological interventions or diagnoses.

l-Theanine is an amino acid found in green tea leaves and has been shown in rodent models to block the binding of l-glutamic acid to glutamate receptors (_RS_)-α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methylisoxazole-4-propionic acid (AMPA), kainate, and _N_-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR12)]. l-Theanine can pass through the blood–brain barrier and begins decreasing in concentration 5 h after administration [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR13)]. The amino acid increases the secretion of neurotransmitters such as dopamine and serotonin in the central nervous system 30 min after oral administration [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR14)]. l-Theanine intake reduces the heart rate (HR) and salivary immunoglobulin A (sIgA) in response to acute stress, attributable to changes in sympathetic activation signals [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR15)]. It is characterized by its ability to induce relaxation when consumed. Apart from its ability to act as a neurotransmitter and decrease blood pressure (BP), l-theanine can stimulate the generation of alpha brainwaves [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR16)]. Increases in brainwave alpha power is considered to be indicative of relaxation [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR16), [17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR17)]. Frontal region alpha waves are observed during non-rapid eye movement (REM) sleep and meditation [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR17)]. Juneja et al. reported that alpha waves were generated in the occipital and parietal regions of the brain surface of human participants within 40 min of oral l-theanine administration [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR16)]. Kobayashi et al. found that after a single dose of l-theanine, individuals with higher anxiety emitted significantly stronger alpha brainwaves than did individuals with lower anxiety [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR18)], indicating a greater effect. These electroencephalography (EEG) studies have shown that l-theanine had a direct effect on the brain and relaxed the mind without inducing drowsiness [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR16), [18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR18)].

With the reported success that l-theanine has had in promoting relaxation and reducing signs of stress, it is possible that a single-dose administration may have an efficacious role for individuals facing an acute stressor. The objective of this study was to investigate the efficacy of AlphaWave®l-Theanine in response to acute stress as assessed by EEG, salivary cortisol, BP, and HR in a moderately stressed and otherwise healthy adult population. It was hypothesized that in response to a task designed to induce stress, a single dose of AlphaWave®l-Theanine would result in reduced psychological indicators of stress relative to placebo. This study population represents the average North American experiencing the daily stresses of life associated with the activities and responsibilities of work and daily living. Participants were required to have regular sleep–wake cycles, which was important to decrease confounding variables that may have impacted study results. This population self-reported being moderately stressed with no pathologies during the global SARS-CoV-2 pandemic.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422)Methods

This randomized, triple-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover study was conducted at the KGK Science Inc. clinical site, London, ON, Canada, from 15 June 2020 to 25 September 2020. The Natural and Non-Prescription Health Products Directorate, Health Canada, Ottawa, Ontario, approved this study on 19 December 2019, and research ethics board approval was granted from the Institutional Review Board (IRB) Services, Aurora, Ontario, on 10 January 2020 (Pro00041119). All participants provided written informed consent to participate in the study prior to initiation of any study procedures. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki guidelines and its subsequent amendments and was carried out in compliance with the International Council for Harmonization of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH) Guideline for Good Clinical Practice (GCP). The trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov ([NCT04706494](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/NCT04706494)).

### Study Participants

Participants were men and women aged 19–60 years. All participants had moderate levels of stress as assessed by scores of 14–26 on the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR19)]. Participants were required to have regular sleep–wake cycles defined as a bedtime between 9:00 pm and 12:00 am and between 7 and 9 h of sleep nightly for at least 3 weeks prior to enrollment. Sleep schedule, diet, supplement use, and exercise were maintained throughout the study, and participants were required to abstain from exercise for 24 h prior to study visits.

Participants were excluded if they had any of the following: self-reported epilepsy, seizures, or clinical diagnosis of anxiety or depression; employment that called for shift work that would disrupt normal circadian rhythm or travel across one or more time zones during the 3 weeks prior to enrollment or during the study; known allergies to the test product; a history of alcohol or drug abuse within 12 months prior to enrollment, reported high alcohol intake defined as > 2 standard drinks/day, use of nicotine or tobacco products within 60 days of enrollment, use of medical cannabis or chronic use of cannabinoid products more than twice a week (occasional use was assessed on a case-by-case basis by the medical director); prescribed use of antiepileptics, antiseizure, sedatives or hypnotics, or antibiotics within 30 days of enrollment, or use of l-theanine, melatonin, valerian root, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), tart cherry, amla (_Phyllanthus emblica_), ashwagandha (_Withania somnifera_), _Rhodiola_, shatavari (_Asparagus racemosus_), or ginseng supplements within 7–14 days of enrollment; cognitive impairment and/or inability to give informed consent, or chronic health conditions including but not limited to diabetes, hypertension, autoimmune or immune compromised, kidney, liver or thyroid disease, significant gastrointestinal tract disease, blood or bleeding disorder, or any other condition that in the opinion of the medical director may have adversely affected their ability to complete the study or its measures, or posed significant risk to the participant.

### Intervention

The investigational product(IP), AlphaWave®l-Theanine (200 mg), and placebo (microcrystalline cellulose, hydroxypropyl methyl cellulose) were provided as capsules by Ethical Naturals, CA, USA. AlphaWave®l-Theanine capsules also contained non-medical ingredients of microcrystalline cellulose, hydroxypropyl methyl cellulose, and silicon dioxide. All study products were identical in appearance (size, color, taste, texture, and packaging) to make them indistinguishable to participants and study personnel. Participants were administered a single capsule with 250 mL of room-temperature water by a trained clinical coordinator. The time of dosing was recorded, and the timing of pre- and post-dose measurements (HR, BP, salivary cortisol, and EEG), questionnaires (State-Trait Anxiety Inventory [STAI] and visual analog scale [VAS]), and mental arithmetic task (MAT) was based on the dose time.

### Electroencephalogram (EEG)

EEG data were collected with a GRAEL 4K-EEG amplifier and 32-electrode Quik-Cap (Compumedics Neuroscan, NC, USA). For each EEG recording, participants completed a 12-min alpha task consisting of 3 min with eyes open, 3 min eyes closed, 3 min open, and 3 min closed. During the eyes-open conditions, participants were fixated on an “X” on the wall. EEG data were filtered with a 0.1–50 Hz linear finite impulse filter, and down-sampled from 512 to 256 Hz. Data were cleaned with an independent component analysis and visual inspection to remove artifacts from eye blinks, movement, and noise. The power spectrum was analyzed using fast Fourier transform (FFT) with a 1 s Hamming window with 500 ms overlap. Frequencies of interest were the alpha band (8–12 Hz) and theta band (4–7 Hz).

### Outcome Measures

The efficacy of a single dose of AlphaWave®l-Theanine was assessed by EEG, salivary cortisol, BP, HR, the STAI, and a VAS of self-reported stress. Relevant EEG channels were averaged to calculate whole-scalp and frontal region alpha power and midline theta power. Whole-scalp alpha power was averaged across the entire scalp, frontal region alpha power was averaged across the frontal channels only, and midline theta was the average theta power between the Fz and FCz electrodes. Salivary cortisol was collected with the Salimetrics high-sensitivity salivary cortisol enzyme-linked immunoassay (ELISA) kit and analyzed by London Health Sciences Centre core laboratory (London, ON, Canada).

Safety outcomes included post-emergent adverse events, vital signs (BP and HR), clinical chemistry, and hematology. Hematology (white blood cell count with differential, red blood cell [RBC] count, hemoglobin, hematocrit, platelet count , RBC indices [mean corpuscular volume, mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH), MCH concentration, red cell distribution width, mean platelet volume]), liver function (alanine aminotransferase [ALT], aspartate aminotransferase [AST], total bilirubin), kidney function (creatinine, electrolytes [Na, K, Cl], and estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR]), and random glucose were analyzed from blood drawn at all visits by Dynacare (London, ON, Canada) using standard procedures.

### Study Procedures

At screening, eligibility was assessed by the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), medical history, vital signs, anthropometric measurements, and hematology and clinical chemistry parameters. Eligible participants were dispensed a saliva collection kit and instructed on use. Participants returned for their baseline visit and were randomized to one of two treatment sequences. Immediately upon waking on the morning of clinic days 1 and 2, participants were required to collect a saliva sample according to the instructions provided. In the study clinic, participants were provided a standardized meal 2 h prior to IP administration. One hour prior to IP administration (−1 h), baseline measures were collected for HR, BP, alpha task EEG, salivary cortisol, STAI, and a VAS of stress. Participants then completed a 10-min mental arithmetic test (MAT) with simultaneous HR and BP measures. During the MAT, participants were asked to verbally perform serial subtractions of 7 from 700 while keeping pace with a metronome at 90 beats/min. Incorrect responses were corrected, and participants were asked to start again from 700. With a neutral tone, the clinic staff encouraged the participant to go faster and keep pace with the metronome throughout the test [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR20)]. Following the MAT, saliva was collected, and participants completed the stress VAS and STAI questionnaire (−30 min). Participants were administered a single dose of AlphaWave®l-Theanine or placebo. Forty-five minutes after the single dose, participants completed the MAT with simultaneous HR and BP measures, followed by collection of salivary cortisol, alpha task EEG, stress VAS, and the STAI questionnaire (1 h). At 3 h post-dose, alpha task EEG was collected. At the end of each clinic day, adverse events (AEs), vital signs, hematology, and clinical chemistry parameters were measured for safety outcomes.

After a 7-day washout, participants returned to the clinic for the second period of the crossover and were administered the alternate product. All assessments from the first study period were repeated.

### Statistical Analysis

The planned total sample size was 16, with eight randomized to each sequence. With this sample size, it was possible to detect a difference in mean change in salivary cortisol levels of 1.94 mmol/L and a difference in mean change in relative alpha of 4% in a crossover design at an unadjusted overall two-sided alpha of 5%, 80% power, and 20% attrition rate. The sample size estimate for salivary cortisol was based on findings from White et al. evaluating the effects of an l-theanine-based nutrient drink on stress among healthy adults using a similar study design [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR21)]. The difference in mean change in salivary cortisol between l-theanine and placebo was −1.08 mmol/L, with a pooled standard deviation of 2.26 mmol/L. The sample size for the difference in mean change in relative alpha is based on Ahn et al. [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR22)], who evaluated the effectiveness of a wearable EEG device in assessing stress. The pooled standard deviations for relative alpha power (for left and right) before and after an arithmetic test were 3.62% and 3.28%, respectively.

The intention-to-treat population consisted of all participants who received either the IP or placebo and for whom any post-randomization efficacy information was available. Assessment of mean change in outcomes between AlphaWave®l-Theanine versus placebo was conducted using a linear mixed effects model. The model included treatment, sequence, and period as fixed effects and subject as a random effect while controlling for the period-dependent baseline value. A within-group analysis of efficacy endpoints was done using Student’s paired _t_ test or, in the case of intractable non-normality, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Within-group analyses were compared to baseline (0 min). HR and BP were measured at 3-min intervals for 15 min. At each time point, these outcomes were compared between groups using repeated-measures linear mixed effects models.

A descriptive analysis was provided for post-emergent AEs which were presented along with the system organ class (SOC), preferred term (PT), and lowest-level term (LLT) by study arm. The number of participants with at least one AE was compared between study arms using Fisher’s exact test. For each group, the change in each blood parameter from screening to end of study was assessed using a paired Student’s _t_ test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test if not normally distributed.

### Safety

All post-emergent AEs were categorized as “unrelated” or “unlikely” to be related to the IP. There were no clinically relevant changes in hematology or clinical chemistry from screening to day 8 in participants enrolled in this study, with the exception of elevated AST and ALT liver enzymes in one participant. The incident finding was classified as unlikely to be related to the product and did not have an impact on study findings. With the exception of this participant, all markers out of laboratory range were deemed not clinically significant by the medical director.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422)Discussion

This clinical study assessed the efficacy and safety of a single dose of AlphaWave®l-Theanine on whole-scalp and frontal alpha power, midline theta power, and salivary cortisol in moderately stressed and otherwise healthy adults in a population with moderate levels of self-reported stress. The study was conducted during the global SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, at a time when there was an accentuation of the daily stresses of life when many people across the world were experiencing higher than their usual levels of stress. Following a task-induced stress protocol and a single dose of AlphaWave®l-Theanine, healthy adults showed significant increases in whole-scalp and frontal region alpha power in their brain and reductions in salivary cortisol. To our knowledge, this is the first study to investigate the effects of l-theanine in a population of healthy adults reporting moderate levels of stress.

The stress model used in this study was successful in eliciting an acute stress reaction as evidenced by the physiological and subjective indications of stress. The expected physiological changes during a stress test are increases in HR and BP. The study results suggest that participants demonstrated these physiological responses. These physiological changes were confirmed by significant increases in self-reported stress and state anxiety pre-dose. Study findings suggest that the MAT test protocol was effective in inducing an acute, stressful event for the participants in this study and support its use in future clinical trials in the nutraceutical industry.

The effect of the stress test was observed in EEG measured alpha waves through nonsignificant reductions in whole-scalp and frontal alpha power at 1 h post dose. Increases in brainwave alpha power is considered to be reflective of relaxation [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR16), [17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR17)]. Frontal region alpha waves are observed during non-REM sleep and meditation [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR17)]. When participants received the single dose of AlphaWave®l-Theanine, they responded with significantly increased frontal region alpha power during the EEG recording at 3 h. In addition to the improvement in frontal region alpha power, there were significant within-group increases in whole-scalp and frontal alpha power over the full EEG recording and during the higher arousal state, eyes-open portions with AlphaWave®l-Theanine that were not observed when participants consumed placebo. This is significant because there is greater arousal and activation with visual stimulation from eyes open compared to eyes closed, resulting in expected differences in alpha power [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR23)]. Previous studies have reported approximately 40% lower alpha power with eyes open compared to closed [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR23)]. By examining the eyes-open and eyes-closed portions of the alpha task separately, the effects of AlphaWave®l-Theanine in two arousal states were assessed. Participants were exposed to task-induced stress 1 h after consumption of the IP. The results of this study are supported by previous reports of direct effects of l-theanine on alpha waves in the occipital and parietal regions of the brain [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR14), [16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR16), [18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR18)]. The current study investigated the effects of a single 200 mg dose of AlphaWave®l-Theanine. A previous study investigated the effects of lower, 50 mg doses of l-theanine on alpha power and showed increases in a time-dependent manner for 105 min [[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR24)]. The current work observed relaxation effects that extended 3 h post-dose, therefore demonstrating the efficacy of AlphaWave®l-Theanine for longer periods of time than previously shown. Future work should continue to investigate dose- and time-dependent effects of AlphaWave®l-Theanine.

Supporting the efficacious changes to whole-scalp and frontal alpha power, there was a significant reduction in salivary cortisol with a single dose of AlphaWave®l-Theanine relative to the placebo, immediately following the stress-inducing task 1 h post-dose. Cortisol plays a crucial role in appropriating the functions that are essential in curbing those that are nonessential or detrimental to the flight-or-fight situation and enhances brain activity. Biologically active cortisol circulates in serum, and salivary cortisol is indicative of circulating levels and can be used as a noninvasive biomarker of stress in clinical research [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR25), [26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR26)]. Cortisol has a diurnal profile, with the onset of the circadian rise occurring in the early morning with the acrophase of the profile upon awakening and the levels decreasing thereafter until reaching a nadir in the late afternoon [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR27)] in those who have a relatively consistent sleep–wake cycle. The enrollment of participants who reported consistent sleep–wake cycles ensured the integrity of the results reported herein. The decrease in the cortisol levels is consistent with what would be expected in both the placebo and the IP group, as it would reflect the cortisol decrease in the diurnal profile. However, there was a greater decrease in cortisol when participants were given a single dose of AlphaWave®l-Theanine versus when they received placebo. Interestingly, a previous study observed that reductions in salivary cortisol were only significant 3 h after a single l-theanine dose and not at the 1-h time points [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR21)]. Studies have indeed shown that an inverse relationship exists between alpha power and cortisol levels [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR28)]. Interestingly, cortisol appears to not always provide the same response when cortical activity is examined. For example, Tops et al. found the opposite response to one of their previous studies when examining the effects of cortisol administration and cortical activity [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR29)]. A likely explanation for this finding is that cortisol is just one of the many factors that impacts alpha power, and it does not provide the full story. Indeed, alpha activity is not only associated with arousal state, but indexes the operation of selective attention [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR30)]. With l-theanine supplementation, alpha amplitude has been demonstrated to be lower in the pre-response and in response to visual and auditory cues compared to placebo [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR31)]. The current study suggests that the l-theanine formulation used in this study showed efficacy as early as 1 h after AlphaWave®l-Theanine administration. Future work is warranted to investigate the long-term effects of a single dose of AlphaWave®l-Theanine, as well as the possibility of using AlphaWave®l-Theanine in longer-term studies in populations that are vulnerable to stress or populations that have received a diagnosis such as general anxiety disorder.

There is long-term potential for l-theanine supplementation for acute and chronic stress management based on the results of this study and previous work [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR32), [33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR33)]. Following the MAT task, there was a significant increase in self-reported state anxiety and no significant changes to trait anxiety. These findings are expected, as state anxiety is reflective of a temporary response to a specific situation, and trait anxiety is a general tendency and personality feature to react to stressful situations in a certain way [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR34)]. Four weeks of supplementation with 200 mg of l-theanine has been shown to improve trait anxiety scores [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8475422#CR35)], suggesting that continued supplementation with AlphaWave®l-Theanine may have positive effects on trait anxiety as well, which may be an important application in longer-term stress management.

This is a randomized, triple-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover study published in Neurology and Therapy (2021) investigating the efficacy of a single 200 mg dose of AlphaWave® L-Theanine on stress in healthy, moderately stressed adults. The study was conducted at KGK Science Inc. in London, Ontario, Canada from June to September 2020, during the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic.

**Methods:** 16 participants (aged 19-60) with moderate stress (PSS scores 14-26) were enrolled. The crossover design involved two periods with a 7-day washout. Participants received either 200 mg AlphaWave® L-Theanine or placebo. A mental arithmetic test (MAT) was used to induce acute stress. Outcomes measured included EEG (alpha and theta power), salivary cortisol, blood pressure, heart rate, self-reported stress (VAS and STAI), and safety parameters.

**Key Results:**
- AlphaWave® L-Theanine led to a significantly greater increase in frontal region alpha power 3 h post-dose compared to placebo during eyes-open portions (p=0.038). Within-group increases were 70.6% (whole recording) and 56.1% (eyes-open).
- Whole-scalp alpha power showed significant between-group increases at 3 h post-dose during eyes-open portions (p=0.050). Within-group increases were 109.0% (whole) and 50.6% (eyes-open).
- Significantly greater decreases in salivary cortisol were observed 1 h post-dose with AlphaWave® L-Theanine compared to placebo (p<0.001), with a -42.4% within-group change vs -32.6% for placebo.
- The MAT successfully induced stress as evidenced by increased heart rate, blood pressure, state anxiety, and self-reported stress.
- No significant between-group differences in state anxiety or self-reported stress post-dose.
- The product was safe and well-tolerated, with all adverse events categorized as unrelated/unlikely related.

**Conclusions:** A single dose of AlphaWave® L-Theanine significantly increased frontal region alpha power (indicative of relaxation) and reduced salivary cortisol compared to placebo in response to an acute stress challenge, suggesting a calming response in moderately stressed but otherwise healthy adults. The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04706494).
